We ask what exogenous predictors, from constituents' trading to alternative data, add to pooled E-mini S\&P~500
realized-variance forecasts for every regular-hours half-hour bar. Against an OLS heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR)
benchmark, the full set lowers QLIKE loss significantly in all 6 model classes, by
6.0--9.0\% (penalized linear models) and 11.2--14.9\% (tree
ensembles), and beats augmented HAR models. The gain concentrates in the FOMC calendar and the futures' realized
moments; beyond them, only boosted trees gain, slightly. Under squared error, a few crash days offset it. In 0DTE
straddles, full-set forecasts beat passive selling but seldom significantly beat HAR forecasts.

\label{sec:rh_intro}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Realized variance within the trading day.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Realized variance, the sum of squared high-frequency returns, made volatility observable and forecastable
    \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003, BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}, and the heterogeneous autoregressive
    (HAR) model of \citet{Corsi2009}, a regression of realized variance on its own averages over several past
    horizons, has become the benchmark for forecasting it.
  \item Within the trading day volatility follows a pronounced diurnal pattern \citep{AndersenBollerslev1997}, and
    pooled models that fit one forecasting equation across the intraday intervals, after a diurnal adjustment, have
    carried the approach to that horizon \citep{EngleSokalska2012,ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}. Like the HAR model,
    they forecast volatility from its own past; we ask what predictors beyond its lagged realized variances add.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Research question.} We investigate whether exogenous predictors improve pooled forecasts of the
  realized variance of front-month E-mini S\&P~500 futures on every regular-hours half-hour bar of the trading day.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item We call exogenous every predictor outside the HAR components of the target and the calendar dummies. The
    46 exogenous series fall into 8 groups drawn from the futures' own higher-order
    realized moments and trading activity; the intraday trading of the index's constituents, through their realized
    moments, liquidity and order-flow imbalance; option-implied volatility; the calendar of FOMC announcements; and
    alternative data, namely sentiment and attention on StockTwits and the net option vega bought by
    non-market-makers (volatility demand).
  \item Alternative data of this kind have mostly been used to forecast daily realized volatility
    \citep{AudrinoSigristBallinari2020,CaporinPoli2017}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Design.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Each model class is estimated as one pooled model on the 13 regular-hours bars of the day,
    $\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$ (bars ending 10:00 to 16:00 ET), as in the intraday volatility models of
    \citet{EngleSokalska2012} and \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}.
  \item Its predictors, the HAR components of the target and trailing averages of every exogenous series, are
    computed on the futures' full grid of 48 half-hour intervals, overnight included, so that the
    forecasts use the information that accumulates outside regular hours \citep{StroudJohannes2014}.
  \item For bar $i \in \mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$ of day $t$ the forecast is
    \[
      \hat y_{t,i} = f_{m,\mathcal X,\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}(\bm x_{t,i}), \qquad
      \mathcal X \in \{\mathrm{HAR}, \mathrm{Full}\},
    \]
    for model classes $m$ from two families, the penalized linear models (ridge regression, the lasso and the
    elastic net) and the tree ensembles (LightGBM, XGBoost and the random forest). The exogenous series are the exact
    difference between the two predictor sets.
  \item Every model is re-estimated at every bar on a rolling window of 3{,}000 trading days
    ($39{,}000$ bars), with hyperparameters fixed before the evaluation span and then frozen
    (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Benchmark and evaluation.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The primary benchmark is ordinary least squares on the HAR benchmark set, pooled on the same bars (the OLS
    row of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}); on this set the penalized linear models choose penalties close to zero and
    reproduce its forecast.
  \item Every forecast is compared with this benchmark, and each class's full predictor set with the HAR benchmark
    set of the same class, the paired comparison that isolates what the exogenous series add.
  \item Accuracy is the average QLIKE loss over the 33{,}527 regular-hours bars of the 2{,}579 trading days
    from 2 January 2014 to 30 April 2024, with Diebold--Mariano tests on the daily average losses
    \citep{DieboldMariano1995}. QLIKE weighs an error relative to the forecast and, like squared error, ranks
    forecasts consistently despite noise in the realized-variance proxy \citep{Patton2011}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Contributions.}

\item \textbf{Application to 0DTE straddles} (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On each day with a same-day SPXW expiration we buy or sell one zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) at-the-money

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Realized variance and the HAR model.} Realized variance, the sum of squared high-frequency returns,
  makes volatility observable and forecastable \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003,
  BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}, and the heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) model of \citet{Corsi2009}, which
  regresses next-day realized variance on its averages over the past day, week, and month, has become the benchmark
  for forecasting it. Its extensions add jumps \citep{AndersenBollerslevDiebold2007}, signed semivariances
  \citep{PattonSheppard2015}, leverage \citep{CorsiReno2012}, and the measurement error of realized variance
  \citep{BollerslevPattonQuaedvlieg2016}, and the panel HAR of \citet{BollerslevHoodHussLebedev2018} estimates a
  single pooled regression across a cross-section of assets. These are models of daily variance. We carry the HAR
  structure to the intraday interval, pool it across the intervals of one index rather than across assets, and ask
  how much a large set of exogenous predictors adds to it.
\item \textbf{Pooled intraday forecasting and overnight information.} Intraday volatility follows a pronounced
  U-shaped pattern across the trading session, and scaling intraday returns or realized variances by a diurnal
  factor is standard practice \citep{AndersenBollerslev1997,TaylorXu1997}; \citet{AndersenSuTodorovZhang2024}
  estimate this curve for the S\&P~500 futures around the clock and find that volatility outside U.S. trading hours
  matters more in the later part of their sample. With this scaling, one model can be estimated across the intervals
  of the regular session: \citet{EngleSokalska2012} estimate a multiplicative component GARCH model of intraday
  volatility, with daily, diurnal, and stochastic intraday components, pooled across a large cross-section of
  stocks, and \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024} fit machine-learning models of realized volatility across all
  intraday buckets of the day, with predictors built from realized volatility alone. Both leave the overnight return
  out of estimation, and so do we (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods}). Yet information from outside the session helps
  forecast it: after-hours realized variance \citep{ChenYuZivot2012} and overnight information, including the
  realized volatility of related assets that trade while the home market is closed \citep{TodorovaSoucek2014},
  improve volatility forecasts, and for the S\&P~500 futures \citet{StroudJohannes2014} argue that deleting the
  overnight returns removes important information. These studies forecast daily or session volatility; we carry the
  idea to the intraday interval by computing our predictors over the futures' full intraday grid, overnight
  intervals included (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}).
\item \textbf{Machine learning for realized volatility.} Applications of bagging, the lasso, boosting, random
  forests, and neural networks to realized volatility \citep{HillebrandMedeiros2010,AudrinoKnaus2016,
  MittnikRobinzonovSpindler2015,LuongDokuchaev2018,RahimikiaPoon2020} preceded the comparison of these methods with
  the HAR model for daily realized volatility in \citet{christensen2023machine}, much as \citet{gu2020empirical}
  compared linear, penalized, tree-based, and neural-network models for returns; \citet{BrancoRubesamZevallos2024}
  find that nonlinear models rarely beat linear ones. Most of this work targets daily volatility; we compare
  penalized linear models with tree ensembles on every regular-hours interval.
\item \textbf{Dense or sparse signals.} In macroeconomic, microeconomic, and financial data, the posterior over
  predictive models does not typically concentrate on a single sparse model \citep{GiannoneLenzaPrimiceri2021}, and
  a characteristics-sparse stochastic discount factor cannot adequately summarize the cross-section of expected
  stock returns \citep{KozakNagelSantosh2020}; \citet{ShenXiu2025} ask whether machine-learning methods can learn
  weak signals. That our exogenous signal is dense and weak, spread thinly over many series, is a hypothesis we
  test, not a premise: ridge regression suits a dense signal and the lasso a sparse one, and we compare penalized
  linear models with tree ensembles across the number of exogenous series and the length of the training window
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi}; Appendix~\ref{app:rh_fi_scaling}). Unlike the complex models of
  \citet{KellyMalamudZhou2024}, which have more parameters
% 2026-10-28 (v2 of Sections 6-7, author approved preliminarily): pointer for the v2 layout. Was: (Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi})
  than observations, ours have far fewer predictors than training observations.
  % 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): optional KMZ clause (coordinator: one clause; the author has not yet decided on
  % the complexity argument, plan "Pending author decisions"); delete the sentence if the author drops KMZ. No number
  % is quoted: the grid's c = P/T is at most \rhcxCMax (\rhcxCMaxMain for the full set at W = 3,000), macros of
  % generated/rehaul_complexity_numbers.tex, which the preamble does not \input today.
\item \textbf{Alternative data.} Sentiment, attention, and news measures have mostly been used to forecast daily
  realized volatility \citep{AudrinoSigristBallinari2020,CaporinPoli2017}; at the intraday horizon,
  \citet{BehrendtSchmidt2018} relate Twitter sentiment and activity to the intraday volatility of individual stocks.
  We ask what such data add to a pooled intraday model of the index's realized variance, next to the futures' own
  realized moments, the trading of the index's constituents, implied volatility, and the FOMC calendar.
\item \textbf{Economic evaluation of volatility forecasts and 0DTE options.} A long tradition ranks volatility
  forecasts by the profits of trading options on them, buying (selling) straddles when the price implied by the
  forecast exceeds (falls short of) the market price \citep{EngleHongKaneNoh1993,NohEngleKane1994,
  BandiRussellYang2008}; statistical gains need not survive transaction costs
  \citep{HarveyWhaley1992,ChanJhaKalimipalli2009}. Because the variance risk premium is positive on average
  \citep{CarrWu2009,BollerslevTauchenZhou2009}, zero-beta at-the-money straddles and delta-hedged index options lose
  money on average \citep{CovalShumway2001,BakshiKapadia2003}, which makes the unconditional short straddle the
  natural benchmark for a strategy that trades straddles on a variance forecast. A recent literature studies the
  pricing, trading, and volatility effects of zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options on the S\&P~500
  \citep{BandiFusariReno2023,BeckmeyerBrangerGayda2023,DimErakerVilkov2024}, and \citet{ChongTodorov2026} ask
  whether equity and 0DTE options markets agree about volatility and trade their disagreement. Nearest to our market
  and bar length, \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026} predict the half-hourly delta-hedged returns of S\&P~500 index
  options from contract characteristics, Greeks, and option-implied measures of the index's return distribution,
  and sort the contracts into long--short portfolios. Our forecasts belong to the realized volatility literature,
  and options enter only as an application: one 0DTE at-the-money straddle a day through the closing half hour,
  long or short as the forecast for that interval exceeds or falls short of the implied variance
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}).
\end{itemize}

  and the half-hour intervals of day $t$ by $i = 1, \dots, M$; every interval is stamped by its end in Eastern time,
  and $i = c$ denotes the closing interval, 15:30--16:00~ET. With $r_{t,i,k}$ the one-minute log-price change of the
  front-month contract in the $k$-th non-missing minute of interval $(t,i)$, $k = 1, \dots, N_{t,i}$
  ($N_{t,i} \le 30$), the realized variance of the interval is \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003}
  \[
    \RV_{t,i} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{t,i}} r_{t,i,k}^2 ,
  \]
  which we forecast on every regular-hours interval, the bars ending 10:00 to 16:00~ET
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}).
\item \textbf{Exogenous series.} The pooled models use 46 exogenous series in 8 groups.
  Appendix Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_dictionary} defines each series, and Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_sources} gives the
  sources and the construction.
  % 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): the display of the seven sums and the sentence that names them moved to Appendix
  % app:rh_dp_sources (A_data_predictors.tex).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Realized moments} (7 series): one-minute sums of the futures over the interval other than
    $\RV_{t,i}$, the target: the sums of the returns, of their absolute values, cubes and fourth powers, the positive
    realized semivariance, the bipower variation and the first-order realized autocovariance.
  \item \textbf{Liquidity} (14 series): the futures volume, the number of observed minutes
    $N_{t,i}$\ifrawseries{} (\sername{numobs})\fi, and equal- and value-weighted cross-sectional averages over the
    S\&P~500 constituents of turnover (total, buyer- and seller-initiated), the effective and quoted spreads, and
    order-flow imbalance.
  \item \textbf{Equal- and value-weighted market moments} (6 and 6 series): the same averages of
    realized moments of the constituents' 5-minute returns.
  \item \textbf{Sentiment} (3 series): StockTwits attention (posts in the half hour), the sentiment score of
    the posts tagged bullish or bearish, and their number.
  \item \textbf{Implied volatility} (3 series): the Cboe VIX, VIX3M and VVIX indices.
  \item \textbf{Volatility demand} (4 series): the net vega bought by customers other than market makers in
    Cboe option volume.
  \item \textbf{FOMC} (3 series): an indicator for a scheduled Federal Open Market Committee statement on
    day $t$ and the proximity measures $1/(1+n^{+}_{t,i})$ and $1/(1+n^{-}_{t,i})$, with $n^{+}_{t,i}$ and
    $n^{-}_{t,i}$ the number of intervals until the next and since the last scheduled statement. The proximity
    measures follow the pre-announced meeting calendar, so all three series are known before the interval begins;
    the meeting scheduled for \rhdsFomcSchedMeeting{} is the next statement until the action announced on
    \rhdsFomcReplaced{} replaced it (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}).
  \end{itemize}
  Our data end on \rhdsSampleEnd. The file of the implied volatility indices ends on \rhdsVixVendorLast{} and is
  extended with the hourly closes of a free feed; the FOMC release file ends with the statement of \rhdsFomcFileLast{}
  and is completed with the \rhdsFomcAdded{} scheduled statements that follow; the volatility-demand feed ends on
  \rhdsVdLast{} (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_sources}).
\item \textbf{Interval grid, sessions and cleaning.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The interval grid $\mathcal{G}$ holds the intervals with an observed realized variance outside the weekend
    break, Friday 20:00 to Sunday 18:30. Lag operators step back through $\mathcal{G}$, overnight sessions included:
    $(t, i - j)$ is the $j$-th interval of $\mathcal{G}$ before $(t, i)$, which may lie on an earlier day.
  \item Early-close sessions stay in $\mathcal{G}$ but leave the estimation and evaluation samples of the pooled
    models and the option-trading sample; their intervals after the 13:00~ET close also leave the window of the
    target's diurnal factor (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}).
  \item On NYSE holidays the E-mini trades a shortened session that ends at about 13:00~ET. The regular-hours intervals
    of these sessions stay in $\mathcal{G}$, in the 13-bar estimation sample and in the window of the target's
    diurnal factor, but are not scored; dropping them from the sample and the window changes the every-bar
    comparisons of the full predictor set with the HAR benchmark by 0.13--0.14 percentage points in the
    linear models (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_robust_holiday}).
  \item A print outside the domain of its series, such as a nonpositive spread or futures volume, is set to missing.
    For each exogenous series $u$ we record the availability indicator $a_{t,i} = \mathbf{1}\{u \text{ observed in }
    (t,i)\}$ before any filling, forward-fill $u$ over at most \rhdsFfillCap{} intervals to compute its trailing
    statistics, and impute every interval with $a_{t,i} = 0$ (step~4 of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}). A trailing
    average that holds no observed interval enters at its neutral value (step~6), as the averages of the
    volatility-demand series do after their feed stops (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_sessions}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Samples.} Appendix Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_samples} lists the samples. The estimation samples and the
  evaluation span are set out in Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_setup}, the option-trading sample in
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_strategy}, and the sample of the closing-interval models in
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing_sample}.
\end{itemize}

% 2026-10-17 (user): prose rewritten in the style of Zhang, Zhang, Cucuringu, and Qian (2024).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Trailing averages on the full grid.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, every predictor is a trailing average
  of a transformed series $\tilde u$ over $k$ samples, lagged by one sample:
  \[
    \bar u^{(k)}_{t,i} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \tilde u_{t,i-j}, \qquad
    k \in \mathcal{K} = \{1, 5, 25, 125, 625, 3125\},
  \]
  6 horizons in base 5. A sample is one interval of the full grid $\mathcal{G}$, overnight
  sessions included: the models are estimated on the 13 regular-hours bars of each day
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}), but the averages of a regular-hours bar include the intervals of the
  overnight session before it. With each value average we form the same average of the availability indicator,
  $\bar a^{(k)}_{t,i}$, the share of the $k$ intervals on which the series was observed.
\item \textbf{Notation.} In tables and figures we drop the overbar and the interval index.
  \ifrawseries
  We refer to each exogenous series by its column name in the data (Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_dictionary}): for instance,
  $\ser{vix}{\mathrm{VIX}}^{(25)}$ is the transformed VIX averaged over the 25 intervals before the forecast
  interval; the implied volatility series are \sername{vix}, \sername{vix3m} and \sername{vvix}; the suffixes
  \sername{_ewstock} and \sername{_vwstock} mark the equal- and value-weighted constituent aggregates (e.g.,
  \sername{ofi_ewstock} and \sername{spread_vwstock}); and the FOMC series are \sername{fomc_day},
  \sername{fomc_until_inv} and \sername{fomc_since_inv}. We write $\bar a^{(k)}(u)$ for the availability average of
  series $u$.
  \else
  For instance, $\mathrm{VIX}^{(25)}$ is the transformed VIX averaged over the 25 intervals before the forecast
  interval. We denote the implied volatility series by $\mathrm{VIX}$, $\mathrm{VIX3M}$ and $\mathrm{VVIX}$, label
  the equal- and value-weighted constituent aggregates with the superscripts EW and VW (e.g.,
  $\mathrm{OFI}^{\mathrm{EW}}$ and $\mathrm{Spread}^{\mathrm{VW}}$), denote the announcement predictors by
  $\mathrm{FOMC}$, and write $\bar a^{(k)}(u)$ for the availability average of series $u$.
  \fi
\item \textbf{HAR benchmark.} The HAR benchmark set holds the HAR components of the target, $\bar y^{(k)}_{t,i}$, the
  same trailing averages of the winsorized target $\tilde y$ (6 columns), and the calendar vector
  $\bm D_{t,i}$ (6 columns): five day-of-the-week dummies and the hour of the interval-end stamp,
  entered as an integer, not as a set of dummies. The estimation sample holds no overnight interval, so
  $\bm D_{t,i}$ has no overnight indicator; and every interval in it falls on a weekday, so the five dummies sum to one
  and are not identified separately from the intercept: the OLS fit is the minimum-norm least-squares solution
  (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_linear}).
\item \textbf{Full predictor set.} The full predictor set adds, for each of the 46 exogenous series
  of Section~\ref{sec:rh_data} (the FOMC group included), the standardized value averages (step~6 below) and the
  availability averages $\bar a^{(k)}$ at every horizon, so that it has
  \[
    564= \underbrace{6}_{\bar y^{(k)}}
      + \underbrace{6}_{\bm D_{t,i}}
      + \underbrace{46\times 6}_{\bar u^{(k)}}
      + \underbrace{46\times 6}_{\bar a^{(k)}}
  \]
  candidate columns. The penalized linear models fit a screened subset of them, leaving out columns that are
  constant or exact duplicates on the estimation window, columns of a series with too few prints off its mode, and
  availability averages that move no more than missing observations at random would; each solver applies the
  screens on its own schedule (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_linear}). The tree ensembles use every column.
\item \textbf{Transformations.} Each exogenous series passes through six steps. Every statistic in them is computed
  from earlier intervals only; Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_transform} gives the formulas and the constants.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Diurnal adjustment.} The raw series $u_{t,i}$ is divided by a time-of-day factor $b^{(u)}_{t,i}$: its
    mean (nonnegative series) or standard deviation (signed series) on interval $i$ over the prior days
    $\mathcal{D}_{t,i}$ of the target's factor $s^2_{t,i}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}), bounded relative to
    the factor's own trailing median. The implied volatility indices, the StockTwits sentiment score and the FOMC
    series are not adjusted.
  \item \emph{Variance stabilization.} A map chosen by what the series measures: the square root for variances,
    turnover and the effective spread, signed power roots for the higher moments and the autocovariance, the identity
    for the other signed series and absolute returns, and the logarithm otherwise. The volatility-demand series,
    whose standard-deviation divisor sits at its floor, take instead an inverse hyperbolic sine of the raw series,
    scaled by a trailing average of its absolute value.
  \item \emph{Winsorization.} A clip at rolling quantiles of the series' preceding 240 intervals, at the
    levels of the target's winsorization (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}). The bounds need a value on each of
    those intervals, so a series is not clipped where its prints leave a gap longer than the fill cap within the
    window: VIX3M and VVIX never are, VIX and the constituent aggregates on part of the sample. The FOMC series are
    not winsorized: the statement-day indicator passes through unchanged, and the proximity measures are
    deterministic ramps, each the extreme of its own trailing window between statements.
  \item \emph{Imputation.} An interval with $a_{t,i} = 0$ takes the median of the series' earlier observed
    transformed values, and before the series starts its first observed value; $a_{t,i}$ itself enters through
    $\bar a^{(k)}$.
  \item \emph{Trailing averages:} $\bar u^{(k)}_{t,i}$, $\bar a^{(k)}_{t,i}$ and $\bar y^{(k)}_{t,i}$ for
    $k \in \mathcal{K}$.
  \item \emph{Robust standardization.} Each value average is centred and scaled on the rolling window
    $\mathcal{W}_{t,i}$, the $W$ rows of the estimation sample before $(t,i)$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}),
    imputed rows included:
    \begin{gather*}
      z^{(k)}_{t,i} = \frac{\bar u^{(k)}_{t,i}
          - \operatorname{med}\bigl\{\bar u^{(k)}_{t',i'} : (t',i') \in \mathcal{W}_{t,i}\bigr\}}
        {\max\bigl\{\mathrm{IQR}^{(k)}_{t,i},\ 0.01\,\overline{\mathrm{IQR}}^{(k)}_{t,i},\
          \mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t,i}\bigr\}}, \\
      \mathrm{IQR}^{(k)}_{t,i} = \mathrm{IQR}\bigl\{\bar u^{(k)}_{t',i'} : (t',i') \in \mathcal{W}_{t,i}\bigr\},
    \end{gather*}
    where $\overline{\mathrm{IQR}}^{(k)}_{t,i}$ is the largest $\mathrm{IQR}^{(k)}$ up to $(t,i)$ and
    $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t,i}$ a causal floor, the interquartile range of the average over the earlier rows whose
    $k$ intervals were all observed. The median and the interquartile range are recomputed at every row; the rows of
    the first window, all before the first forecast, take that window's statistics
    (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_scale}).
    \begin{itemize}
    \item The availability averages are not standardized; the HAR components and the calendar columns follow the same
      rule with $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)} = 0$.
    \item \emph{Late start.} For a series whose first print comes after the start of the sample,
      $z^{(k)}_{t,i} = 0$ on every row whose window $\mathcal{W}_{t,i}$ holds a row whose $k$-interval average
      reaches back before the day of that print. Because the window spans 39{,}000 bars (about
      3{,}000 trading days), late series enter late: on the bars scored from 2 January 2014 to
      30 April 2024, the value averages are live on 56.0--58.4\% of bars for the VIX, 25.0--27.3\% for
      VIX3M, 28.8--31.2\% for StockTwits attention, 17.3--19.7\% for its sentiment and tag count,
      7.0--7.6\% for volatility demand and 0.0--2.0\% for VVIX (ranges over $k$).
    \item \emph{No observation.} $z^{(k)}_{t,i} = 0$ whenever the $k$-interval average holds no observed interval,
      $\bar a^{(k)}_{t,i} = 0$, so the averages of a feed that has stopped are neutral.
    \item The step equalizes interquartile ranges, not variances, and scales each row on its own trailing window;
      the penalized linear models therefore standardize the columns again within their estimation window
      (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_linear}).
    \end{itemize}
  \end{enumerate}
\item \textbf{No look-ahead.} Every statistic indexed by $(t,i)$ uses intervals before $(t,i)$ only: the trailing
  averages, the diurnal factors and their bounds, the winsorization bounds, the imputation medians, the routing of
  step~2 and the standardization statistics. The FOMC proximity measures use the pre-announced calendar
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}). Two inputs use later intervals, and neither looks ahead of a forecast: the first print
  that fills the intervals before a series starts (step~4), which the late-start rule sets to zero, and the statistics
  that scale the rows of the first standardization window, all of which precede the first forecast.
\end{itemize}

\section{Methods}
\label{sec:rh_methods}

\subsection{Forecasting design}
\label{sec:rh_methods_setup}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Target.} We index days by $t$ and the 30-minute intervals of a day, overnight included, by
  $i = 1, \dots, M$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}). The regular-hours intervals, those ending 10:00 to 16:00~ET, form the
  set $\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$ of 13 bars, and $c \in \mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$ is the closing half hour,
  15:30--16:00~ET. Following \citet{AndersenBollerslev1997}, we remove the diurnal pattern with the trailing mean
  realized variance of the same interval of the day,
  \[
    s^2_{t,i} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal D_{t,i}|}\sum_{t' \in \mathcal D_{t,i}} \RV_{t',i},
  \]
  where $\mathcal D_{t,i}$ holds the last $n_{\mathrm{d}}$ days $t' < t$ with interval $i$, at least
  $\underline n_{\mathrm{d}}$ of them, which every scored interval has; the intervals after the 13:00 close of NYSE
  early-close sessions are left out of $\mathcal D_{t,i}$, those of the shortened futures sessions on NYSE holidays
  are not (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}). The regression target is the square root of the adjusted
  realized variance, $y_{t,i} = (\RV_{t,i}/s^2_{t,i})^{1/2}$, winsorized at the lower and upper empirical quantiles
  $\underline Q_{t,i}$ and $\overline Q_{t,i}$ of its preceding $n_{\mathrm{w}}$ values,
  $\tilde y_{t,i} = \clip(y_{t,i}, \underline Q_{t,i}, \overline Q_{t,i})$ (window lengths and quantile levels:
  Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_samples}). A forecast $\hat y_{t,i}$ of $\tilde y_{t,i}$ becomes a variance forecast
  without recalibration,
  \[
    \hat\sigma^2_{t,i} = \hat y_{t,i}^{\,2}\, s^2_{t,i},
  \]
  which leaves the downward Jensen bias of squaring uncorrected; it is scored against the unwinsorized $\RV_{t,i}$.
  For the closing interval we write $\RV_t \equiv \RV_{t,c}$ and $\hat\sigma^2_t \equiv \hat\sigma^2_{t,c}$, with
  $\mathcal F_t$ the information observed through 15:30~ET on day $t$ and
  $\E_t[\cdot] \equiv \E[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal F_t]$.
\item \textbf{Pooled estimation on the regular-hours bars.} Each model is estimated once for all regular-hours bars:
  its estimation sample is $\mathcal I = \mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$, one observation per bar, as in intraday
  volatility forecasting \citep{EngleSokalska2012, ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}, while its predictors, the HAR
  components and trailing averages of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}, are computed on the full grid of $M$ intervals,
  whose overnight intervals also carry information \citep{ChenYuZivot2012, StroudJohannes2014, TodorovaSoucek2014}.
  We write $(t,i) \ominus j$ for
  the $j$th observation of $\mathcal I$ before $(t,i)$; unlike the grid lag $(t, i-j)$ of Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}, it
  skips the intervals outside $\mathcal I$. The forecast of interval $(t,i)$ is formed at the start of the interval,
  from the information available then, by a model fitted on the rolling window
  \[
    \mathcal W_{t,i} = \{(t,i) \ominus j : j = 1, \dots, W\}, \qquad W = 39{,}000,
  \]
  the bars of about 3{,}000 trading days. Every model is refitted at every bar, by least squares on
  $\tilde y$ over $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, the penalized regressions adding their penalty. NYSE early-close sessions are
  not in the estimation sample; the shortened regular-hours sessions of NYSE holidays are, and they are forecast but
  not scored (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}).
\item \textbf{Frozen hyperparameters.} Hyperparameters are chosen once, before the first forecast, and held fixed at
  every bar of the evaluation, with no re-tuning. The linear penalties minimize the validation MSE of $\tilde y$ on
  the last pre-sample fold (validation year 2013): each candidate is fitted on a full window of $W$ observations, which ends an embargo gap before the
  validation year \citep{gu2020empirical}. Each tree ensemble keeps one configuration, transferred unchanged from an
  Optuna search on an earlier design of this panel. Appendix~\ref{app:rh_tuning} discloses how both were obtained
  (the late-starting series are still zero in the penalties' validation year) and checks them
  (Table~\ref{tab:rh_tuning}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation spans.} All forecasts are out of sample. The main evaluation runs over
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$, the $T_{\mathrm{oos}} = |\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}| = 2{,}579$ NYSE trading days
  from 2 January 2014 to 30 April 2024 (20 early-close sessions excluded), and scores every
  regular-hours bar of these days, 33{,}527 bars.

%   Comparisons that involve the closing-interval models of Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing}, whose forecasts start later,
%   use the subset $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}} \subset \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ of the
%   $T_{\mathrm{close}} = \rhoosDays$ days from \rhoosSpanStart{} to \rhoosSpanEnd{} on which all of them exist; the
%   option days of the application lie in it (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_strategy}).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Models}
\label{sec:rh_methods_models}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, coordinator: the paper keeps its bullet structure): the forecast-label sentence, prose
% before the list, became the first bold-lead item below; wording unchanged.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Forecast labels.} We label a forecast $f_{m,\mathcal X,\mathcal I}$ by its model class $m$, its
  predictor set $\mathcal X$ and its estimation sample $\mathcal I$; every forecast of the main text has
  $\mathcal I = \mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$.
\item \textbf{Predictor sets.} The HAR set ($\mathcal X = \mathrm{HAR}$) holds the HAR components
  $\bar y^{(k)}_{t,i}$, $k \in \mathcal K$, the means of $\tilde y$ over the $k$ grid intervals before $(t,i)$, and
  the calendar vector $\bm D_{t,i}$ of five weekday dummies and the hour of the bar-end stamp, which enters as an
  integer (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}). The full set ($\mathcal X = \mathrm{Full}$),
  $\bm x_{t,i} \in \mathbb R^{p}$ with $p = 564$, adds for every exogenous series $u$ the trailing averages
  $\bar u^{(k)}_{t,i}$ of its values and $\bar a^{(k)}_{t,i}$ of its availability indicator.
\item \textbf{Primary benchmark: OLS on the HAR set.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, the HAR model of interval $(t,i)$ is
  \[
    \hat y_{t,i} = \beta_0 + \sum_{k \in \mathcal K} \beta^{(k)}\, \bar y^{(k)}_{t,i} + \bm\delta^{\top} \bm D_{t,i} ,
  \]
  pooled over the regular-hours bars and fitted by OLS on $\mathcal W_{t,i}$. Its forecast
  $f_{\mathrm{OLS},\mathrm{HAR},\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}$ is the primary benchmark. Every row is a weekday, so the
  five weekday dummies sum to one and are collinear with the intercept; we take the minimum-norm least-squares
  solution, whose fitted values and forecasts are those of any least-squares solution, for instance with one dummy
  dropped.
\item \textbf{Penalized linear regressions.} Ridge \citep{HoerlKennard1970}, the lasso \citep{Tibshirani1996} and the
  elastic net \citep{ZouHastie2005}, which weights the two penalties equally, add an $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$ or mixed
  penalty on $\bm\beta$ to the sum of squared errors over $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, as in the penalized HAR of
  \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}. The penalty acts on the coefficients of the columns standardized within
  $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, so that it does not depend on a column's spread \citep{FriedmanHastieTibshirani2010}; on the full
  set the HAR-set columns carry the lighter weight $\omega_j = 0.01$ against $\omega_j = 1$ for the other
  predictors, and the intercept is not penalized. On the HAR set alone the selected penalties, \ensuremath{10^{-3}}
  (ridge), \ensuremath{10^{-8}} (lasso) and \ensuremath{10^{-7}} (elastic net), are negligible, and the three
  forecasts coincide with the benchmark. Estimators, column screens and solvers: Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_linear}.
\item \textbf{Tree ensembles.} To capture nonlinearities and interactions, we fit gradient-boosted regression trees on
  the squared error \citep{Friedman2001}, with LightGBM \citep{Ke2017} and XGBoost \citep{Chen2016}, and a random
  forest \citep{Breiman2001}, fitted with Intel's oneDAL engine. The trees use every column of their predictor set
  (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_trees}).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Forecast evaluation and tests}
\label{sec:rh_results_eval}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Losses.} The QLIKE loss \citep{Patton2011} of the forecast of a scored interval is
  \[
    L_{t,i} = \QLIKE\bigl(\RV_{t,i},\, \hat\sigma^2_{t,i}\bigr)
      = \frac{\RV_{t,i}}{\hat\sigma^2_{t,i}} - \log\frac{\RV_{t,i}}{\hat\sigma^2_{t,i}} - 1
      = \frac{y_{t,i}^2}{\hat y_{t,i}^{\,2}} - \log\frac{y_{t,i}^2}{\hat y_{t,i}^{\,2}} - 1 ,
  \]
  in which the diurnal factor cancels ($y_{t,i}$ unwinsorized). QLIKE is our primary loss. Like the squared error
  $(\RV_{t,i} - \hat\sigma^2_{t,i})^2$, which we also report, it ranks forecasts consistently when the realized
  variance is a noisy proxy \citep{Patton2011}; unlike the squared error, it depends on the forecast only through the
  ratio $\RV_{t,i}/\hat\sigma^2_{t,i}$, so a few of the largest realizations cannot dominate it. $\overline{\QLIKE}$
  ($\bar L$) and the MSE average the interval losses over a scored set $\mathcal S$, the bars of the days of a span,
  and the daily loss $L_t$ averages $L_{t,i}$ over the bars of day $t$ in $\mathcal S$.
  % 2026-10-26 (coordinator; author: no 16:00-bar results in the main text): was "a scored set S, every bar or the
  % closing bar of the days of a span" (the closing bar alone is scored in Appendix app:rh_closing).
\item \textbf{Relative loss and out-of-sample $R^2$.} A forecast $A$ is compared with a reference $B$, the benchmark
  unless noted otherwise, by $\Delta\% = 100\,(\bar L^{A}/\bar L^{B} - 1)$. Following \citet{CampbellThompson2008},
  \[
    R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{(t,i) \in \mathcal S} \bigl(\RV_{t,i} - \hat\sigma^2_{t,i}\bigr)^2}
      {\sum_{(t,i) \in \mathcal S} \bigl(\RV_{t,i} - \overline{\RV}_{t-1,i}\bigr)^2},
  \]
  where $\overline{\RV}_{t-1,i}$ is the mean realized variance of interval $i$ over every earlier day from
  5 January 1998.
\item \textbf{Tests.} Two forecasts are compared by the \citet{DieboldMariano1995} test on the daily loss differential
  $d_t = L^{A}_t - L^{B}_t$, with the small-sample correction of \citet{HarveyLeybourneNewbold1997} and a
  \citet{NeweyWest1987} long-run variance with lag $q_{\mathrm{NW}} = \lfloor 4\,(T/100)^{2/9} \rfloor$ on a span of
  $T$ days: $q_{\mathrm{NW}} = 8$ on $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$. $\DM < 0$ favours $A$, % 2026-10-26 (coordinator; author: no 16:00-bar results in the main text): was "... on T_oos and \rhoosDMLag on T_close" (Appendix app:rh_closing)
  and ``significant'' means significant at the 5\% level. We test
  every forecast against the benchmark $f_{\mathrm{OLS},\mathrm{HAR},\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}$ and, within each class
  $m$, $f_{m,\mathrm{Full},\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}$ against $f_{m,\mathrm{HAR},\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}$, the
  paired measure of what the exogenous predictors add. The model confidence set \citep{HansenLundeNason2011}, the
  test of superior predictive ability \citep{Hansen2005} and StepM \citep{RomanoWolf2005} account for the number of
  comparisons. Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_methods_tests} gives every statistic in full.
\end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Overview.} Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} reports the MSE, the average QLIKE loss and $R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}}$ of
  the six model classes on the HAR benchmark set and on the full predictor set.
\item \textbf{Against the primary benchmark.} The full predictor set lowers the average QLIKE loss of every model
  class below that of the OLS on the HAR benchmark set.
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-26 (coordinator, D13): the percentages and the tree DMs now come from the patched Table 1
  % (rehaul_oos_vs_ols_numbers); were the pre-patch ablation macros \rhabRidgeFullAllPct, \rhabLassoFullAllPct,

  \item Penalized linear models, whose HAR-set forecast is the benchmark: $-$6.0\% (ridge regression),
    $-$9.0\% (lasso) and $-$6.7\% (elastic net), with $\DM={}$$-$6.28,
    $-$6.34 and $-$7.36.
  \item Tree ensembles: 11.2--14.9\%, with $\DM={}$$-$10.35,
    $-$9.95 and $-$9.65 for LightGBM, XGBoost and the random forest.
  \item The reduction is significant for 6 of the 6 full-set forecasts.
  \item On the HAR benchmark set alone the tree ensembles stay within 0.9\% of the
    benchmark, so the trees' gain comes from the added predictors rather than from a nonlinear use of the HAR terms.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Within each class.} The paired comparison of $f_{m,\mathrm{Full},\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}$ with
  $f_{m,\mathrm{HAR},\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_eval}; the DM column of
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}) isolates what the exogenous predictors add to a given model $m$.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The full set has the lower loss in 6 of the 6 classes, 6 of them
    significantly.
  \item The tree ensembles gain more from the same predictors than the linear models: $-$14.1\% for
    LightGBM, $-$14.6\% for XGBoost and $-$11.3\% for the random forest ($\DM={}$$-$10.26,
    $-$9.94 and $-$9.74). % RECHECK (D13): "gain more ... than the linear models"
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Squared-error loss.} Under squared error the comparison reverses: on every bar the full set raises the
  MSE in all 6 classes, by 100.6 to 117.7\% for the penalized
  linear models and by 10.9 to 20.0\% for the tree ensembles, and lowers
  $R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}}$ (Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}). A handful of days in the COVID-19 crash account for the difference
  (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_results_calib}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On 2014--2019 the full set has the lower every-bar MSE in all classes (\ensuremath{-}10.8 to
    \ensuremath{-}8.9\% for the linear models).
  \item On 2020--2024 the 5 days with the largest excess squared error of the full set, all between
    12 March 2020 and 2 April 2020, carry 92--94\% of that excess for the linear
    models and 92--101\% for the trees; without the days from 24 February 2020 to 30 April 2020,
    the full set has the lower every-bar MSE on 2020--2024 in all classes, each significantly.
  \item The excess is not a level bias (the bias term is at most 0.1\% of any forecast's MSE) but
    one of scale: on 2020--2024 the full-set forecasts move too much in levels.
    % 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): parked -- the Mincer--Zarnowitz slopes, in Appendix app:rh_results_calib. Was:

    % the HAR benchmark set."
  \item QLIKE scores an error relative to the forecast and grows only logarithmically in over-prediction, so the crash
    bars weigh little in it, and in logs the full-set forecasts are well scaled. QLIKE, which is robust to noise in
    the realized-variance proxy \citep{Patton2011}, remains the primary loss.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{FOMC statement days}
\label{sec:rh_results_channels}
% 2026-10-28 (author: v2 of Sections 6-7 approved preliminarily): new subsection, from drafts/06_results_DRAFT.tex
% (v2 of 26 Oct). The previous Section 6.2 ("Which predictors carry the gain?", rewritten 27 Oct around the consolidated
% statement) moves to Section 7, which now carries that title; its text is parked verbatim at the end of this
% subsection. The draft's Section 6.3 ("Beyond the HAR, the realized moments and the FOMC calendar") is not used: its
% content is Section 7's opening, Section 7.2 and Section 7.3. Bullet title changed from the draft's "The gain does
% not depend on the FOMC calendar" (the calendar alone delivers two-thirds of the trees' gain; Section 7.1).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Day types.} The Federal Reserve publishes its meeting calendar in advance, so whether a day carries a
  scheduled FOMC statement is known before every forecast of that day. We split $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ into the
  81 statement days and the 2{,}498 other days, the ordinary days, and score each part with the
  tests of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}. The split is set by the calendar, not by the losses, and every class and predictor
  group is reported under it (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_channels}).
\item \textbf{The statement afternoons} (Figure~\ref{fig:rh_channels}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The bars from 14:30 to 16:00~ET of the statement days, 1.0\% of the scored bars, carry
    51--78\% of the full set's every-bar QLIKE gain in the penalized linear
    models and 59--63\% in the tree ensembles.
  \item The statement is released at 14:00~ET. The HAR benchmark, which knows the weekday and the bar but not the
    calendar, cannot anticipate the rise in variance that follows, and QLIKE penalizes such under-prediction heavily,
    so a few hundred bars move the average; the largest differential is at the 14:30 bar.
  \item On ordinary days the trees' cumulative loss differential declines steadily, without the jumps of the statement
    days; the linear models' declines too, but unevenly, giving back part of its gain in some years.
    % 2026-10-28 (coordinator; claim check on the patched numbers): the draft's "On ordinary days the cumulative loss
    % differential declines steadily, without the jumps of the statement days" fails for the linear models (the
    % elastic net gives back 18% of its ordinary-day gain, with adverse ordinary days near the largest statement-day
    % move); it holds for the trees.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Beyond the FOMC calendar} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_corr}). Three corrections ask what the other
  predictors add beyond the calendar: the full set against HAR\,+\,FOMC, the HAR benchmark set with the FOMC series
  added; the full set refitted without the FOMC series against the HAR benchmark; and the full set against the HAR
  benchmark on ordinary days alone.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item They lower the loss by 2.4--4.0\% in the penalized linear models and 4.0--6.1\% in the tree
    ensembles, each significantly, and agree within 2 percentage points in each of the 5
    classes in which all three were run.
  \item The FOMC calendar thus adds an event component of its own, concentrated on the statement afternoons, to a
    gain that is present without it. Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi} asks which predictors carry each part.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Two groups carry the gain.} The FOMC calendar and the futures' realized moments, added to the HAR

\item \textbf{Evidence.} Three kinds, each reported for every class and predictor group.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Accuracy: the predictor-group ablations of Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation}, with the design of

  \item Use: each model's attribution, its TreeSHAP shares \citep{lundberg2020local} or standardized coefficient

\subsubsection{FOMC calendar}
\label{sec:rh_fi_event}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{It carries the statement days} (Tables~\ref{tab:rh_ablation} and~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl}). On every
  bar the FOMC series, added alone to the HAR benchmark set, deliver
  65--68\% of the trees' gain, and removing them from the full set
  raises the loss by 3.1--10.3\%. On statement days they recover
  93--104\% of the full set's gain in the linear models and 100--108\% in the trees, and
  removing them raises the loss by 28.2--173.0\%. The reading is concentrated for both model types; no other
  group recovers more than 15\% of it.
\item \textbf{The lasso wins.} On statement days the lasso's full-set loss differs from the ridge's by
  $-$31.9\% ($\DM={}$$-$8.42) and from the elastic net's by $-$31.8\%
  ($\DM={}$$-$7.69), as a signal in one series predicts; the lasso's top-ranked series, \ensuremath{\ser{fomc_until_inv}{\mathrm{FOMC}^{\mathrm{next}}}},
  is the proximity to the next statement.
\item \textbf{The models use it on few bars.} Over the span the FOMC calendar holds only
  1.4--2.3\% of the trees' attribution; on statement days \ensuremath{\ser{fomc_until_inv}{\mathrm{FOMC}^{\mathrm{next}}}} holds
  25.4\% of LightGBM's, on other days 1.06\% (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_fi_cond}).
\item \textbf{A cost on ordinary days for the linear models.} A linear term in the FOMC series also moves the forecasts
  of ordinary days: added alone, the series raise the ordinary-day loss of the penalized linear models by
  0.4--0.7\%, while the trees, which can confine the series' effect to the statement bars, pay no such
  cost ($-$0.3 to $-$0.1\%).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Realized moments}
\label{sec:rh_fi_ordinary}
\label{sec:rh_results_bench}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Not an augmented HAR} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation}, Panels~B--D). The futures' realized moments,
  computed from the same one-minute returns that define the target, are the natural augmented HAR. Added to the HAR
  benchmark set they lower the every-bar loss in every class ($-$1.9\% for the OLS), by about as much as
  the three classical extensions estimated together ($-$2.7\%; Panel~C). Yet the full set is
  significantly more accurate than the HAR benchmark set plus the realized moments in six of the
  six classes (Panel~D).
\item \textbf{They carry most of the ordinary-day gain} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl}). Added alone to the HAR
  benchmark set, the futures' realized moments lower the ordinary-day loss by $-$3.8,
  $-$3.3 and $-$3.9\% in the ridge, lasso and elastic net, nearly all or more of the
  full set's ordinary-day gain, and by 4.6--4.9\% in the trees, 77--88\% of theirs. Removing
  them from the full set is the only removal that raises the ordinary-day loss significantly in every class; on every
  bar it raises the loss by 1.5--2.0\% ($\DM={}$2.58 or larger). The
  reading is concentrated in all 3 linear classes and all 3 trees
  (Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl_full}).
  % 2026-10-28 (author, Table tab:rh_channels_abl legibility): the per-class readings, the add-alone sum and the counts
  % of significant removals moved to the appendix table tab:rh_channels_abl_full; pointers here and in the next item.
\item \textbf{The other groups repeat their information} (Tables~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl}
  and~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl_full}). The constituents' realized moments and the liquidity
  measures each lower the trees' ordinary-day loss on their own, by 2.3--4.1\% (on every bar,
  $-$3.3\% for the value-weighted market and XGBoost), and the groups' separate gains sum to
  2.9--3.3 times the trees' joint gain, but removing any one of them from the full set changes the
  gradient-boosted trees' ordinary-day loss by at most 0.2\%, none significantly. The
  redundancy reading holds in all 3 linear classes and in XGBoost; it fails for LightGBM, which
  has a second significant removal, and cannot be applied to the random forest, whose other removals were not run
  (the trees' removals other than the FOMC calendar's are on the design before the FOMC fix;
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_channels}). The groups are largely correlated proxies of the volatility information that the
  futures' own moments measure most directly.
  % 2026-10-28 (coordinator; claim check on the patched numbers): was "... sum to \rhchOrdSumRatioRng{} times the joint
  % gain, but removing any one of them from the full set costs little. The redundancy reading holds in
  % \rhchLinOrdNRedTest{} of the three linear classes and \rhchTreeOrdNRedTest{} of the three trees: the groups are
  % largely correlated proxies ..." (the tree count 1 of 3 read as a rejection for the forest, which was not tested).
\item \textbf{Averaging beats selection on ordinary days.} On ordinary days the lasso's full-set loss lies
  0.8\% above the ridge's and 1.6\% above the elastic net's
  ($\DM={}$2.28 and 3.35), the reverse of the statement days: the realized moments
  enter as several correlated columns, which averaging uses better than selection.
\item \textbf{Not a common factor of all the series} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_factor}). We add to the HAR benchmark set the
  first $k$ principal components, or partial-least-squares components, of the value averages of the 43
  non-FOMC exogenous series, standardized and re-estimated each day in the rolling window, and fit by OLS at every bar.
  With $k \le 3$ the factor-augmented HAR recovers none of the full set's ordinary-day gain (at best
  $R_k = 0.00$, PLS, $k = 1$), although the first three components hold 43.6\% of the
  series' variance, and ten components recover $R_{10} = 0.27$. The leading components largely repeat the
  HAR terms; the gain sits in particular series, the realized moments, rather than in the series' common variation.
  % The RULE's mechanical reading is "\rhfaReading" (R_10 < 0.5); the text gives the reason rather than the label.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Other predictor groups}
\label{sec:rh_fi_rest}
\label{sec:rh_results_beyond}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Small, and only in the boosted trees} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation}, Panel~D, last row;
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_results_beyond}). Against HAR\,+\,RM\,+\,FOMC the full set changes the every-bar loss of the
  ridge, lasso and elastic net by 0.1, $-$0.6 and
  $-$0.6\%, none significantly ($p \geq{}$0.161), and that of
  LightGBM and XGBoost by $-$1.6 and $-$1.8\%
  ($\DM={}$$-$4.92 and $-$5.26); the random forest's
  $-$0.5\% is not significant ($p$-value 0.096). On ordinary days the trees'
  remainder is $-$1.6, $-$1.8 and $-$0.6\%.
\item \textbf{A few series, from several groups} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_beyond_ladder}). No single remaining group is
  indispensable: removing any group other than the FOMC calendar and the realized moments changes the every-bar loss
  by at most 0.5\%. Yet a few series carry the boosted trees' remainder, and they come from several
  groups. LightGBM's top five are the value- and equal-weighted constituents' absolute returns, the value-weighted
  effective spread, the VIX and the value-weighted constituents' third moment; XGBoost ranks StockTwits sentiment
  first, then the same constituent series and the VIX. In follow-up tests outside the pre-specified design, scored
  on ordinary days, LightGBM and XGBoost refitted on HAR\,+\,RM\,+\,FOMC plus their own top five series recover
  shares of 0.72 and 0.91 of the remaining gain (LightGBM's top series alone
  0.75), and ten principal components of the six remaining groups 0.35 and
  0.37.
\item \textbf{Sparse, not dense.} In the terms of \citet{GiannoneLenzaPrimiceri2021}, the remainder is sparse in
  series and scattered across groups.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item A dense linear signal would show in the ridge, which keeps and shrinks every series; yet the ridge's full set
    changes its ordinary-day loss against HAR\,+\,RM\,+\,FOMC by 0.2\%
    ($p = 0.752$). In the boosted trees five series recover more of the remainder than ten
    principal components of all of them, and under the reading fixed before the ladder was scored XGBoost's
    remainder is concentrated and LightGBM's intermediate ($R = 0.94$ with twenty
    series): neither is dense.
  \item No group is indispensable, yet the top series come from four or five groups: series in different groups
    appear to measure much the same thing (both models rank the equal- and the value-weighted constituents'
    absolute returns among their top five). Where averaging beats selection, it does so among the correlated
    columns of the futures' realized moments (Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi_ordinary}).
  \end{itemize}

\subsection{Robustness}
\label{sec:rh_results_robust}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Estimation window.} The window length $W$ of 3{,}000 trading days was chosen after the
  six candidate windows from 1{,}000 to 3{,}500 trading days had been
  scored out of sample on $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$; it is not a pre-sample choice. Appendix~\ref{app:rh_robust_window}
  reports every window.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Every bar: the comparison does not depend on the window. Across the candidate windows the every-bar gain of the
    full-set elastic net over its HAR-set forecast lies between \ensuremath{-}6.7\% and
    \ensuremath{-}5.2\%, significant at each, and with a window of 3{,}500 days the full set
    remains significantly more accurate on every bar in 6 of the 6 classes
    (Table~\ref{tab:rh_robust_w3500}).
% 2026-10-26 (coordinator; author: no 16:00-bar results in the main text): moved to Appendix app:rh_robust_window. Was:
%   \item The 16:00 bar: comparisons are window-sensitive; the same elastic-net change at 16:00 ranges from
%     \rhwsEnetClosePctMin{}\% to \rhwsEnetClosePctMax{}\% across the windows.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Multiple comparisons.} Adjusting for the number of comparisons leaves the every-bar result intact: under
  QLIKE the 90\% model confidence set \citep{HansenLundeNason2011} holds 2 of the
  10 distinct pooled forecasts (LightGBM on the full predictor set and XGBoost on the full predictor set), and StepM \citep{RomanoWolf2005} rejects
  equal accuracy of the full and HAR benchmark sets in 6 of the 6 classes (SPA
  $p$-value \ensuremath{<}0.001; \citealp{Hansen2005}), against none under squared error
  (Tables~\ref{tab:rh_mcs} and~\ref{tab:rh_mcs_spa}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Economic application}
\label{sec:rh_econ}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc; audit front-3, results-18): parked -- the lead of 2026-10-25 (the forecasts framed as
% closing-half-hour forecasts; the straddle said to pay on the half hour's realized variance). Was: "Our forecasts
% target the realized variance of the closing half hour, and that target has a direct counterpart in the options
% market: a same-day-expiring straddle bought at the start of the closing half hour and held to the close pays off on
% the variance realized over that half hour, against the variance implied by its price. We therefore value the
% forecasts as the literature on the economic evaluation of volatility forecasts does (Section~\ref{sec:rh_related}),
% by the returns of the straddle trades they signal; the main strategy uses each forecast only through the sign of its
% difference from the implied variance."
% 2026-10-26 (integration, coordinator: bullet structure): the lead paragraph recast as a bold-lead item, content kept.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A trade on the closing-bar forecast.} The pooled models forecast every regular-hours bar, and their
  15:30 forecast of the closing bar has a counterpart in the options market: a same-day-expiring S\&P~500 straddle
  traded at 15:30 ET and held to the close.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Its payoff is set by the index's move over that half hour, so a forecast of the half hour's realized
    variance, set against the variance implied by the straddle's price, signals which side to take.
  \item As in the literature on the economic evaluation of volatility forecasts (Section~\ref{sec:rh_related}), we
    value the forecasts by the returns of the trades they signal; each forecast enters only through the sign of its
    difference from the implied variance \citep{FlemingKirbyOstdiek2001}.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

% 2026-10-28 (author: conventional titles). Was: \subsection{The straddle strategy}
\subsection{Trading strategy}
\label{sec:rh_econ_strategy}
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved to A_econ.tex (app:rh_econ_details) -- the T_opt identity (expirations minus
% early closes), the held-out expirations and the non-option days of T_oos.
\item \textbf{Sample.} The strategy trades on $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}} \subset \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$, the
  $T_{\mathrm{opt}} = 866$ trading days of the evaluation span with a same-day SPXW expiration, early-close days
  excluded (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_econ_details}). Its first 252 days only initialize the sizing rules of
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_econ_sizing}; every statistic of this section is computed on the remaining 614
  post-warmup days, $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}$.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved to A_econ.tex (app:rh_econ_details) -- the quote screen (outage rule), the
% entry-price formulas and the settlement display; the payoff and the return are written as one display below.
\item \textbf{Position.} With $S_t$ the underlying print on the option chain at 15:30 ET, we trade the call and the
  put at the nearest strikes with live quotes, $K_C = \min\{K \ge S_t\}$ and $K_P = \max\{K \le S_t\}$: an
  at-the-money straddle when $K_C = K_P$, otherwise a narrow strangle on the two strikes bracketing $S_t$, which we
  also call the straddle. It is held unhedged to cash settlement at the official S\&P~500 close
  $S^{\mathrm{close}}_t$, and its return on the mid-quote premium $P_t$, the sum of the two legs' mid-quotes, is
  \[
    R_t = \frac{\bigl(S^{\mathrm{close}}_t - K_C\bigr)^+ + \bigl(K_P - S^{\mathrm{close}}_t\bigr)^+}{P_t} - 1
      \;\ge\; -1 .
  \]
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved to A_econ.tex (app:rh_econ_details) -- the recovery of the implied
% volatility on the days with a failed vendor solve (the Black--Scholes display).
\item \textbf{Signal.} With $\mathrm{IV}^C_t$ and $\mathrm{IV}^P_t$ the legs' implied volatilities at 15:30 ET, quoted
  per hour, $\mathrm{IV}_t = (\mathrm{IV}^C_t + \mathrm{IV}^P_t)/(2\sqrt2)$ is the implied volatility over the closing
  half hour and $\mathrm{IV}_t^2$ its implied variance (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_econ_details} treats the vendor's
  failed solves). The sign strategy holds
  \[
    q_t = \sign\bigl(\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2\bigr), \qquad r_t = q_t R_t ,
  \]
  long when the forecast variance $\hat\sigma^2_t$ of the closing bar (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}) exceeds
  the implied variance and short otherwise (ties go short); $\mathrm{IV}_t^2 - \hat\sigma^2_t$ is the forecast of the
  half hour's variance risk premium \citep{CarrWu2009,BollerslevTauchenZhou2009}.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc; D2; audit results-12): added -- the two benchmark strategies, and the HAR-set
% forecasts counted once (the pooled ridge, lasso and elastic net on the HAR benchmark set equal the OLS).
\item \textbf{Benchmarks.} The unconditional short straddle, $q_t \equiv -1$, and the sign strategy of the benchmark
  forecast, the OLS on the HAR benchmark set pooled over the 13 regular-hours bars
  (Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}). On the HAR benchmark set the pooled ridge, lasso and elastic-net forecasts coincide with
  the OLS (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_main}, note b), so the six HAR-set strategies hold four distinct
  forecasts.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved to A_econ.tex (app:rh_econ_details) -- the display of r^ba_t.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc; audit numbers-13, results-14): parked -- the half-spread over all 866 option days
% printed beside the post-warmup Sharpe ratios. Was: "\item \textbf{Transaction costs.} Executing at the quoted bid or
% ask rather than the mid-quote imposes a median half-spread cost of \cmSvCostStraddle\% of the straddle premium. No
% additional commissions or exchange fees are deducted."
\item \textbf{Execution.} At quoted prices a purchase pays the sum of the legs' asks and a sale receives the sum of
  their bids; settlement is in cash, so the spread is paid at entry only (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_econ_details}). The
  median quoted half-spread is 2.5\% of the premium on the 614 post-warmup days
  (2.9\% on all 866 days of $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$). No commissions or fees are
  deducted.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Performance measures}
\label{sec:rh_econ_measures}
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved to A_econ.tex (app:rh_econ_sharpe) -- the values of A_y, N_y and c_y, the
% equal-weight rationale, the alternative definitions, and note D6 (resolved; its disclosure is now text there).
% Moved to A_econ.tex: the hit rate and position counts (not used in this section), the elementary score and its
% decision-threshold property (app:rh_econ_rankcorr), and the compounding measures (app:rh_econ_compounding).
\item \textbf{Sharpe ratio.} With $T = 614$ the number of post-warmup days in $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}$
  and $\mathcal Y$ their 4 calendar years,
  \[
    \SR = \sqrt{q}\;\frac{\bar r}{\mathrm{sd}(r)},
    \qquad
    q = \frac{T}{\sum_{y \in \mathcal Y} c_y},
  \]
  where $\bar r$ and $\mathrm{sd}(r)$ are the mean and standard deviation (divisor $T - 1$) of the $T$ daily returns,
  each day with weight $1/T$, and $c_y$ is the fraction of calendar year $y$ that the sample covers, so that
  $q = 225.5$ is the average number of option days per calendar year (SPXW expirations were listed on Mondays,
  Wednesdays and Fridays until spring 2022 and on every weekday from 16~May~2022). The ratio of a single year,
  $\SR_y = \sqrt{A_y}\,\bar r_y/\mathrm{sd}_y(r)$, takes the mean and standard deviation of the $N_y$ returns of year
  $y$ and annualizes by that year's own number of option days per calendar year, $A_y = N_y/c_y$. The risk-free
  return over the 30-minute holding period is negligible and omitted. Appendix~\ref{app:rh_econ_sharpe} gives the
  alternative definitions and when this one was adopted.
% 2026-10-28 (D19, standard pooled Sharpe): the equal-year mean of the SR_y (D6) is now a robustness column
% (tab:rh_econ_sharpe_defs). Was: "\item \textbf{Sharpe ratio.} With $\mathcal Y$ the \rheNYears{} calendar years of
% $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}$, \[ \SR = \frac{1}{|\mathcal Y|}\sum_{y \in \mathcal Y} \SR_y, \qquad \SR_y =
% \sqrt{A_y}\;\frac{\bar r_y}{\mathrm{sd}_y(r)}, \qquad A_y = \frac{N_y}{c_y}, \] where $\bar r_y$ and
% $\mathrm{sd}_y(r)$ are the mean and standard deviation (divisor $N_y - 1$) of the $N_y$ daily returns of year $y$ and
% $c_y$ is the fraction of the calendar year that the sample covers, so that $A_y$ is the year's number of option days
% per calendar year. Each year enters with equal weight at its own trading frequency (SPXW expirations were listed on
% Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays until spring 2022 and on every weekday from \rheSplitDate). The risk-free return
% over the 30-minute holding period is negligible and omitted. Appendix~\ref{app:rh_econ_sharpe} gives the
% alternative definitions and when this one was adopted."
\item \textbf{Tests.} Every statement about a difference of Sharpe ratios, $\Delta\SR = \SR(r^A) - \SR(r^B)$, uses
  the studentized circular block bootstrap test of \citet{LedoitWolf2008} (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_methods_tests}).
  % 2026-10-28 (D19, standard pooled Sharpe): was "uses a paired circular block bootstrap of $\Delta\SR$ itself
  % (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_methods_tests})."
  A statement about
  a mean daily return, or about the mean of the return differential $\Delta_t = r^A_t - r^B_t$, uses the
  $t$-statistic with the Newey--West long-run variance at bandwidth $S = 33$ and fixed-$b$ critical values
  \citep{KieferVogelsang2005,LazarusLewisStockWatson2018}. The two tests answer different questions: a strategy can
  have a significantly higher Sharpe ratio than another without a significantly higher mean return.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:rh_conclusion}
% 2026-10-26 (author requirement, relayed by the coordinator): bold-lead items with nested sub-items; the wording is
% that of the same day's rewrite (not committed before), split into sub-items and tightened to the one-page budget,
% so nothing is parked for this step.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Exogenous predictors in intraday realized variance forecasts.} We ask what exogenous predictors, from
  the futures' own realized moments and the constituents' trading to the FOMC calendar, implied volatility and
  alternative data, add to pooled forecasts of the E-mini S\&P~500's realized variance on every regular-hours bar,
  against OLS on the HAR benchmark set.
% 2026-10-26: "all ... each significant" backed by \rhorAfLower = \rhorAfLowerSig = \rhorAfPairs (Table 1).
\item \textbf{The exogenous predictors improve the forecast of every bar} (Section~\ref{sec:rh_results}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The full set lowers the average QLIKE loss in all 6 model classes, each reduction significant at
    the 5\% level, by 6.0--9.0\% (penalized linear models) and 11.2--14.9\%
    (tree ensembles) against the OLS benchmark.
  \item The gain survives the HAR benchmark augmented with the futures' realized moments (significantly in
    six of the six classes), the classical HAR extensions and a window of
    3{,}500 days (6 of 6 classes).
    % 2026-10-26 (coordinator; author: no 16:00-bar results in the main text): dropped "; it is weakest at the closing half hour (significant in \rhcaNLowerSigCloseSpan{} of
    % \rhorAfPairs{} classes)".
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{The gain is concentrated} (Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi}). The FOMC calendar
% 2026-10-28 (v2 of Sections 6-7, author approved preliminarily): pointer for the v2 layout. Was: (Sections~\ref{sec:rh_results_ablation} and~\ref{sec:rh_fi}), now one section
  carries most of the trees' gain and the futures' realized moments come second; the 10
  highest-ranked series retain 95--98\% of it, and the linear models do best with
  10 series. The signal sits in a few series rather than spreading thinly over many.
% 2026-10-26 (audit correctness-4, front-11): the option-day live share of StockTwits attention alone (100%) parked;
% the evaluation bars are the reach that matters, and the training-window share is \rhfilStwWinPct.
\item \textbf{Beyond the two groups, a small gain in the boosted trees.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The other 36 series change no penalized linear model's loss significantly and that of
    LightGBM and XGBoost by $-$1.6 and $-$1.8\%, through a few
    series from several groups rather than a factor common to them.
% 2026-10-28 (author, alternative-data edit: the claim is about the 36 series beyond HAR + RM + FOMC). Was:
% \item \textbf{Alternative data add little, even when live.}
%   \begin{itemize}
  \item Under our causal construction the StockTwits and volatility-demand series are live on
    17.3--31.2\% and 7.0--7.6\% of the scored bars; on those bars they change the
    loss little, and volatility demand raises that of the linear models.
  \item Their share of the trees' attribution rises in their live years (StockTwits
    0.8--1.3\%, from at most 27\% of the training window), but use is not
    accuracy.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{QLIKE and squared error.} Under squared-error loss the full set is not more accurate (its mean squared
  error is higher in 6 of 6 classes, significantly in 0),
  a difference carried almost entirely by 5 days of the COVID-19 crash; without the crash window it is
  significantly lower in 6 classes.
% 2026-10-26: "the full-set strategies beat the short straddle" backed by \rhemFullVsShortSig (D6 bootstrap); the
% count against the RTH13 OLS-HAR strategy awaits \rhPending{rhemFullVsOlsHarSig}; "no significant market beta" by
% \rhebBetaSigFull = 0.
\item \textbf{An application to 0DTE straddles} (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Signed by the forecast of the closing bar's variance against implied variance, one at-the-money SPXW
    straddle a day earns annualized Sharpe ratios of 1.54--1.88 at mid-quotes
    (1.18--1.52 at bid/ask) on the full set, against 0.32 for the short
    straddle, significantly more in 3 of the 6 classes; against the HAR strategy, in
    1.
  \item The gain is earned on the days the strategies buy and rests on their 10 best days; no strategy has a
    significant market beta.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Comparison with machine-learning option portfolios.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026} trade decile long--short portfolios of S\&P~500 index options of all
    maturities, re-formed every half hour on forecasts of delta-hedged returns, over eight months of
    2015. Their Sharpe ratios (31.27 and 38.47 annualized) are gross, at
    mid-quotes; by their account quoted spreads would erase much of the profit.
  \item Ours come from one unhedged straddle a day, are far smaller, are reported at bid/ask too, and rest on a few
    days.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Scope and extensions.} One index and one futures contract; a window fixed after an out-of-sample
  comparison of windows, all reported in the online appendix; NYSE-holiday sessions kept in the estimation sample; a
  short option sample (614 days). Extensions: the sessions after 30 April 2024, other markets, density
  forecasts, and trades entered at earlier bars from the every-bar forecasts already produced.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Replication package}
\label{app:rh_repro}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Contents.} The code that builds the design matrices from the data, fits every model and writes every
  forecast, and the generators that turn the stored forecasts into the numbers, tables and figures of the paper. Its
  README maps each number, table and figure to its generator and inputs.
\item \textbf{Numbers.} The numbers in the text are macros written by these generators
  (\texttt{writeup/\allowbreak make\_*.py}) to files in \texttt{writeup/\allowbreak generated/}; one switch
  (\texttt{REHAUL\_\allowbreak FINAL\_\allowbreak RUN}, \texttt{writeup/\allowbreak final\_run.py}) points them at the
  final forecasts.
\item \textbf{Fits.} The pooled linear models are fitted by
  \texttt{experiments/\allowbreak pooled\_\allowbreak linear\_\allowbreak rerun\_\allowbreak 2026\_10\_19\_13.py} and
  the tree ensembles by \texttt{experiments/\allowbreak pooled\_\allowbreak trees\_\allowbreak rerun\_13.py}, the
  random forest with Intel's oneDAL engine
  (Intel Extension for Scikit-learn).
\item \textbf{Software.} \texttt{requirements.txt} names the packages, with a version range for each; it is not a
  pinned lock file. The package does not record hashes of the design matrices, the CPU class of the fits or their
  compute time.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Data sources}
\label{app:rh_dp_sources}
\begin{itemize}
% From 03_data.tex (2026-10-26): the display of the futures' realized moments and the sentence that names them.
% Sums read off the column names: the builder of data/core_stats.parquet is not in the repo
% (live/close_signal/features.py:1-25); sumpret2 = positive semivariance is an assumed reading; bipower unnormalized.
\item \textbf{Realized moments.} With $r_{t,i,k}$ the one-minute log-price changes of Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}, the
  7 realized-moment series are the one-minute sums
  % 2026-10-19 (user): raw parquet names for now (\ifrawseries, paper_rehaul.tex preamble): each sum is named by its
  % column of data/core_stats.parquet. The \else branch is the display of the symbols.
  \ifrawseries
  \begin{gather*}
    \sername{sumret}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}, \quad \sername{sumabsret}_{t,i} = \sum_k |r_{t,i,k}|, \quad
    \sername{sumret3}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^3,\\
    \sername{sumret4}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^4, \quad
    \sername{sumpret2}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^2\,\mathbf{1}\{r_{t,i,k} > 0\},\\
    \sername{sumbipow}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} |r_{t,i,k}|\,|r_{t,i,k-1}|, \quad
    \sername{sumautocov}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} r_{t,i,k}\, r_{t,i,k-1}.
  \end{gather*}
  \else
  \[
    \sum_k r_{t,i,k}, \quad \sum_k |r_{t,i,k}|, \quad \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^3, \quad \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^4, \quad
    \mathrm{RS}^{+}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^2\,\mathbf{1}\{r_{t,i,k} > 0\},
  \]
  \[
    \mathrm{BV}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} |r_{t,i,k}|\,|r_{t,i,k-1}|, \qquad
    \mathrm{AC}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} r_{t,i,k}\, r_{t,i,k-1}.
  \]
  \fi
  The third sum is the unnormalized realized skewness of \citet{AmayaChristoffersenJacobsVasquez2015} (before the
  division by $\RV^{3/2}_{t,i}/\sqrt{N_{t,i}}$), the fourth the realized quarticity without the factor $N_{t,i}/3$,
  $\ser{sumpret2}{\mathrm{RS}^{+}}_{t,i}$ the positive realized semivariance of
  \citet{BarndorffNielsenKinnebrockShephard2010}, $\ser{sumbipow}{\mathrm{BV}}_{t,i}$ the bipower variation of
  \citet{BarndorffNielsenShephard2004} without its $\pi/2$ factor, and $\ser{sumautocov}{\mathrm{AC}}_{t,i}$ the
  first-order realized autocovariance. The realized variance itself is the target and not a predictor.
\item \textbf{Liquidity.} From the front-month futures contract we take the total contract volume traded in the half
  hour and the number of observed one-minute intervals $N_{t,i}$\ifrawseries{} (\sername{numobs})\fi. From intraday
  data on the S\&P~500 constituents, 1993 to 2024, we form equal- and value-weighted cross-sectional aggregates of
  share turnover, buyer-initiated turnover, seller-initiated turnover, the effective spread, the quoted spread and
  order-flow imbalance. Constituent turnover is the number of shares traded in the half hour divided by the prior
  day's shares outstanding; buyer- and seller-initiated turnover aggregate the trades by their estimated direction.
  The effective spread is the average percentage deviation of the transaction price from the prevailing mid-quote,
  and the quoted spread the average percentage bid--ask spread. Equal-weighted aggregates are simple cross-sectional
  averages; value-weighted aggregates weight each constituent by its prior-day market capitalization. For each
  weighting ($\ser{ofi_ewstock}{\mathrm{OFI}^{\mathrm{EW}}}$ and $\ser{ofi_vwstock}{\mathrm{OFI}^{\mathrm{VW}}}$),
  order-flow imbalance is
  \[
    \mathrm{OFI}_{t,i} = \frac{\mathrm{Buy}_{t,i} - \mathrm{Sell}_{t,i}}{\mathrm{Buy}_{t,i} + \mathrm{Sell}_{t,i}}
      \in [-1, 1],
    \qquad \text{missing if } \mathrm{Buy}_{t,i} + \mathrm{Sell}_{t,i} = 0 ,
  \]
  with $\mathrm{Buy}_{t,i}$ and $\mathrm{Sell}_{t,i}$ the aggregate buyer- and seller-initiated turnover of interval
  $(t,i)$.
  % loading.py:161-180, built on the unfilled legs.
\item \textbf{Market moments.} For each weighting, the 6 constituent moments are the realized variance,
  realized skewness, realized quarticity, absolute variation, bipower variation and positive semivariance, computed
  from 5-minute log returns rather than the one-minute changes of the futures moments. The constituent groups omit
  the signed return sum and the realized autocovariance; the futures group omits the realized variance, which is the
  target.
\item \textbf{Sentiment.} StockTwits message streams, from 2009 for all posts and 2010 for
  posts tagged by their users: attention, the number of posts in the half hour; the sentiment score, $1$ when every
  tagged post is bullish and $-1$ when every tagged post is bearish; and the sentiment count, the number of posts
  tagged bullish or bearish.
