\subsection{FOMC calendar}
\label{app:rh_dp_fomc}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Statements.} The scheduled statement times come from the release file, which ends with the statement of
  \rhdsFomcFileLast, and from the \rhdsFomcAdded{} scheduled statements that follow it up to the end of our data. The
  statement-day indicator equals 1 on every interval of a day with a scheduled statement. The distances
  $n^{+}_{t,i}$ and $n^{-}_{t,i}$ count half-hour intervals on the grid less the weekend break.
\item \textbf{The pre-announced calendar in March 2020.} The release file holds the statements that were issued, and
  the meeting scheduled for \rhdsFomcSchedMeeting{} is not among them: the Federal Reserve replaced it with the
  action announced on Sunday, \rhdsFomcReplaced. The proximity measures follow the calendar that was public at each
  interval. Until that announcement, $n^{+}_{t,i}$ counts the intervals to that meeting's scheduled statement; from
  the announcement on, $n^{+}_{t,i}$ counts to the next statement issued, on
  \rhdsFomcNextIssued, and $n^{-}_{t,i}$ counts from the first interval after the announcement. No statement is added,
  so the statement-day indicator is unchanged.
\item \textbf{No winsorization.} The statement-day indicator passes through every step unchanged. The proximity
  measures, after the logarithm of step~2, are deterministic ramps that rise or fall monotonically between
  statements, so each value is an extreme of its own trailing window and a rolling quantile clip would bind on most
  intervals, holding the series behind its true value. They skip the winsorization of step~3; every other step
  applies.
\item Both rules change only the two proximity series. Forecasts built before them (some robustness and ablation
  arms, marked where they are reported) count to the next statement issued in early 2020 and clip the proximity
  measures.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Sessions, cleaning and missing values}
\label{app:rh_dp_sessions}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Grid.} The grid $\mathcal G$ starts at the first observed realized variance; the weekend break it leaves
  out runs from Friday 20:00 to Sunday 18:30~ET:
  \[
    (t,i) \in \mathcal{G} \iff \RV_{t,i} \text{ observed and } (t,i) \notin (\text{Fri } 20{:}00,\ \text{Sun } 18{:}30) .
  \]
\item \textbf{Early closes.} The early-close sessions stay in the grid $\mathcal G$, on which every trailing average is
  computed, but the pooled models neither estimate on nor score any interval of them, and the option-trading sample
  leaves them out. The intervals after their 13:00~ET close leave the window $\mathcal D_{t,i}$ of the target's
  diurnal factor $s^2_{t,i}$; the diurnal factors of the exogenous series keep them.
\item \textbf{Holiday sessions.} On full NYSE holidays the cash market is closed and the E-mini trades a shortened
  session that ends at about 13:00~ET. Its regular-hours intervals, which carry little variance, are rows of the
  13-bar estimation sample and enter the windows $\mathcal D_{t,i}$ of the target's diurnal factor at their
  times of day; they are forecast but never scored, which is why each pooled model has 33{,}970 forecasts
  and 33{,}527 scored bars over the evaluation span. Because the estimation window counts rows, its
  39{,}000 rows span slightly fewer than 3{,}000 trading days. In the robustness check of
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_robust_holiday}, the holiday sessions leave the estimation sample and the windows $\mathcal D_{t,i}$, while
  every trailing average is still computed on the full grid; the linear models are refitted with their frozen
  penalties, and the every-bar comparisons of the full predictor set with the HAR benchmark change by
  0.13--0.14 percentage points.
\item \textbf{Domain rule.} Before any other step, a print outside the domain of its series is set to missing: a
  nonpositive quoted or effective spread, total turnover, futures volume, observation count or index level, and a
  negative value of a series that cannot be negative. The rule removes \rhdsInvalidPrints{} prints,
  \rhdsInvalidVolume{} of them zero futures volumes on intervals that carry one-minute price changes.
\item \textbf{Availability and filling.} For each exogenous series the availability indicator $a_{t,i}$ is recorded
  before any filling. The series is then forward-filled over at most \rhdsFfillCap{} intervals, and the diurnal
  factors, the variance-stabilizing scale and the winsorization bounds are computed on the filled series; every
  interval with $a_{t,i} = 0$ then takes the imputed value of step~4 (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_transform}). A gap
  longer than the cap stays missing in these statistics.
\item \textbf{No observation.} A series whose feed stops is unobserved from its last print on, and its availability
  averages fall to zero. Wherever a $k$-interval average holds no observed interval, its standardized value is set to
  zero (step~6 of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}). In the pooled models this rule acts, on at least one interval, on
  \rhdsUnobsCols{} of the \rhdsValueCols{} value averages of the full predictor set over the whole sample and on
  \rhdsUnobsColsEval{} of them within the evaluation span from \rhdsEvalStart: on every horizon of the volatility-demand
  series once their feed has stopped, and on the shorter horizons of the series that do not print on every interval
  (volatility demand, the implied volatility indices, the constituent aggregates and the StockTwits series) where the
  averaging window falls in a gap between their prints.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Transformations of the exogenous series}
\label{app:rh_dp_transform}
% 2026-10-26 (coordinator: the paper keeps its bullet structure): the lead sentence as a bold-lead item.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Order.} Steps 1 to 4 of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors} are applied to each exogenous series $u$ in this
  order; step~5 forms the trailing averages, and step~6 (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_scale}) standardizes them.
\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Diurnal adjustment.} Each raw series is divided by a time-of-day factor estimated over the prior-day set
  $\mathcal D_{t,i}$ of $s^2_{t,i}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}) and bounded relative to its own trailing
  median:
  \[
    \tilde u_{t,i} = \frac{u_{t,i}}{b^{(u)}_{t,i}}, \qquad
    b^{(u)}_{t,i} =
    \begin{cases}
      \clip\bigl(\operatorname{mean}_{t' \in \mathcal{D}_{t,i}} u_{t',i},\ 0.5\,\rho_{t,i},\
        2\,\rho_{t,i}\bigr), & u \ge 0,\\[2pt]
      \max\bigl\{\clip\bigl(\operatorname{sd}_{t' \in \mathcal{D}_{t,i}} u_{t',i},\ 0.5\,\rho_{t,i},\
        2\,\rho_{t,i}\bigr),\ 0.1\,\bar\sigma^{(u)}_{t,i}\bigr\}, & u \text{ signed},
    \end{cases}
  \]
  \begin{itemize}
  \item where $\rho_{t,i}$ is the median of the 250 most recent unbounded factors of interval $i$
    (at least 20 of them), and $\bar\sigma^{(u)}_{t,i}$ the median of the nonzero trailing standard
    deviations $\operatorname{sd}_{t'' \in \mathcal{D}_{t',i'}} u_{t'',i'}$ over all intervals $(t',i')$ up to
    $(t,i)$, every time of day pooled (before the first such standard deviation the adjusted value is undefined and
    is imputed as in step~4);
  \item a series is signed when the quantity it measures can be negative, not when its sample has a negative value
    (Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_dictionary});
  \item $b^{(u)}_{t,i} = 1$ whenever the factor of a nonnegative series is zero or undefined; and
  \item the implied volatility indices, the StockTwits sentiment score and the FOMC series are not adjusted.
  \end{itemize}
\item \emph{Variance stabilization.} The first matching rule of
  \[
    g(v) =
    \begin{cases}
      \sqrt{v} & \text{squared returns, realized variance, turnover,}\\
        & \text{bipower variation, effective spread},\\
      \sign(v)\,|v|^{1/2} & \text{autocovariance},\\
      v^{1/3} & \text{cubed returns},\\
      \sign(v)\,|v|^{1/4} & \text{fourth-power returns},\\
      v & \text{other signed series, absolute returns},\\
      \log \max(v, \ensuremath{10^{-12}}) & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
  \]
  replaces $\tilde u_{t,i}$ by $g(\tilde u_{t,i})$.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item A signed series without a power rule is routed at interval $(t,i)$ to an inverse hyperbolic sine of the raw
    series when its standard-deviation divisor sat at its floor on at least 50\% of its intervals
    since its first print and before $(t,i)$, at least 250 of them. This routes the volatility-demand
    series, on almost all of their intervals (Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_dictionary}), and no other series:
    \[
      \tilde u_{t,i} = \operatorname{asinh}(u_{t,i} / \kappa_{t,i}), \qquad
      \kappa_{t,i} = \max\bigl\{ e_{t,i-1},\ 0.01\operatorname{med}_{j \ge 1} e_{t,i-j} \bigr\},
    \]
    where $e_{t,i}$ is an exponentially weighted moving average of $|u|$ over the nonzero intervals ($u \ne 0$) with
    a half-life of 12{,}000 such intervals (nominally 250 days of 48
    intervals).
  \item The FOMC statement-day indicator passes through unchanged, and the FOMC proximity measures take the logarithm
    (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \emph{Winsorization.} With $\mathcal U_{t,i} = \{\tilde u_{t,i-j} : j = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{w}}\}$ the
  preceding $n_{\mathrm{w}} = 240$ intervals of the grid, all times of day pooled,
  \[
    \tilde u_{t,i} \leftarrow \clip\bigl(\tilde u_{t,i},\ \underline Q^{(u)}_{t,i},\ \overline Q^{(u)}_{t,i}\bigr),
  \]
  where $\underline Q^{(u)}_{t,i}$ and $\overline Q^{(u)}_{t,i}$ are the empirical 1st and
  99th percentiles of $\mathcal U_{t,i}$, the levels of the target's winsorization
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The bounds are defined only when all $n_{\mathrm{w}}$ values of $\mathcal U_{t,i}$ exist, after the forward
    fill of at most \rhdsFfillCap{} intervals; otherwise the interval is not clipped. Series whose prints leave longer
    gaps are therefore clipped only where a full window of values precedes the interval: VIX3M and VVIX, which print
    only part of the day, never; the VIX and the constituent aggregates on part of the sample; the futures' own
    moments and liquidity series, which print on every interval of the grid, throughout.
  \item The FOMC series are not winsorized (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \emph{Imputation.} An unobserved interval takes the expanding median of the series' earlier observed
  transformed values; $a_{t,i}$ enters the model separately, through its trailing averages:
  \[
    \tilde u_{t,i} \leftarrow
    \begin{cases}
      \tilde u_{t,i}, & a_{t,i} = 1,\\
      \operatorname{med}\mathcal{A}_{t,i}, & a_{t,i} = 0,\ \mathcal{A}_{t,i} \ne \emptyset,\\
      \tilde u_{(1)}, & a_{t,i} = 0,\ \mathcal{A}_{t,i} = \emptyset,
    \end{cases}
  \]
  where $\mathcal{A}_{t,i} = \{\tilde u_{t',i'} : (t',i') \prec (t,i),\ a_{t',i'} = 1\}$, $(t',i') \prec (t,i)$ means
  that $(t',i')$ is an interval of the grid strictly before $(t,i)$, and $\tilde u_{(1)}$ is the transformed value on
  the series' first observed interval. The late-start rule of step~6 keeps $\tilde u_{(1)}$ out of every forecast.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Activity indicator (not in the pooled models).} A series is mode-inflated at interval $(t,i)$ when it has
  at least 250 observed prints strictly before $(t,i)$ and their most frequent value, $m_{t,i}$,
  accounts for at least 20\% of them. On every interval at which the series is mode-inflated,
  \[
    \chi_{t,i} =
    \begin{cases}
      \mathbf{1}\{u_{t,i} \ne m_{t,i}\}, & a_{t,i} = 1,\\
      \chi^{\circ}_{t,i}, & a_{t,i} = 0,
    \end{cases}
  \]
  where $\chi^{\circ}_{t,i}$ is the more frequent value of $\chi$ on the series' earlier observed intervals (0 on a
  tie), and $\chi_{t,i} = 0$ elsewhere. Under this rule 5 series are mode-inflated at some interval:
  the number of observations, the 3 StockTwits series (on part of the sample) and the FOMC statement-day
  indicator; the volatility-demand series never are. The pooled models carry no trailing averages of $\chi$; the
  evidence requirement of the penalized linear models (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_linear}) uses the same threshold of
  250 intervals, and the closing-interval panel of the earlier model set carries the averages
  (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing_predictors}).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Robust standardization}
\label{app:rh_dp_scale}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Window and statistics.} The rows are those of the estimation sample, the 13 regular-hours bars
  of each day. Row $(t,i)$ is scaled with the median and the interquartile range of the $W = 39{,}000$ rows
  before it, $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, imputed rows included, so both are recomputed at every row; the rows of the first
  window take that window's statistics, and all of them precede the first forecast. The denominator of
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}, step~6, takes the largest of three scales: the window's interquartile range; a
  relative floor, 0.01 times the largest interquartile range of the column up to $(t,i)$; and the
  causal floor $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t,i}$. A scale below \ensuremath{10^{-12}} is replaced by 1 before the causal floor
  applies.
\item \textbf{The causal floor} $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t,i}$ is the interquartile range of the column over the
  earlier rows whose $k$-interval average holds only observed intervals (the availability mask eroded over about
  $\lceil k \cdot 13/ 46\rceil$ rows of the sample). When at least 250
  earlier rows exist and one value accounts for at least 20\% of them, rows at that value are left out.
  The floor is re-evaluated every 480 rows and held in between, and it equals 1 until
  8 such rows exist. It guards against a window that holds mostly imputed values, whose interquartile
  range collapses.
\item \textbf{Columns.} The availability averages $\bar a^{(k)}$ keep their $[0, 1]$ scale. The HAR components and the
  calendar columns are scaled by the same rule without the causal floor ($\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)} = 0$).
\item \textbf{Late start.} For a series whose first print comes after the first day of the sample, an interval is live
  for horizon $k$ when its $k$-interval average holds no interval before the day of the first print. The standardized
  value $z^{(k)}_{t,i}$ is set to 0 on every row whose window $\mathcal W_{t,i}$ holds a row that is not live; since
  liveness only switches on, these are the first $L + W$ rows, $L$ the first live row. A late series therefore enters
  a forecast only once a full window of live averages exists, and because the rows before that point stay at zero,
  the estimation windows of the following years hold few rows on which the series varies (none at the first such
  forecast). The availability averages are not affected.
\item \textbf{Live shares on the option days.} On the closing bars of the 614 post-warmup option days of
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}, the value averages are live on 100.0\% of bars for the VIX,
  96.1--100.0\% for VIX3M, 100.0\% for StockTwits attention, 72.6--81.9\% for its
  sentiment and tag count, 31.6--31.9\% for volatility demand and 0.0--9.0\% for VVIX (ranges over $k$).
  The first prints are in 2006 (VIX), 2009 (VIX3M), 2009 (StockTwits
  attention), 2010 (sentiment and tag count), 2011 (volatility demand) and 2012
  (VVIX); the one-interval averages turn live in 2018, 2021, 2021,
  2022, 2022 and 2024, respectively.
\item \textbf{No observation.} After the late-start rule, $z^{(k)}_{t,i} = 0$ on every row whose $k$-interval average
  holds no observed interval ($\bar a^{(k)}_{t,i} = 0$); the scaler's statistics are computed before either rule and
  are not changed by them.
\item \textbf{Why the linear models standardize again.} The step equalizes each column's interquartile range, not its
  variance: the ratio of a column's standard deviation to its interquartile range varies with its tails, its skewness
  and its share of zeros, and each row is scaled with its own trailing window, so the columns of an estimation window
  are not standardized on that window. The step serves the data: it limits the influence of outliers and keeps each
  series comparable over time. The penalized linear models therefore also standardize every column within their own
  estimation window (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_linear}), so that the penalty treats every column alike.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Selection splits}
\label{app:rh_methods_splits}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved from 05_methods.tex ("Hyperparameter-selection splits"); the displays now use
% the lag on the estimation sample, (t,i) \ominus j (audit design-3: the grid lag (t, i-j) of Section 3 steps through
% every grid interval, overnight included, while the final pre-sample fold counts rows of the 13-bar design: fit
% [8202, 47202), gap 325, validation [47527, 50777), results/window_sweep_2014start_2026-10-22/w3000/run_info.json).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Pre-sample split.} In line with \citet{gu2020empirical}, a split runs forward in time: an estimation
  subsample, an embargo gap of $n_{\mathrm{gap}}$ observations and a validation subsample of $n_{\mathrm{val}}$
  observations. For a split whose validation subsample ends just before $(t,i)$, with $(t,i) \ominus j$ the $j$th
  observation of the estimation sample before $(t,i)$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}),
  \begin{gather*}
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{est}}_{t,i} = \{(t,i) \ominus j : j = n_{\mathrm{val}} + n_{\mathrm{gap}} + 1, \dots,
      n_{\mathrm{val}} + n_{\mathrm{gap}} + W\}, \\
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t,i} = \{(t,i) \ominus j : j = n_{\mathrm{val}} + 1, \dots,
      n_{\mathrm{val}} + n_{\mathrm{gap}}\}, \qquad
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{val}}_{t,i} = \{(t,i) \ominus j : j = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{val}}\}.
  \end{gather*}
  The estimation subsample is a full window of $W$ observations, so that each candidate is fitted on as many
  observations as a forecast. The pooled linear models choose their penalties once on such a split, the last pre-sample fold (validation year 2013),
  with $n_{\mathrm{gap}} = 325$ bars (25 trading days) and
  $n_{\mathrm{val}} = 3{,}250$ bars (250 trading days); the first scored forecast follows
  it. Each candidate penalty $\lambda$ is fitted on $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{est}}_{t,i}$ and scored by the mean squared
  error of $\tilde y$ over $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{val}}_{t,i}$; the minimizer is held fixed at every forecast
  (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_methods_tuning}; grids and picks in Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_methods_hyper}). The
  closing-interval linear models choose theirs on pre-sample folds of the same form
  (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing}).
\item \textbf{Split of the rolling window.} A model that re-selects its hyperparameters during the evaluation, as
  some closing-interval models do, partitions its own window $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, so that the three subsamples together
  hold $W$ observations:
  \[
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{est}}_{t,i} = \{(t,i) \ominus j : j = n_{\mathrm{val}} + n_{\mathrm{gap}} + 1, \dots, W\},
  \]
  with $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t,i}$ and $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{val}}_{t,i}$ as above. No forecast of the main text
  re-selects.
\item \textbf{Use of the subsamples.} The target interval $(t,i)$ never enters any of these sets. During a selection,
  a candidate is estimated on $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{est}}_{t,i}$ and evaluated on $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{val}}_{t,i}$;
  every forecast is estimated on the full window $\mathcal W_{t,i}$.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Penalized linear regressions}
\label{app:rh_methods_linear}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved from 05_methods.tex ("Penalized linear regressions" and its sub-bullets),
% lightly edited. Changed: the typed "100 times" (audit design-15) -> the weight \rhfiBackbonePf itself; the typed
% "alpha = 0.5" -> "the midpoint of [0, 1]"; the ridge solver (audit fidelity-9: under STANDARDIZE_PENALTY the ridge
% re-solves the standardized system every bar with X'X and X'y kept by rank-one updates, which "replaces the
% Sherman-Morrison update", results/standardize_penalty_2026-10-22/RULE_std.txt items 3 and addendum 3); the timing of
% the screens (fidelity-9 and its verifier: ridge applies the constant, evidence and availability screens every bar,
% the exact-duplicate screen at its cold solves; the lasso and elastic net apply every screen at a cold solve and add
% failing columns between them, the lasso also constant and duplicate ones; the trees have no screen). The
% closing-interval clause of the old screen bullet (hour and overnight indicators) is closing-interval material, dropped
% (audit design-13 (g)). Was: see the parked Methods text at the end of 05_methods.tex.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Objectives.} Following the penalized HAR formulation of \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}, the
  estimates at origin $(t,i)$ are
  \begin{align*}
    \hat{\bm\beta}^{\mathrm{ridge}}_{t,i} &= \argmin_{\beta_0, \bm\beta} \sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}}
      (\tilde y_{t',i'} - \beta_0 - \bm x_{t',i'}^\top \bm\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \omega_j\, \beta_j^2, \\
    \hat{\bm\beta}^{\mathrm{enet}}_{t,i} &= \argmin_{\beta_0, \bm\beta} \sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}}
      (\tilde y_{t',i'} - \beta_0 - \bm x_{t',i'}^\top \bm\beta)^2
      + \lambda\alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} \omega_j |\beta_j|
      + \frac{\lambda(1-\alpha)}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{p} \omega_j\, \beta_j^2 ,
  \end{align*}
  where $\lambda > 0$ sets the overall strength of the penalty, $\alpha \in [0,1]$ is the elastic-net mixing
  parameter and $\omega_j \ge 0$ is predictor $j$'s penalty weight; the intercept $\beta_0$ is not penalized. The lasso
  is $\alpha = 1$, and our elastic net fixes $\alpha$ at the midpoint of $[0,1]$. For ridge, $\lambda$ is the grid
  value reported in Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_hyper}. For the lasso and the elastic net the table reports the
  \texttt{scikit-learn} penalty parameter, and $\lambda$ above is $2n$ times the tabulated value, with $n$ the number
  of observations in the window.
\item \textbf{Penalty weights.} On the full predictor set the HAR-set columns are penalized more lightly than the
  additional predictors:
  \[
    \omega_j =
    \begin{cases}
      \underline\omega = 0.01& j \in \text{HAR set}, \\
      1 & j \text{ an additional predictor}.
    \end{cases}
  \]
  A penalized regression on the HAR set alone uses $\omega_j = 1$ for every predictor.
\item \textbf{Standardization within the estimation window.} The penalties apply to standardized coefficients
  \citep{Tibshirani1996, FriedmanHastieTibshirani2010}. Each predictor column is centred and scaled by its mean $m_j$
  and standard deviation $s_j$ over $\mathcal W_{t,i}$; the objectives above are solved for the coefficients
  $\gamma_j$ of the standardized columns $(x_j - m_j)/s_j$, with the weights $\omega_j$, and transformed back,
  $\beta_j = \gamma_j / s_j$, the intercept absorbing the centring. Without this step the penalty on a column's
  contribution to the forecast would scale with $1/s_j^2$ for ridge and $1/s_j$ for the lasso, so that columns with
  little spread, such as long-horizon averages, would be penalized far more heavily for no economic reason. The robust
  standardization of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors} does not achieve this: it equalizes interquartile ranges rather
  than variances, and its scale factors are not those of the estimation window. For ridge, $m_j$ and $s_j$ are those
  of the current window at every bar; for the lasso and the elastic net they are recomputed at every cold solve of the
  homotopy below and held fixed in between. Solving in standardized coordinates gives the same estimates as penalizing
  the raw columns with weights $\omega_j s_j$ ($\ell_1$) and $\omega_j s_j^2$ ($\ell_2$), and keeps the systems the
  solvers work on well conditioned.
\item \textbf{Screens.} Only a screened subset $\mathcal J_{t,i}$ of the predictors enters a fit:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item columns that are constant within $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, or exact duplicates of an earlier retained column, are
    left out;
  \item a column of an exogenous series enters only if the series' own one-interval column differs from its modal
    value on at least 250 intervals of $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, the evidence requirement of the activity
    indicator (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_transform}); a $k$-interval average repeats each observation $k$ times, so its own
    count would overstate the evidence;
  \item an availability average over $k > 1$ intervals is a proportion, with sampling resolution $\sqrt{p(1-p)/k}$
    at its window mean $p$. It is left out when its standard deviation over $\mathcal W_{t,i}$ does not exceed that
    resolution, or when the standard deviation of its difference from an earlier retained availability average of the
    same horizon does not exceed $\sqrt 2$ times the resolution at the pair's mean: its movement is then no larger than
    independent missing observations would produce. These are mostly the long-horizon availability averages of
    regular-hours series, which record the trading calendar rather than the series.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Timing of the screens.} The HAR set is exempt from the second and third screens. Ridge applies the first screen's constant columns and the
  other two screens at every bar, and the exact duplicates at each of its cold solves (below). The lasso and the
  elastic net apply every screen at each cold solve; between cold solves, a retained column that fails the evidence or
  the availability screen, or, for the lasso, becomes constant or an exact duplicate, is left out at once and the
  solver restarts cold. The tree ensembles use every column.
\item \textbf{Solvers.} With $\bm X_{t,i}$ stacking the rows $(1, \bm x_{t',i'}^\top)$, $(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}$,
  on the retained columns, ridge solves at every bar the normal equations of the current window in standardized
  coordinates, with the cross-products $\bm X_{t,i}^\top \bm X_{t,i}$ and $\bm X_{t,i}^\top \tilde{\bm y}$ updated by
  rank one as observations enter and leave $\mathcal W_{t,i}$ and recomputed from the current window at fixed
  intervals, its cold solves. The lasso and the elastic net update the active set and
  the coefficients by exact online homotopy \citep{Garrigues2008}, adding the entering observation and dropping the
  leaving one at each step. The homotopy restarts from a cold solve on the current window at fixed intervals; between
  restarts, after each update we check the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker conditions of the current window's problem, and where
  they fail the solution is replaced by a cold solve on the current window, from which the homotopy continues. The OLS
  benchmark is the minimum-norm least-squares solution on the window (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_models}).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Tree ensembles}
\label{app:rh_methods_trees}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved from 05_methods.tex ("Tree ensembles" and its sub-bullets), lightly edited;
% the forest engine added (audit correctness-9: results/pooled_rf_skx_2014start_w3000/RULE_rf_skx.txt, ENGINE and
% CONFIG; experiments/pooled_trees_rerun_13.py:248-256).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Gradient boosting} \citep{Friedman2001}, implemented with LightGBM \citep{Ke2017} and XGBoost
  \citep{Chen2016}, minimizes the squared-error loss $\tfrac12 (\tilde y - F)^2$ over boosting rounds $b = 1, \dots, B$
  with learning rate $\eta$. Each regression tree $f_b$ partitions the predictor space into $J$ leaves with leaf weights
  $\bm w$, where leaf $j$ contains the observation subset $\mathcal R_j$ of size $n_j = |\mathcal R_j|$. When the
  $\ell_1$ leaf penalty $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} = 0$, the additive update and the optimal leaf weight are
  \begin{align*}
    F_b &= F_{b-1} + \eta f_b, \\
    w_j^\ast &= -\frac{\sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal R_j}\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)}
      {n_j + \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}} .
  \end{align*}
  At round $b$, tree $f_b$ is grown to minimize the regularized second-order objective
  \[
    \sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}} \Bigl[\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)
      f_b(\bm x_{t',i'}) + \tfrac12 f_b(\bm x_{t',i'})^2\Bigr]
    + \gamma^{\mathrm{tree}} J + \lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_1
    + \tfrac12 \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_2^2 ,
  \]
  where $\gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}$ penalizes each leaf and $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}}, \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}$
  shrink the leaf weights. Every leaf must contain at least $n_{\min}$ observations ($n_j \ge n_{\min}$), the minimum
  leaf size in LightGBM and, under the unit Hessian of the squared-error loss, the minimum child weight in XGBoost.
\item \textbf{Random forest} \citep{Breiman2001}: the equally weighted average of $B$ regression trees $f_b$, each
  grown on a bootstrap sample of the estimation window with a random subset of the predictors tried at each split,
  \[
    \hat y_{t,i} = \frac1B \sum_{b=1}^{B} f_b(\bm x_{t,i}).
  \]
  The forest is fitted with Intel's oneDAL engine (Intel Extension for Scikit-learn), whose splits search histograms of
  256 bins of each predictor rather than every threshold, % -> \rhtuRfBins
  with the configuration selected for the stock \texttt{scikit-learn} forest (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_tuning}).
\item \textbf{Implementation.} Each method keeps one configuration (Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_hyper}), refitted at every bar
  on $\mathcal W_{t,i}$ with a fixed random seed. The trees are invariant to monotone transformations of a column, so
  they are not standardized again within the window, and they use every column, with no screen.
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Scope of the tuning.} The tuning of the main text only has to put off-the-shelf estimators in the
  forecasting regime; it is not a search for the best configuration, and every comparison of the main text holds the
  hyperparameters fixed. This subsection discloses how the frozen values were obtained and reports four checks of
  them on the final design (Table~\ref{tab:rh_tuning}).
\item \textbf{Linear penalties: the selection fold.} The penalties are selected once, on the split of
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_splits}: the last pre-sample fold (validation year 2013). Under the late-start rule of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}, the value
  averages of a series that starts late are zero until a full window of its data exists. In the selection fold this
  holds for all 10 late-starting series, % -> \rhtuNLateSeries
  VIX, VIX3M, VVIX, the StockTwits series and the volatility-demand series; the first of their averages to
  go live, the one-interval VIX average, does so in 2018 (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}). The full-set penalties are therefore selected on a design without the implied-volatility series or any alternative
  data, and then govern those columns once they go live. The same holds for the trees' pre-sample check below.
\item \textbf{Tree configurations: transferred from an earlier design.} The configuration of each tree method is the
  best trial of an Optuna search \citep{Akiba2019} (for the random forest, trial 255 of
  400) on the 1998--2002 pre-sample of an earlier design of this panel: % -> \rhtuTreeSearchSpan
  all 48 intervals of the day, overnight included, a HAR ladder of base 2, % -> \rhtuTreeHarBase
  1{,}144 columns without the FOMC series, % -> \rhtuTreeNCols
  the data before the corrections of Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}, a masked robust scaler and a window of
  24{,}000 intervals. The configurations are used unchanged on the final design (13 regular-hours
  bars, 564 columns, $W = 39{,}000$), the minimum leaf size $n_{\min}$ included, which is not
  rescaled to the longer window.
\item \textbf{The forest engine.} The forest's configuration was selected with the stock \texttt{scikit-learn} forest,
  which tries every threshold; the forest of the main text is fitted with Intel's oneDAL engine, which splits on
  histograms (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_methods_trees}) and is several times faster. On the selection fold its validation
  MSE is within 0.27 percent of the stock forest's at the same window, % -> \rhtuRfMseDiffPct
  and its validation forecasts are nearly perfectly correlated with the stock forest's (Table~\ref{tab:rh_tuning}).
\item \textbf{Check 1: neighbouring penalties.} Each full-set penalized regression is rerun over the whole evaluation
  with its penalty one grid step below and one above the frozen value, the HAR-set forecasts unchanged. At every
  neighbouring penalty the full set's every-bar QLIKE remains significantly below the HAR set's
  (Table~\ref{tab:rh_tuning}).
\item \textbf{Check 2: annual re-tuning.} For each year from 2014 to 2024, % -> \rhtuAnnFirstYear, \rhtuAnnLastYear
  each penalty is re-selected by the same procedure on a split whose validation subsample is the
  250 trading days before the year, using only data before the year, and is applied to the bars of
  that year. From its first live year on, a late-starting series is live in the validation subsample, so the
  re-selected penalties see the implied-volatility series and the alternative data. In every class the full set's
  every-bar gain over the HAR set stays significant (Table~\ref{tab:rh_tuning}).
\item \textbf{Check 3: a pre-sample neighbourhood of each tree configuration.} On the validation year of the
  selection fold only, with a refit at the first bar of every day on the $W$ observations before it, each tree method
  is fitted at its transferred configuration, at 4 further seeds of it, % -> \rhtuTreeNSeeds
  and at variants that move one hyperparameter at a time: the number of leaves (LightGBM) or the depth, the learning
  rate halved and doubled (boosting), half and twice the trees, the minimum leaf size rescaled to the window (for the
  forest also halved), and for the forest the share of predictors tried at a split. For the forest the transferred
  configuration is within noise of the best variant (Diebold--Mariano test of the best variant against it, on the
  daily validation MSE, $p \ge 0.05$). For LightGBM the best variant, a doubled learning rate, and for XGBoost the best
  variant, twice the boosting rounds, have a significantly lower validation MSE than the transferred configuration,
  but not a significantly lower validation QLIKE. This check uses no data after the pre-sample and changes no
  configuration.
\end{itemize}

% 2026-10-28 (author: conventional titles). Was: \subsection{Calibration and the squared-error loss}
\subsection{Calibration and squared-error loss}
\label{app:rh_results_calib}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): from drafts/2026-10-25_close_accuracy.tex (items "QLIKE and squared-error loss
% disagree" and "The linear models at the closing half hour after 2020: a level shift"); the draft's first item, the
% closing half hour on both spans (Table tab:rh_close_accuracy), goes to the closing-interval appendix (APPENDIX agent).
% The draft's T_oos (2020-2024) is written as \rhcaYearsOos or T_close here: T_oos is Table 1's span (audit results-1).
% Every class name, direction and "all"/"every"/"none" is asserted in make_rehaul_close_accuracy.py (claims()).
% Note E33 (05_methods.tex) can be closed: MAE and the calibration diagnostics are computed for the forecasts of
% Table 1 (Table tab:rh_calibration).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{QLIKE and squared-error loss disagree.} On every bar the full predictor set lowers the average QLIKE
  loss in all 6 classes (Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}) but raises the MSE in all of them (by
  100.6 to 117.7\% for the penalized linear models and
  10.9 to 20.0\% for the tree ensembles) and lowers $R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}}$;
  at 16:00 the MSE rises in 6 of the classes, none significantly.
\item \textbf{Diagnostics} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_calibration}, Figure~\ref{fig:rh_calibration}). Mincer--Zarnowitz
  regressions of the realized variance on the forecast, in levels and in logs \citep{MincerZarnowitz1969}, with
  Newey--West standard errors, and two exact decompositions of the losses:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item the MSE into a bias, a slope and a disturbance term,
    \[
      \mathrm{MSE} = \bigl(\overline{\RV} - \overline{\hat\sigma^2}\bigr)^2 + (1 - b)^2\,\Var\bigl(\hat\sigma^2\bigr)
        + \bigl(1 - R^2_{\mathrm{MZ}}\bigr)\Var(\RV),
    \]
    with $b$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{MZ}}$ the slope and $R^2$ of the levels regression;
  \item the average QLIKE loss into a level and a dispersion term,
    \[
      \overline{\QLIKE} = \bigl(\bar r - 1 - \ln\bar r\bigr) + \bigl(\ln\bar r - \overline{\ln r}\bigr),
      \qquad r_t = \RV_t/\hat\sigma^2_t ,
    \]
    where the first term vanishes when $\bar r = 1$ and is what a constant rescaling of the forecast can remove, and
    the second is unchanged by such a rescaling.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Not a level bias.} The bias term is at most 0.1\% of the MSE of any pooled forecast
  on every bar of 2020--2024, and the ratio of mean realized to mean forecast variance lies between
  0.96 and 1.05.
\item \textbf{Not before 2020.} On 2014--2019 the full predictor set has the lower MSE on every bar in all
  6 classes (\ensuremath{-}10.8 to \ensuremath{-}8.9\% for the linear models) and at 16:00,
  and the lower MAE in all of them; the levels slope of the linear models on the full set is
  0.99--1.00, not significantly different from one.
\item \textbf{Scale on 2020--2024.} On every bar of 2020--2024 the full-set forecasts move too much in levels:
  the slope is 0.56--0.58 for the penalized linear models and 0.74--0.78 for the tree
  ensembles, each significantly below one, against 0.99 and 0.92--0.94 on the HAR
  benchmark set. The slope term is 35.9--40.8\% of the linear models' full-set MSE and
  12.7--17.7\% of the trees', against at most 1.4\% on the HAR benchmark
  set, and over-predictions carry 63.1--67.0\% of the linear models' full-set squared error
  (21.5--26.7\% on the HAR benchmark set). By forecast decile (Figure~\ref{fig:rh_calibration}), the
  full-set elastic net under-predicts in its bottom decile and over-predicts in its top decile, which carries
  97\% of its squared error.
\item \textbf{A handful of days in the COVID-19 crash.} The 5 days with the largest excess squared error of
  the full set, all between 12 March 2020 and 2 April 2020, carry 92--94\% of the full
  set's excess squared error on every bar of 2020--2024 for the penalized linear models and
  92--101\% for the tree ensembles. The largest full-set forecast of the elastic net, for the bar
  ending at 10:00 ET on 23 March 2020, is $2064\times 10^{-6}$,
  4.1 times the realized variance of that bar ($501\times 10^{-6}$; HAR
  benchmark set $627\times 10^{-6}$). Without the days from 24 February 2020 to
  30 April 2020, the full predictor set has the lower every-bar MSE on 2020--2024 in all 6 classes
  (\ensuremath{-}7.3 to \ensuremath{-}5.2\% for the linear models,
  \ensuremath{-}9.0 to \ensuremath{-}6.0\% for the trees) and the lower MAE, each
  statistically significant at the 5\% level.
\item \textbf{Calibrated in logs.} QLIKE behaves like a loss on $\ln r_t$: it weights an error by its size relative to
  the forecast and grows only logarithmically in over-prediction, so the bars of the crash, which dominate the squared
  error, weigh little in it. In logs the full-set forecasts are well scaled (slope 0.98--0.99 for the
  linear models on every bar of 2020--2024) and more informative than the HAR benchmark set of the same class
  ($R^2$ of 0.81 for the linear models and 0.82 for the trees,
  against 0.79--0.80).
\item \textbf{The linear models at the closing half hour after 2020: a level shift.} At 16:00 on
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}}$ (2020--2024), the full-set forecasts of the penalized linear models lie below the
  HAR-set forecast (a median log ratio of \ensuremath{-}6.9 to \ensuremath{-}5.6\%, against
  \ensuremath{-}3.1 to \ensuremath{-}2.1\% on 2014--2019), they fall short of the
  realized variance more often (52.1--52.9\% of days, against 47.7\%), and
  $\bar r$ rises from 1.092 to 1.165--1.183. QLIKE penalizes under-prediction more than
  over-prediction, and the level term of the decomposition above accounts for 64--76\% of their
  increase in QLIKE (from 0.0040 to 0.0123--0.0150), while the dispersion term rises less
  (from 0.1097 to 0.1122--0.1159). Most of the linear models' added closing-half-hour loss
  on $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}}$ is thus one that a constant rescaling of their forecasts would remove. The tree
  ensembles' full-set forecasts of the closing half hour are also lower and their level term also rises (from
  0.0005--0.0019 to 0.0039--0.0059), but their dispersion term falls by more (from
  0.1095--0.1112 to 0.1044--0.1064), so their QLIKE falls.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Ablation design}
\label{app:rh_results_ablation}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): from drafts/2026-10-25_ablations.tex ("Design", "Augmented HAR benchmarks",
% "Late-starting series"); typed counts replaced by \rhdmNSeriesPooled and \rhfiNBuckets, the 3,000-day rule by
% \rhorWindowDays, the "[check]" placeholder on the volatility-demand feed resolved (\rhabLiveVdSpxOcLast), and the
% clause on the HAR-block penalty weight dropped (no macro; Section 5 and Appendix app:rh_hyper state the penalties).
% The draft's result paragraphs are condensed in Section 6 (sec:rh_results_ablation).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Groups and arms.} The 46 exogenous series form the 8 groups of
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_dictionary}. For each group $g$ we fit two models in every class:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item the full set without $g$ (all of $g$'s trailing averages $u^{(k)}$ and availability shares $\bar a^{(k)}$
    removed), which measures what $g$ contributes given everything else;
  \item the HAR benchmark set with $g$ added, which measures what $g$ contributes on its own.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Hyperparameters and coverage.} Hyperparameters stay those of the full set: the linear penalties chosen on
  the last pre-sample fold (validation year 2013) for the full predictor set, and the single frozen configuration of each tree method. The random
  forest, the most expensive class, is fitted for the 8 additions and for the removal of the realized
  moments. Panel~D of Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation} restates the full-set row of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}.
\item \textbf{Augmented HAR benchmarks.} The first group, the futures' own realized moments, is the natural augmented
  HAR: it adds the return, absolute variation, skewness, quarticity, positive semivariance, bipower variation and
  autocovariance of the same one-minute E-mini returns that define the target. We also fit the three classical
  extensions of the HAR model by OLS, each built from the same one-minute data and passed through the same diurnal
  adjustment, variance-stabilizing transform and trailing averages as every other series; a fourth model adds all
  three.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The semivariance HAR of \citet{PattonSheppard2015} adds the positive and negative realized semivariances
    $\mathrm{RS}^{\pm}$ of the last half hour; the negative semivariance is $\mathrm{RS}^{-} = \RV - \mathrm{RS}^{+}$,
    exact on every bar of the data.
  \item The HARQ model of \citet{BollerslevPattonQuaedvlieg2016} adds the interaction of the last half hour's realized
    variance with the square root of its realized quarticity $\mathrm{RQ} = (N/3)\sum_k r^4_{t,i,k}$ (in the
    volatility units of the design, $\sqrt{\RV\,\mathrm{RQ}^{1/2}}$).
  \item The leverage HAR of \citet{CorsiReno2012} adds the negative part of the half-hour return, $\min(r_{t,i}, 0)$,
    at every HAR horizon.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Late-starting series.} The implied-volatility, sentiment and volatility-demand series start after the
  data, and a series enters as zero until the rolling window holds 3{,}000 trading days of its history
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}). In the evaluation span this rule binds for most of the sample:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item the VIX enters on 19~April 2018 (its longest average on 18~July 2018), VIX3M on
    6~July 2021, and VVIX on 12~February 2024;
  \item StockTwits attention on 11~February 2021 and the other StockTwits series on 19~April 2022;
  \item the volatility-demand series on 16~November 2022 (their feed stops on 31~August 2023);
  \item before those dates the groups contribute only their availability shares, so the rows of these groups in
    Panels~A and~B measure the series over the later part of the span only; Panel~E scores them on the bars on which
    their value averages are live.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{FOMC statement days and ordinary days}
\label{app:rh_channels}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Day types.} Sections~\ref{sec:rh_results_channels} and~\ref{sec:rh_fi} score the forecasts of
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} separately on two kinds of day. Statement days are the 81 days of
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ with a scheduled FOMC statement, from the calendar of Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}
  (unscheduled meetings excluded), with 1{,}053 of the 33{,}527 scored bars; ordinary days are the other
  2{,}498. The Federal Reserve publishes its meeting calendar in advance, so the type of a day is known before
  every forecast of it. No other split is used for inference; the splits by bar of the day are descriptive. Loss,
  benchmarks and tests are those of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}, with the Diebold--Mariano test on the daily average loss
  over the days of the type (Newey--West lag 8 on both types).
\item \textbf{Order of the analyses.} The day split was introduced after the every-bar results of
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} and of the predictor-group ablations had been seen.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Before the split was formalized, an exploratory rescoring by day type of the ablation forecasts on the design
    before the FOMC fixes of Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc} had shown the pattern reported in
    Sections~\ref{sec:rh_results_channels} and~\ref{sec:rh_fi}: a large share of the every-bar gain on the afternoons
    of the statement days; a gain on ordinary days in which the futures' realized moments are the largest single
    group and the only one whose removal costs much; and the lasso ahead of the ridge and the elastic net on statement
    days but behind them on ordinary days.
  \item A written rule then fixed the day types, the tests, the readings below and their thresholds, and the factor
    test, before any forecast on the fixed design was scored by day type. Every number the paper reports by day type
    comes from the fixed design under that rule; the exploratory numbers are not reported. Every model class and every
    predictor group is reported; none was dropped after scoring.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Readings} (Tables~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl} and~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl_full}). On each day type,
  with the joint gain that of the full set over the HAR benchmark on that day type, the gain is
  \begin{itemize}
  \item concentrated if one group, added alone to the HAR benchmark set, recovers at least three-quarters of the joint
    gain and removing it from the full set raises the loss significantly;
  \item spread across correlated proxies (redundant) if the groups' separate gains sum to more than one and a half
    times the joint gain and removing at most one group raises the loss significantly;
  \item mixed otherwise.
  \end{itemize}
  The penalized linear models are read by the majority of the ridge, lasso and elastic net, the trees by LightGBM and
  XGBoost, with the random forest where its arms exist. The rule applies the two definitions in this order. Both can
  hold, when one group carries the gain and the others repeat its information, so Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi} reports
  where each holds. The three corrections of Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_corr} agree for a class when they lie within
  2 percentage points of one another; a disagreement is reported, not resolved.
\item \textbf{The factor test} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_factor}, Figure~\ref{fig:rh_factor}). Fixed by the same rule and
  scored primarily on ordinary days: the OLS on the HAR benchmark set plus the first $k$ principal components
  ($k = 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20$) or partial-least-squares components ($k = 1, 2, 3$) of the 258 value averages
  of the 43 exogenous series outside the FOMC group, standardized in each window, the loadings recomputed
  once a trading day and the regression at every bar, on the window of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item With $k = 0$ it reproduces the OLS row of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} on every bar (largest relative difference
    $4 \times 10^{-14}$). The share $R_k$ of the gain recovered is measured against the lower loss of the full-set ridge
    and elastic net.
  \item Reading: a shared factor if some $k \le 3$ has $R_k \ge 0.75$ and a loss not significantly
    above the full set's; dense beyond a few factors if $R_{10} < 0.5$ and the full set beats the
    ten-component model significantly; intermediate otherwise. On ordinary days it is ``dense beyond a few factors''.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Tables and coverage.} Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl} reports every group's change added alone and
  removed, for every class on both day types, with the joint gain and the readings by model type;
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_abl_full} repeats it in full, with the per-class readings, the add-alone gains summed over
  the groups against the joint gain and the counts of significant removals; Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_sparse}
  the lasso against the ridge and the elastic net and the feature-count ladder by day type;
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_channels_corr} and Figure~\ref{fig:rh_channels} the three corrections and where the gain falls.
  Two gaps are marked in the tables: the random forest is fitted for the additions and for removing the realized
  moments only (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_results_ablation}), and the trees' removals other than that of the FOMC group are
  on the design before the FOMC fixes, against the full set on that design.
\item \textbf{Added after the rule.} Not pre-registered, each requested by the author after the results it follows and
  specified in a dated addendum to the ablation rule, or in a rule of its own, before its forecasts were scored:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item the reference HAR\,+\,RM\,+\,FOMC, the HAR benchmark set with the futures' realized moments and the FOMC
    calendar (Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation}, Panel~D; Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_beyond}), after the results by day
    type;
  \item the tests beyond that reference (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_results_beyond}), after the results against it.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

% 2026-10-27 (coordinator, author request): the follow-up tests beyond HAR + RM + FOMC, cited from Section 6.2
% (sec:rh_results_ablation, "What remains"). Rules: results/ablations_2014start_w3000/RULE.txt addendum G

% "each remaining group ... lowers": \rhab{Lgbm,Xgb}AddRmFomc{Ew,Vw,Liq,Iv,Sent,Vd}{All,Ord}Pct all negative (Panel A);
% "the groups overlap": \rhab{Lgbm,Xgb}BeyondRatioOrd > 1; "for both trees": \rhbyFAgreement = agree. No macro in a
% loaded file for the base's column count (132; \rhbyFLNBase is in the unwired linear factor file) or for the factor
% test's reading thresholds (RULE.txt section 1); the table notes print the count, not the thresholds.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Design.} Requested by the author after the results by day type and against HAR\,+\,RM\,+\,FOMC
  (Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation}, Panel~D), not part of the pre-specified design; the design and reading rule of each
  test were fixed before it was scored (the table notes state the designs and the readings).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Base: HAR\,+\,RM\,+\,FOMC, the HAR benchmark set with the futures' realized moments and the FOMC calendar. The
    remaining groups are the equal- and value-weighted constituent markets, liquidity, implied volatility, sentiment
    and volatility demand.
  \item The FOMC-patched design of Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation}, with the full set's frozen hyperparameters,
    re-estimated at every bar.
  \item Primary span: ordinary days, the trading days without a scheduled FOMC statement.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{By group} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_ablation_beyond}). Each remaining group, added alone to the base, lowers the
  loss of LightGBM and XGBoost (Panel~A). On ordinary days the six one-group gains sum to 2.90
  (LightGBM) and 2.63 (XGBoost) times the full set's gain over the base (row ``Sum of the six
  rows''): the groups overlap.
\item \textbf{How many series} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_beyond_ladder}). Each tree is refitted on the base plus its own top
  $k$ remaining series, ranked on its 2013 pre-sample fit. The top five recover shares of
  0.72 (LightGBM) and 0.91 (XGBoost) of the full set's ordinary-day gain over the
  base, and LightGBM's top series alone 0.75. The reading fixed before scoring is ``concentrated''
  for XGBoost and ``intermediate'' for LightGBM.
\item \textbf{Not a common factor} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_beyond_factor}). The six groups are replaced by a few components
  of their series' value averages, with loadings re-estimated once a trading day on the rolling window. Three
  partial-least-squares components recover 0.32 (LightGBM) and 0.36 (XGBoost)
  of the ordinary-day gain, ten principal components 0.35 and 0.37; the reading
  fixed before scoring is ``dense beyond a few components'' for both trees. Together with the ladder: the remaining gain sits in a
  few specific series, not in a few components common to the six groups, although the component block holds the
  series' value averages only, whereas the ladder's rungs also carry their availability shares.
\item \textbf{The linear models.} They have no gain beyond the base to decompose: against HAR\,+\,RM\,+\,FOMC the full
  set changes the ordinary-day loss of the ridge, lasso and elastic net by 0.2,
  0.0 and $-$0.6\%, none significantly
  ($p \geq{}$0.194).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Construction}
\label{app:rh_fi_compute}
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-28 (SHAP on the patched design): "on the design with the FOMC fixes" added; the trees' SHAP values and the
% linear coefficients at W = 3,000 are now those of the FOMC-patched walks (D13). Was: "... the HAR components and the
% calendar dummies), explained at monthly origins."
\item \textbf{Models.} The pooled intraday models of the final design (rolling window of 3{,}000 trading
  days, 39{,}000 bars; full predictor set of 564 predictors in 48 groups: each of the
  46 exogenous series with its 12 predictors, the HAR components and the calendar dummies),
  on the design with the FOMC fixes of Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}, explained at monthly origins.
\item \textbf{Origins.} $k = 1, \dots, K$, $K = 126$: one every 21 trading days, at the
  10:00 bar, from 2~January~2014 to 5~April~2024. Origin $k$'s model forecasts its block
  $\mathcal O_k$, the 21 trading days up to the next origin (the last block: 18 days);
  the blocks partition all $|\mathcal O| = 33{,}970$ bars from 2~January~2014 to 30~April~2024.
\item \textbf{Sample.} The 33{,}970 bars include the bars of the shortened futures sessions held on NYSE
  holidays, which the models are estimated on but Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} does not score (it scores 33{,}527 bars
  on the same dates); every share in Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi} and here is computed over all explained bars.
\item \textbf{Tuning.} The linear penalties were chosen on the last pre-sample fold, which ends on 31~December~2013, and
  the tree configurations on an earlier development sample (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_hyper}), so no explained bar lies in
  a tuning sample.
\item \textbf{Tree ensembles} (LightGBM, XGBoost, random forest). At each origin the model is refit on the
  39{,}000 bars before it, as its every-bar walk refits at that bar, and held for the block.
  Path-dependent TreeSHAP values \citep{lundberg2020local} of every bar $(t,i) \in \mathcal O_k$, on the scale of the
  forecast, add up to it, and a group's value sums its predictors' values:
  \[
    \hat y_{t,i} = \phi_{k,0} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{t,i,j}, \qquad
    \phi_{t,i,A} = \sum_{j \in A} \phi_{t,i,j}, \qquad
    s_A = \frac{I_A}{\sum_{B} I_B}, \quad I_A = \frac{1}{|\mathcal O|} \sum_{(t,i) \in \mathcal O} |\phi_{t,i,A}| ,
  \]
  with $\phi_{k,0}$ the model's expected forecast over its own training sample (the trees' node covers), so no
  background sample is chosen.
\item \textbf{Linear models} (ridge, lasso, elastic net). The walk's own coefficients at each origin on the
  window-standardized predictors, which the penalty acts on, $\gamma_{k,j} = \hat\beta_{k,j}\,\mathrm{sd}_{k,j}$, and
  a group's share $S_A = \sum_k \sum_{j \in A} |\gamma_{k,j}| / \sum_k \sum_{j} |\gamma_{k,j}|$; penalties as frozen
  for this window (ridge \ensuremath{10^{3}}, lasso \ensuremath{10^{-4}}, elastic net \ensuremath{10^{-3}}), with the penalty factor
  0.01 on the HAR components and the calendar dummies.
\item \textbf{Classes}, fixed before any SHAP value was computed. Standard (12 groups): the HAR components,
  the calendar dummies, the futures' seven realized moments, the VIX, and the futures' volume and trade count.
  Non-standard: the other 36 series (constituent liquidity, the equal- and value-weighted market
  moments, StockTwits sentiment, volatility demand, the FOMC calendar, VVIX and VIX3M).
% 2026-10-28 (v2 of Sections 6-7, author approved preliminarily): added -- the comparison convention of the main-text
% bullet "Questions and measures" (08_feature_importance.tex), the one part of it this subsection did not already state
% (origins and blocks, the holiday sessions, the tuning samples, s_A, S_A and the classes are in the items above).
\item \textbf{Comparisons.} Each model is described by its own shares; models of different types are compared on the
  exogenous total, the exogenous series' shares of their sum. A share measures how much a series moves the forecast,
  not how much it improves its accuracy.
\item \textbf{Intervals.} 95\% moving-block bootstrap over the origins (blocks of 12
  origins, about a year; 2{,}000 resamples), paired across models. They measure the variation over the span's
  origins, not the sampling error of one fit.
\item \textbf{Correlated predictors.} Between correlated predictors (the equal- and value-weighted versions of a
  series, a series' value and availability averages) the credit follows the trees' split choices; summing over a
  group removes the split within the group, not the split between groups.
\item \textbf{Checks.} SHAP explains each origin's refit held for its block, whereas the walks refit at every bar; the
  two coincide at the origin bars. There the refits equal the walks' forecasts bit for bit at 126,
  126 and 126 of the 126 origins (LightGBM, XGBoost, random forest). The
  linear coefficients are the walks' own (their replayed forecasts match to \ensuremath{4.4\times 10^{-16}}). XGBoost computes SHAP
  values in single precision: they add up to the forecast within \ensuremath{3.7\times 10^{-6}} (tolerance \ensuremath{10^{-5}});
  LightGBM's and the forest's within \ensuremath{5.1\times 10^{-14}}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Question.} Does the gain from the exogenous series grow with the number of series a model sees and
  with the length of its training window, and does the number of series worth keeping grow with the window? If the
  exogenous signal were dense and weak, more data per coefficient would let more of the weak series pay for
  themselves, so the best number of series would rise with the window.
\item \textbf{Design.}
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-28 (v2 of Sections 6-7, author approved preliminarily): the every-bar ladder left Section 7 for Appendix
  % app:rh_fi_ladder. Was: "The feature-count ladder of Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi} at rolling windows ..."
  \item The feature-count ladder of Appendix~\ref{app:rh_fi_ladder} at rolling windows of $W = 1{,}000$, 2{,}000,
    3{,}000 and 3{,}500 trading days ($T = 13\,W$, from 13{,}000 to 45{,}500 bars), with the rungs
    $k = 0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 46$: each rung keeps the 12 columns of the HAR benchmark set and all
    columns of the top $k$ exogenous series, so it has $P = 12+ 12\,k$ predictors (564
    for the full set).
  \item The series are ranked separately at each window and for each model, by one fit before the evaluation span
    (explained on the bars of 2013: mean absolute SHAP value for the trees, $\sum |\beta|\,\mathrm{sd}$ for
    the linear models), the first-training-window ranking of \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026}.
  \item LightGBM and XGBoost on their frozen configurations at every window (minimum leaf sizes not rescaled with
    $T$); ridge, lasso and elastic net on each window's own frozen penalty (ridge \ensuremath{10^{4}} at $W =
    1{,}000$, \ensuremath{10^{3}} at the other windows; lasso \ensuremath{10^{-3}} and \ensuremath{10^{-4}}; elastic net
    \ensuremath{10^{-2}} and \ensuremath{10^{-3}}).
  % 2026-10-28 (v2 of Sections 6-7, author approved preliminarily): the origins are defined in Appendix
  % app:rh_fi_compute, no longer in Section 7. Was: "... monthly origins of Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi} and held ..."
  \item Each rung is refitted at the 126 monthly origins of Appendix~\ref{app:rh_fi_compute} and held for
    the next 21 trading days. The full rung equals the every-bar walk at every origin
    (20 of 20 window--model gates).
  \item Gain $G(W, k)$: the QLIKE of the same window's $k = 0$ rung minus the rung's, $\times 10^3$, on the
    33{,}527 scored bars of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} and on the 16:00 bar; Diebold--Mariano tests against $k = 0$
    (HLN, Newey--West lag 8). Figures~\ref{fig:rh_cx_features} and~\ref{fig:rh_cx_data}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Feature scaling} (fixed $T$). At the main window the trees' gain rises with the number of series and
  is nearly complete at 10 (LightGBM at $W = 3{,}000$: 8.73 at $k = 5$,
  24.28 at $k = 10$, 25.53 for the full set). The linear models' gain is
  hump-shaped in the number of series (ridge: 9.94, 12.92 and
  6.86).
\item \textbf{Data scaling} (fixed $k$; Figure~\ref{fig:rh_cx_data}). The trees gain most from the first doubling
  of the window. LightGBM at $k = 10$: 6.00 at $W = 1{,}000$, 22.32 at
  2{,}000, 23.83 at 3{,}500; its full set: 15.67, 23.23,
  25.53, 24.50. At the shortest window LightGBM's top ten keep much less of its
  full set's gain than at the longer ones, its top 20 nearly all of it (15.81); XGBoost's top ten
  keep nearly all of it at every window (20.80 against 20.85 at $W =
  1{,}000$). The linear models' gain at $k = 10$ also rises with the window (ridge
  8.89 to 13.52); their full set's does not change monotonically with the
  window (ridge 10.10, 7.64, 6.86,
  12.18).
\item \textbf{Does the best number of series rise with the window?} On every bar it rises for
  XGBoost ($k^\ast = 20$, 20, 46, 46 at the
  four windows). It rises for LightGBM (the full set, $k^\ast = 20$, at every
  window). It rises for the lasso ($5$, 10,
  10, 10) and falls for the elastic net
  ($46$, 10, 10, 10). It
  falls for the ridge ($46$, 20, 10,
  10). At the 16:00 bar it rises with the window for none of the models,
  falls for LightGBM, XGBoost and elastic net and is not monotone for ridge and lasso. The dense-and-weak prediction
  therefore holds on every bar for LightGBM, XGBoost and lasso and at the 16:00 bar for none. For the
  linear models the best number of series is largest at the shortest window, where the tenfold larger penalty favors
  the full set, and smaller after it.
\item \textbf{Caveats.} The minimum leaf sizes of the trees are not rescaled with $T$, so a shorter window also means
  relatively larger leaves. The window length is confounded with regime averaging: a longer window averages over more
  regimes. The linear penalties also change with the window (tenfold at $W = 1{,}000$), and the rankings are
  refitted at each window, so the series behind a given $k$ differ across windows. The refits are monthly and held for
  21 trading days, not the every-bar walks of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}; holding a fit costs the full
  linear set most. The design precedes the FOMC-calendar patch, and the FOMC calendar is among the top-ranked series of
  the linear models. Four windows and no intervals: the grid is descriptive.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Straddle sample and execution}
\label{app:rh_econ_details}
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved here from 07_economics.tex (The straddle strategy, Option-trading sample;
% moved there on 2026-10-22 from 03_data.tex, "Estimation and evaluation samples").
\item \textbf{Option-trading sample.} The strategy of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_strategy} trades on the subsample
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}} \subset \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_setup}) of trading days with
  a same-day SPXW expiration:
  \[
    T_{\mathrm{opt}} = 866\text{ trading days} = 872\text{ SPXW expirations}
      - 6\text{ early-close days}.
  \]
  The 419 subsequent SPXW expiration dates (413 full trading days) are held out from
  the present analysis. The 216 days of $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ without a same-day SPXW expiration
  enter the statistical accuracy evaluation only.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved here from 07_economics.tex (Position item). Code pointers (2026-10-23, E18):
% the scored straddle frame (notebooks/_write_0dte_nb.py -> results/atm_straddle_0dte_1530/daily_blk2.parquet, read by
% experiments/master_table_close.py and writeup/make_rehaul_economics.py) picks K_C and K_P among the 15:30 contracts
% with a positive mid-quote and drops a day without both legs (run log 2026-10-07: 0 of 1,279 days). The outage rule
% (atm_straddle_lib.pick_nearest_otm_guarded: ATM_MAX_STRIKE_GAP = 10 points, ATM_MIN_LIVE = 10 contracts) is applied
% by notebooks/_write_0dte_experimental_nb.py, whose frame is gated day for day against the scored frame; it drops no
% 15:30 chain (rechecked 2026-10-23 on data/spxw_chain.parquet). The two thresholds are code constants with no macro.
\item \textbf{Quote screen.} Every 15:30 chain in $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$ has a call at or above and a put at or
  below $S_t$ with a positive mid-quote. We also screen each chain for a quote outage, that is, fewer than 10
  contracts with a positive mid-quote or a wider strike more than 10 index points from $S_t$ (more than one strike
  missing near the money); no chain in the sample fails this screen, so no day is dropped for want of quotes;
  early-close days are already outside $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved here from 07_economics.tex (Entry prices). Code: atm_straddle_lib.py:1725-1741
% (settle_package); R = exit / entry - 1 (notebooks/_write_0dte_nb.py:452).
\item \textbf{Entry prices and payoff.} From the legs' bid quotes $b$ and ask quotes $a$ at 15:30 ET, the package
  mid-quote $P_t$, bid $P^{b}_t$ and ask $P^{a}_t$ are
  \[
  P_t = \tfrac12\bigl(b^C_t + a^C_t\bigr) + \tfrac12\bigl(b^P_t + a^P_t\bigr),
  \qquad
  P^{b}_t = b^C_t + b^P_t, \qquad P^{a}_t = a^C_t + a^P_t ,
  \]
  and the package pays $X_t = \bigl(S^{\mathrm{close}}_t - K_C\bigr)^+ + \bigl(K_P - S^{\mathrm{close}}_t\bigr)^+$ at
  the official S\&P~500 close, so that $R_t = X_t/P_t - 1$.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved here from 07_economics.tex (Implied variance). Code pointers (2026-10-23,
% E18): notebooks/_write_0dte_nb.py, iv_hourly_15_30: a leg on a node of the vendor's bisection bracket
% (atm_straddle_lib.censor_vendor_iv / IV_VENDOR_NODES) makes the day "capped"; on a capped day
% atm_straddle_lib.bsm_invert_package_vol(S, K_c, K_p, entry mid, hours_remaining=0.5) inverts the Black-76 price with
% r = 0 on the level S by bisection for the total volatility over the half hour. Run log 2026-10-07: 5 capped days
% (2020-03-13, -16, -18, -20, -23), all recovered; they are days 31-35 of the 866 days of T_opt, inside the warmup.
\item \textbf{Implied volatility on failed solves.} The vendor solves each leg's implied volatility by bisection
  and, when the bisection does not converge, reports a node of its bracket instead of a volatility. On the
  5 days of $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$ on which a leg carries such a node, we recover $\mathrm{IV}_t$
  from the package instead: $\mathrm{IV}_t = \sigma$, the volatility over the remaining half hour at which the
  Black--Scholes value of the package, with a zero interest rate and no dividends, equals its mid-quote
  \citep{BlackScholes1973},
  \[
    P_t = S_t\,\Phi(d_C) - K_C\,\Phi(d_C - \sigma) + K_P\,\Phi(\sigma - d_P) - S_t\,\Phi(-d_P),
  \]
  where $d_j = \bigl(\ln(S_t/K_j) + \sigma^2/2\bigr)/\sigma$ for $j \in \{C, P\}$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal
  distribution function. All of these days lie within the first 252 days of $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$,
  which only initialize the sizing rules, so none of them is a scored day.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): moved here from 07_economics.tex (Execution). Code: master_table_close.py:1168-1183
% (q = +-1); rows.py:1020-1025 (sized q); atm_straddle_lib.py:1325-1344.
\item \textbf{Execution at quoted prices.} At mid-quotes the strategy return is $r_t = q_t R_t$. At quoted bid and
  ask prices, buying the straddle pays the ask $P^{a}_t$ and selling receives the bid $P^{b}_t$; because settlement
  is in cash at expiration, the spread is incurred at entry only:
  \[
  r^{\mathrm{ba}}_t =
  \begin{cases}
  |q_t|\,\bigl(X_t/P^{a}_t - 1\bigr), & q_t > 0,\\
  |q_t|\,\bigl(1 - X_t/P^{b}_t\bigr), & q_t < 0.
  \end{cases}
  \]
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Position sizing}
\label{app:rh_econ_sizing}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, coordinator: bullet structure): the lead sentence and the two rules recast as one
% bold-lead item with sub-items, content kept.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Sized rules.} Besides the sign strategy of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_strategy}, two rules scale the
  position by the size of the variance gap.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Robust clip:} $q_t = \clip\bigl((\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2)/\mathrm{MAD}_t, -1, 1\bigr)$, where
    $\mathrm{MAD}_t = \operatorname{median}_{t'<t}\bigl|\hat\sigma^2_{t'} - \mathrm{IV}_{t'}^2\bigr|$ is the expanding
    median absolute variance gap over earlier days $t' < t$ in $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$.
  \item \emph{Percentile rank:} the sign of the gap scaled by the empirical percentile rank of its magnitude across
    the $t - 1$ preceding days $t' < t$ in $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$:
    \[
      q_t = \sign\bigl(\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2\bigr)\cdot\frac{1}{t-1}\sum_{t'<t}
        \mathbf{1}\bigl\{|\hat\sigma^2_{t'} - \mathrm{IV}_{t'}^2| \le |\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2|\bigr\}.
    \]
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Sizing sample.} Every position $q_t$ uses days $t' < t$ only. The first 252 days of
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$ initialize $\mathrm{MAD}_t$, and every rule, the sign strategy included, is evaluated
  on the remaining 614 post-warmup days.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc; audit results-12): the twelve forecasts count the identical HAR-set linear forecast
% three times; flagged in the text. The medians and counts over the distinct forecasts need new macros (NUMBERS).
\item \textbf{Results.} Across the 12 pooled forecasts, in which the identical HAR-set ridge, lasso and
  elastic-net forecast is counted three times (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_main}, note b), the median mid-quote Sharpe
  ratio is 1.26 under the sign strategy, 1.40 under the robust clip and
  1.43 under the percentile rank. In point estimates the robust clip beats the sign strategy
  ($\SR^{\mathrm{clip}} > \SR^{\mathrm{sign}}$) for 8 of the 12 forecasts.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Compounded wealth}
\label{app:rh_econ_compounding}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Definition.} From initial capital $V_0 = 1$, a fixed fraction $f = 3\%$ of current wealth
  is allocated to the straddle premium each day, which gives the terminal portfolio value and the annualized log
  growth rate
  \[
  V = \prod_{t \in \mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}}\bigl(1 + f\,r_t\bigr),
  \qquad
  G = \frac{252}{614}\sum_{t \in \mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}}\log\bigl(1 + f\,r_t\bigr).
  \]
  At quoted bid/ask prices $r^{\mathrm{ba}}_t$ replaces $r_t$. The maximum drawdown is
  $\max_t\bigl(1 - V_t/\max_{t'\le t}V_{t'}\bigr)$, with $V_t$ the portfolio value at the end of day $t$.
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc; audit results-16): the short straddle's values are not in
% Table tab:rh_pooled_shift_compounding, so the citation now covers the pooled forecasts only (a short-straddle row
% is requested from NUMBERS). Was: "... against \rhpcAW{} and \rhpcAWX{} for the unconditional short straddle, with

% the unconditional short straddle; Table~\ref{tab:rh_pooled_shift_compounding});"
\item \textbf{Results.} Across the 12 pooled forecasts (the HAR-set linear forecast counted three times),
  compounding at $f = 3\%$ over the 614 post-warmup days yields a median terminal value $V$ of
  4.3 at mid-quotes (1.1 to 9.4) and 2.7 at quoted bid/ask prices (0.6
  to 5.8), with maximum drawdowns of up to 45\% and 50\%
  (Table~\ref{tab:rh_pooled_shift_compounding}). The unconditional short straddle ends at $V = 1.1$ and
  0.6, with maximum drawdowns of 52\% and 60\%.
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Quoted spreads.} Trading at quoted bid/ask prices rather than mid-quotes lowers every strategy's Sharpe

    $k = 0.91$, inside the quoted spread.

\item \textbf{Elementary score.} To measure forecast accuracy at the decision threshold $\mathrm{IV}_t^2$, we
  evaluate the elementary score of \citet{Ehm2016} normalized by implied variance,
  \[
  \mathrm{ES}_{1,t} = \Bigl|\frac{\RV_t}{\mathrm{IV}_t^2} - 1\Bigr|\;
    \mathbf{1}\bigl\{\min(\hat\sigma^2_t, \RV_t) \le \mathrm{IV}_t^2 < \max(\hat\sigma^2_t, \RV_t)\bigr\},
  \]
  and denote its mean over the post-warmup days $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}$ by $\overline{\mathrm{ES}}_1$.
  $\mathrm{ES}_{1,t}$ is positive if and only if the forecast $\hat\sigma^2_t$ and the realization $\RV_t$ fall on
  opposite sides of the implied variance, that is, precisely when the sign strategy takes the wrong side.
