\subsection{Profit decomposition}
\label{app:rh_econ_decomp}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A short straddle that turns long on a fifth of the days.} The sign strategies of the six pooled
  forecasts on the full predictor set hold a long straddle on 117 to 146 of the 614
  post-warmup days (19--24\%; Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_longshort}). Because
  \[
    r_t = q_t R_t = -R_t + 2R_t\,\mathbf{1}\{q_t = +1\},
  \]
  each strategy's return is that of the unconditional short straddle plus a gain $\Delta_t = 2R_t\mathbf{1}\{q_t = +1\}$
  over it, and that gain is earned on the long days only.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The unconditional short straddle earns 2.4\% of the premium a day at mid-quotes; the gain on the
    long days adds 9.1--11.6\%, which is 79--83\% of the strategies'
    mean daily return of 11.5--14.1\%.
  \item On its long days the straddle returns 19--30\% of the premium on average at
    mid-quotes and 16--26\% bought at the ask. On the remaining days the short straddle earns
    9--11\% at mid-quotes, against 2.4\% on all days: the long days are the
    days on which the short straddle loses.
  \item The long days account for 39--41\% of the summed mid-quote return
    (42--45\% at quoted bid/ask prices). On the HAR benchmark set the same model
    classes go long on 150 to 193 days, on which the straddle returns only
    0--10\% (gain over the short straddle 0.0--5.0\% a day).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{No better call of the premium's sign, but the large moves.} The position has the sign of
  $\RV_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2$ on 70.7--73.0\% of the days, against 71.8\% for the
  unconditional short straddle, so the forecasts are no better than always selling at calling the sign of the
  realized premium. What they add is in the long days: realized variance exceeds implied variance on
  47--53\% of them, against 28.2\% of all days, yet the long straddle has a
  positive return on only 42--45\% of its long days, so its mean return on those days comes
  from a few large moves.
\item \textbf{Forecast quintiles} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_quintiles}). Sorted by the forecast variance gap
  $\log(\hat\sigma^2_t/\mathrm{IV}_t^2)$, the mean ratio of realized to implied variance rises from quintile to
  quintile for 6 of the 6 full-set forecasts, from 0.73 in the lowest to 1.05 in the
  highest (mean of the six), and for 4 of the six HAR-set forecasts (0.74 to
  1.02): the forecasts rank the closing half hours by their realized variance relative to the implied.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The return of a long straddle is negative in each of the four lower quintiles (\ensuremath{-}13 to
    \ensuremath{-}6\% on average) and 26\% in the highest, where 99\% of the days are long days;
    for the HAR-set forecasts it is 7\%. The sign rule's threshold, $\hat\sigma^2_t =
    \mathrm{IV}_t^2$, falls between the fourth quintile (forecast ratio 0.93) and the fifth
    (1.18).
  \item The highest quintile earns 43\% of the summed mid-quote return of the six full-set strategies
    (40--48\% across them), against 23\% for the HAR benchmark
    set. Across the four lower quintiles, where the strategies are short, the return is not monotone in the forecast.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{About ten days carry the gain over the short straddle} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_bestdays}). The six
  full-set forecasts share 9 of their ten best days and 9 of their ten worst; the
  best days are long straddles on large closing moves, the worst are short straddles on large closing moves.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Without each forecast's ten best days, the Sharpe ratio gain over the unconditional short straddle falls from
    1.21--1.56 to \ensuremath{-}0.54 to \ensuremath{-}0.12 (negative for
    6 of the 6); the ten days earn 107--138\% of the summed return
    gain over the short straddle, so the other long days lose on balance.
  \item The largest, 22~November~2021, returned 1{,}032\% of the premium on a closing-half-hour move of
    \ensuremath{-}0.83\% (realized variance 2.79 times the implied), 12--15\% of each
    full-set strategy's summed return.
  \item Against the HAR-set forecast of the same class the gain is less concentrated: without the forecast's ten best
    days the Sharpe ratio gain falls from 0.56--1.56 to 0.30--0.83,
    and those days carry 47--61\% of the summed return gain over it.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{The days are not scheduled announcements.} Of the 11 days in the union of the six
  forecasts' best days, 1 is an FOMC statement day and 8 carry no tag in our event
  calendar, 5 of them after 26~October~2023, when its macro-release dates end (its FOMC dates are
  complete).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On the 21 FOMC statement days the closing straddle returns 25\% on average
    ($t = 1.02$, the days treated as independent); the full-set forecasts are long on 25\% of them
    and earn \ensuremath{-}6\% a day, against 13\% on the other days.
  \item On the 33 month ends the straddle returns 70\% ($t = 2.79$) and the squared closing move
    averages 1.93 times the implied variance; the forecasts are long on 6\% of them, earn
    \ensuremath{-}58\% a day, and \ensuremath{-}24\% of their summed return comes from these days (3 of the
    worst days are month ends).
  \item On the 33 monthly SPX expirations the straddle returns \ensuremath{-}45\% ($t = \ensuremath{-}4.01$); the
    forecasts are long on 9\% of them and earn 15\% of their summed return there, a gain the
    unconditional short straddle shares.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Calibration and the short tilt} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_longshort}, Panel D). In levels the full-set
  forecasts are close to unbiased on the option days (mean forecast over mean realized variance
  0.95--1.01), but in ratios they are low: the mean of $\RV_t/\hat\sigma^2_t$, the scale that
  minimizes mean QLIKE, is 1.09--1.20, the downward bias of squaring a level forecast
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Multiplying each forecast by a causal estimate of that scale, the mean of $\RV_{t'}/\hat\sigma^2_{t'}$ over the
    earlier option days $t' < t$, changes 55 to 120 positions, all from short to long.
    The straddle's mean return on the changed days is \ensuremath{-}24 to \ensuremath{-}8\%, and the Sharpe ratio
    falls to 0.92--1.32 at mid-quotes and 0.57--0.97 at quoted bid/ask prices
    (below the uncorrected ratio for 6 of the six; the correction raises it for 2 of
    the six HAR-set forecasts). This is a diagnostic, not a strategy of the paper.
  \item A reading consistent with this: a straddle pays the absolute move of the index, so a long position is
    profitable when the expected realized volatility, not variance, exceeds the implied volatility. The sign rule
    $\hat\sigma^2_t > \mathrm{IV}_t^2$ is the same as $\hat y_t\, s_{t,c} > \mathrm{IV}_t$, a comparison of the level
    forecast with the implied volatility, which the uncorrected forecast makes.
  \item The forecast target and the straddle's settlement differ: $\RV_t$, the realized variance of the futures from
    one-minute returns, averages 0.87 of the implied variance (median 0.77), while the squared
    log move of the cash index from $S_t$ to $S^{\mathrm{close}}_t$ averages 1.01 of it, and
    1.15 times the mean of $\RV_t$. Measured on the move that settles the straddle, the implied variance
    carries no premium on average in our sample, which agrees with the short straddle's Sharpe ratio of
    0.32, whose mean daily return is not significantly different from zero ($t = 0.67$).
% 2026-10-28 (D19, standard pooled Sharpe): the short straddle's ratio is now positive; its insignificance added.
% Was: "which agrees with the short straddle's Sharpe ratio of \rheShortSh."
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc; audit numbers-1, results-6, correctness-8): the worthless-expiry share of the parked
% "Concentration of economic gains" item (07_economics.tex) placed here, its "settlement pinning" gloss dropped; the
% share is over the \rhrPoolN{} pooled forecasts (the HAR-set linear forecast counted three times).
\item \textbf{Worthless expiries are not pinning.} $R_t = -1$ exactly when the close settles between the two strikes,
  $K_P \le S^{\mathrm{close}}_t \le K_C$; on 611 of the 614 days the two strikes are 5 index
  points apart, against a median one-standard-deviation implied move over the half hour of 9.6 points.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The straddle expires worthless on 137 days (22.3\%). A normal half-hour log move with the
    implied volatility $\mathrm{IV}_t$ predicts 128 such days (20.9\%; the difference is
    0.90 standard deviations), the empirical distribution of the earlier days' moves scaled by
    $\mathrm{IV}_t$ predicts 132, and the close is uniformly placed between adjacent strikes (mean
    distance to the nearest strike 1.23 points, 1.25 under a uniform;
    Kolmogorov--Smirnov $D = 0.026$, 5\% critical value 0.055).
  \item The full-set forecasts are short on 110--115 of these days, on which the short
    straddle keeps its whole premium; these days supply 37\% of the positive returns of the
    median pooled forecast (34--39\% across the 12 pooled
    forecasts).
  \item Monthly SPX expirations are the exception: 10 of the 33 expire worthless against
    6.1 expected ($1.77$ standard deviations), and the squared closing move averages
    0.40 of the implied variance. Outside them the share is 21.9\% against
    21.0\% expected.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Risk exposures} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_riskreg}; $t$-statistics with Newey--West standard errors at
  bandwidth $S = 33$ and fixed-$b$ critical values, Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_methods_tests}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On the short-straddle return the full-set strategies load 0.23--0.28
    ($t$ from 1.22 to 1.42; $R^2$ 0.06--0.08), with
    $\alpha = 11.0$--13.4\% of the premium a day at mid-quotes (fixed-$b$ $p$ from
    0.005 to 0.025) and 8.3--10.7\% at quoted bid/ask prices
    ($p$ from 0.021 to 0.077). The equal-weight mean of the six returns has
    $\alpha = 12.1\%$ ($p = 0.0100$) at mid-quotes and $9.4\%$
    ($p = 0.040$) at quoted bid/ask prices.
  \item They are short volatility, less so than the short straddle: a basis point of absolute S\&P~500 move over the
    closing half hour changes their return by \ensuremath{-}1.87 to \ensuremath{-}1.40\% of the premium ($t$ from
    \ensuremath{-}3.49 to \ensuremath{-}2.31); for their mean return the coefficient, \ensuremath{-}1.68\%, is
    43\% of the short straddle's \ensuremath{-}3.96\%. The sign of the move does not matter
    (coefficients \ensuremath{-}0.01 to 0.14).
  \item The S\&P~500 daily return and the change in the VIX explain none of their return ($R^2$
    0.00), and with all regressors $\alpha$ is 11.4--13.6\% at mid-quotes and
    8.7--10.9\% at quoted bid/ask prices.
  \item Without each forecast's ten best days, $\alpha$ on the short straddle is \ensuremath{-}0.5 to
    2.1\% ($p \ge 0.43$). The standard errors allow for serial correlation,
    not for a return distribution whose mean rests on ten days. The HAR-set strategies have
    $\alpha = 1.1$--7.0\% ($p \ge 0.082$).
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, coordinator: bullet structure): the closing paragraph of the draft recast as a bold-lead
% item with sub-items, content kept.
\item \textbf{Summary: where the profits come from.} The strategy is a short straddle on most days, and the short
  straddle by itself earns nothing detectable in our sample (0.32 at mid-quotes, \ensuremath{-}0.03 at quoted
  bid/ask prices).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The profit comes from the days on which the full-set forecasts switch to a long straddle: these are the
    closing half hours that the forecasts rank highest in realized relative to implied variance, the ranking is
    monotone across the forecast quintiles, and on these days the straddle earns 19--30\%
    of its premium on average (26\% in the top forecast quintile, against 7\% on the HAR
    benchmark set).
  \item The strategy is not a disguised short-volatility position: it has less than half of the short straddle's
    exposure to the size of the closing move, almost none to its return, and none to the market or the VIX.
  \item But the payoff of the ranking is concentrated in about ten days with closing moves several times the
    implied, the same days for all six forecasts, and only 1 of the 11 an FOMC statement
    day; without them the gain over the short straddle and the regression $\alpha$ disappear.
  \item The forecasts thus time the sign of the closing-half-hour variance premium in a narrow sense, by stepping out
    of the short straddle on a minority of days, and in this sample of 614 days that timing paid through a
    handful of large closing moves that they anticipated, not through a steady premium.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Question.} The sign strategy of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ} holds one straddle over the last half hour of
  the session. We ask whether its returns are a disguised position in the stock market, and what an investor who holds
  the S\&P~500 gains by adding the strategy. The specification below was fixed before any of these statistics was
  computed, except two changes that follow the paper's Sharpe ratio (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}), adopted
  after they had been seen: every Sharpe ratio is annualized by $\sqrt{q}$ in place of $\sqrt{252}$, a common factor
  that moves no test, and the gain of a real-time combination over the market is tested by \citet{LedoitWolf2008} in
  place of a paired block bootstrap of the difference.

% disclosed. Under the registered bootstrap (stats.csv, iv_pb) the inverse-volatility gain is significant at mid for
% the lasso, the elastic net and the random forest (p 0.046-0.049); under Ledoit--Wolf for none (p 0.054-0.061). No
% macro carries the registered count. Was: "The specification below was fixed before any of these statistics was
% computed."
\item \textbf{Returns.} The strategy's daily return $r^{s}_t$ (in percent of the premium, at mid-quotes unless noted)
  is treated as an excess return, as in Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}. The market return $r^{m}_t$ is the
  S\&P~500 close-to-close return of option day $t$, from the previous trading day's close, minus the return of the
  three-month Treasury bill (FRED series DTB3, actual/360). It is a price return: the market's mean excess return
  omits the dividend yield, which leaves the regression slopes and residuals unchanged. We also use $r^{30}_t$, the
  index's own return from 15:30 ET to the close, the window of the trade.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Over the 614 post-warmup days the market's excess return averages 0.011\% a day with a
    standard deviation of 1.12\%, a Sharpe ratio of 0.15 (0.17 over all 684 trading days
    of the same span, with $q = 251.3$). Under the equal-weight mean of the $\SR_y$
    (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_econ_sharpe}), which gives each calendar year, including the partial first and last ones, the
    same weight, it is 0.57.
  \item The decomposition of the maximum Sharpe ratio below holds for the ratio of the pooled daily returns, which is
    the paper's $\SR$: every Sharpe ratio in this subsection is $\sqrt{q}$ times the ratio of the mean to the standard
    deviation of the daily returns, $q$ the average number of days per calendar year of its sample
    (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}), unless it is marked as the mean of the $\SR_y$. All $t$-statistics use
    Newey--West standard errors with bandwidth $S = 33$ and fixed-$b$ critical values
    (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_methods_tests}).

% generator's STANDARD ratio; rhebQAll for the trading days of the span); D6 is the marked alternative. Was: "(\rhebSRmAll{}
% over all \rhebNAll{} trading days of the same span). Under the paper's ratio $\SR$ of
% Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}, which gives each calendar year, including the partial first and last ones, the
% same weight, it is \rhebSRmDSix." and "The decomposition of the maximum Sharpe ratio below holds for the ratio of the
% pooled daily returns, so every Sharpe ratio in this subsection is $\sqrt{252}$ times the ratio of the mean to the

  \end{itemize}
% Parked (plan D2): in the next item, after "($R^2$ at most \rhebRsqFullMax).", Was: "The closing-interval HAR strategy
% ($\beta = \rhebBetaCiHar$, $t = \rhebBetaTCiHar$) and the short straddle ($\beta = \rhebBetaShort$, $t =

% \rhebBetaHarMin{} to \rhebBetaHarMax)."
\item \textbf{No market beta} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_beta}, Panel A). The correlation of the six full-set strategies
  with the market is \ensuremath{-}0.01 to 0.03, and their CAPM betas are \ensuremath{-}0.52 to
  2.92 percent of the premium per percent of market return ($t$ from \ensuremath{-}0.13 to
  0.75); none of the six is significant at the 5\% level, at mid-quotes or at quoted bid/ask prices
  ($R^2$ at most 0.00). The short straddle ($\beta = 4.43$, $t = 1.22$) is no
  different, nor are the four distinct HAR-set forecasts ($\beta$ from 0.14 to
  2.44).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On the 307 days on which the market falls, the full-set strategies earn 13.1 to
    18.7\% of the premium, against 7.2 to 12.6\% on the other days;
    none of the six differences is significant.
  \item On the 62 days with the lowest market return (at most \ensuremath{-}1.29\%) every full-set strategy
    has a negative mean return, \ensuremath{-}15.7 to \ensuremath{-}3.3\% of the premium, against
    14.5 to 17.2\% on the other days ($t$ of the difference from
    \ensuremath{-}2.28 to \ensuremath{-}1.31; significant at the 5\% level for three of
    the six). The short straddle returns \ensuremath{-}22.4\% on these days ($t = \ensuremath{-}1.99$). The
    strategy has no linear exposure to the market, but like the short straddle it mostly is, it loses on the market's
    worst days.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{The convexity is in the trading window, not in the daily return.} In the regression of $r^{s}_t$ on
  $r^{m}_t$ and $(r^{m}_t)^2$ \citep{TreynorMazuy1966}, the coefficient $\gamma$ on the squared market return is
  \ensuremath{-}2.19 to \ensuremath{-}1.36 for the full-set strategies ($t$ from \ensuremath{-}1.53 to
  \ensuremath{-}1.02; none significant), and on the strategies' own long days
  \ensuremath{-}3.45 to 11.32 ($t$ at most 1.11).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Against the index's return over the trade's own half hour the straddle's payoff shows. On their long days
    every full-set strategy loads positively on $(r^{30}_t)^2$, $\gamma$ from 195.08 to
    389.30 ($t$ from 2.38 to 3.67),
    and on their short days negatively, \ensuremath{-}377.20 to \ensuremath{-}270.34 ($t$
    from \ensuremath{-}4.46 to \ensuremath{-}4.35; percent of the premium per squared
    percent of index return). These $t$-statistics are descriptive: the long and short days are not consecutive.
  \item Over all days the full-set strategies are short the squared half-hour move, $\gamma$ from
    \ensuremath{-}122.92 to \ensuremath{-}38.65 ($t$ from \ensuremath{-}2.41 to
    \ensuremath{-}0.55), against \ensuremath{-}274.27 ($t = \ensuremath{-}4.16$) for the short
    straddle, and they carry no slope on its sign ($\beta$ on $r^{30}_t$ with $t$ at most
    0.77).
  \end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Alpha} (Panel B). The CAPM intercept of the full-set strategies is 11.5 to
  14.1\% of the premium a day ($t$ from 2.93 to 3.77, fixed-$b$ $p$ at most
  0.008), with appraisal ratios $\alpha/\sigma_\varepsilon$ of 1.53 to 1.88
  (annualized by $\sqrt{q}$). With a beta near zero, $\alpha$ is close to the mean return and the appraisal ratio
  to the strategy's own Sharpe ratio (1.54 to 1.88).
% 2026-10-28 (D19, standard pooled Sharpe): was "(annualized by $\sqrt{252}$)".
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The short straddle has $\alpha = 2.4\%$ ($t = 0.65$). For the
    four distinct HAR-set forecasts $\alpha$ is 2.4 to 7.4\% ($t$ at
    most 2.05; none significant).
  \end{itemize}
% Parked (plan D2): in the next item, Was: "... ($p$ from \rhebGrsPFullMin{} to \rhebGrsPFullMax), and for the

\item \textbf{Maximum Sharpe ratio of the market and the strategy.} The tangency portfolio of the two reaches
  $(\SR_m^2 + (\alpha/\sigma_\varepsilon)^2)^{1/2}$, 1.54 to 1.88 for the full-set
  strategies against 0.15 for the market alone. Its gain over the market is significant exactly when $\alpha$
  is: the one-asset test of \citet{GibbonsRossShanken1989} rejects $\alpha = 0$ for six of the six at
  the 5\% level ($p$ from 0.002 to 0.012), but not for the short straddle
  ($p = 0.603$).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item In the tangency portfolio the strategy carries 99 to 100\% of the
    volatility. The market's Sharpe ratio over the sample is low, so the in-sample optimum is almost the strategy
    alone; the strategy's leverage is arbitrary, so this share, not a dollar weight, is the allocation.
  \item The paired block bootstrap of the gain, with the weights re-estimated in each resample, gives $p$ from
    \ensuremath{<}0.001 to 0.003 (95\% intervals with lower ends from 0.18 to
    0.43). The gain cannot be negative, so this test rejects in one tail only and its $p$ lies below
    the GRS $p$: for the four distinct HAR-set forecasts it is below 5\% for
    two and the GRS $p$ for none. The GRS test and the $t$-statistic of $\alpha$ are the tests of
    record.
  \end{itemize}

% straddle \rhebRtMvShort{} and \rhebRtIvShort{}."
\item \textbf{Real-time allocation} (Panel C, Figure~\ref{fig:rh_econ_beta_cum}). Each day the weights of the market
  and the strategy are set from the earlier post-warmup days only. After a burn-in of 126 days the
  combinations are evaluated on the 488 days from 17~May~2022, over which the market alone has a Sharpe ratio
  of 0.50 (mean of the $\SR_y$: 0.68). The largest of the strategies' best days, 22~November~2021,
  falls in the burn-in: it moves the estimated weights but not the evaluation.
% 2026-10-28 (D19, standard pooled Sharpe): was "($\SR = \rhebSRmRtDSix$)".
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Mean--variance weights (expanding window, no short positions, neither leg above 90\% of the estimated
    portfolio volatility) reach Sharpe ratios of 1.66 to 1.95 with the full-set
    strategies. The estimated means put the strategy at the cap on every evaluation day, which amounts to a median of

    (\citet{LedoitWolf2008} $p$ from 0.071 to 0.146; with the mean of the $\SR_y$,
    1.76 to 2.03 and bootstrap $p$ from 0.135 to
    0.243).
  \item Inverse-volatility weights over the trailing 63 days, which estimate no means and split the risk
    equally (a median of at most 0.9\% of capital in premium), reach 1.22 to
    1.61; the gain is significant for none of the six (\citet{LedoitWolf2008} $p$ from
    0.054 to 0.169; with the mean of the $\SR_y$, for two under the

  \item With the short straddle the two rules reach 0.90 and 1.34.

  2.99, none significant). The intercept falls to 8.9 to 11.4\% a day ($t$
  from 2.32 to 3.09), the GRS test rejects for four of the six ($p$
  up to 0.053), and the maximum Sharpe ratio is 1.19 to 1.53. In real time
  the mean--variance combinations reach 1.31 to 1.59 and the inverse-volatility ones
  0.94 to 1.33, and none is significantly above the market ($p$ at least
  0.169 and 0.142).
\item \textbf{Without the days that carry the gain} (Panel E). We remove the 11 days in the union of the six
  full-set forecasts' best days (Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_bestdays}) from every series, the market's included. The
  selection uses the strategies' realized returns, so this is a stress test against them.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The betas stay near zero (\ensuremath{-}0.22 to 3.26, $t$ at most 0.96). The
    intercept falls to 5.9 to 8.7\% a day ($t$ from 1.98 to

  ratio over it is low, which makes the tangency portfolio almost all strategy. The strategies' gains over the short
  straddle rest on the 11 days with large closing moves; the $t$-statistics allow for serial correlation, not

  strategies are tested without a correction for multiple testing.

\item \textbf{Summary: market exposure and allocation.} The sign strategy is not a disguised position in the market.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Its betas are near zero and insignificant, and the convexity of the straddle shows in the trade's half hour,
    not in the daily market return.
  \item Its intercept is significant, so in this sample a holder of the S\&P~500 would have given almost all of the
    risk budget to the strategy.
  \item In real time, the combinations reach Sharpe ratios of 1.22 to 1.95 at mid-quotes
    against 0.50 for the market, but over 488 days that gain is not statistically significant for
    either rule, at mid-quotes or at quoted bid/ask prices, or without the 11 days that carry the
    strategies' gain over the short straddle.

\subsection{Relation to intraday option-return prediction}
\label{app:rh_econ_maisch}
% 2026-10-26 (integration, coordinator: bullet structure): the prose recast as bold-lead items with sub-items,
% content kept.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Their design.} \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026} also trade S\&P~500 index options on half-hourly
  machine-learning forecasts, but they forecast the delta-hedged return of each contract from its characteristics
  and sort the contracts into decile long--short portfolios every half hour. Their portfolio returns are computed at
  mid-quotes, and they note that trading each option at its quoted bid and ask prices would erase a large share of
  the profits.
\item \textbf{How ours differs.} Our test differs in three respects:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item the forecast is the variance of the underlying over the closing half hour, set against the straddle's
    implied variance;
  \item the position is a single at-the-money 0DTE straddle a day, entered at 15:30 and held to expiration;
  \item its Sharpe ratios are reported at quoted bid/ask prices as well as at mid-quotes.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Comparability.} Because the two designs differ in horizon, position, and sample period, their Sharpe
  ratios are not directly comparable.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Training sample}
\label{app:rh_robust_train}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Main design.} Every pooled model of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} (ridge regression, the lasso, the elastic
  net, LightGBM, XGBoost and the random forest, each on the HAR benchmark and on the full predictor set) is estimated
  on the 13 regular-hours bars of each day, $\mathcal I = \mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$ (bar ends 10:00 to
  16:00~ET), over a rolling window of 3{,}000 trading days (39{,}000 bars), with its predictors
  computed on the full grid of 48 half-hour intervals, overnight included
  (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}). Estimation on the regular session follows the intraday volatility
  forecasting literature \citep{EngleSokalska2012,ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}. Below, this sample is RTH13.
\item \textbf{A pre-registered comparison.} Before any model was estimated on the other samples, a written rule (one
  for the linear models, one for the trees) fixed two other training samples, the models, their tuning and the tests:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item ALL48: all 48 half-hour intervals of the futures' day, overnight, weekend and holiday
    intervals and early-close sessions included, over the same 3{,}000-day window (144{,}000 rows);
  \item CLOSE: the closing half hour alone (the 16:00 rows of the main design), over 3{,}000 closes; its
    results are in Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_econ_last30}.
  \end{itemize}
  Everything else is the main design's: the predictors, the frozen tree configurations, a refit at every training
  row, and the rule that chooses the linear penalties, applied to each sample's own pre-sample rows (validation year
  2013). Every sample is scored on the same 2{,}579 trading days from 2 January 2014 to 30 April 2024, on the
  16:00 bar and on every regular-hours bar. The linear rule also fixed secondary samples for the penalized linear
  models (a natively built CLOSE, and penalties chosen on the 16:00 validation rows, ALL48@16 and RTH13@16). Samples
  with equal numbers of training rows were added before their models were estimated (for the linear models by a
  dated addendum to the rule).
\item \textbf{Design and table.} The comparison ran on the design before the FOMC fixes of
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}; its RTH13 rows are the forecasts of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} on that design.
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_train_arms} reports every comparison.
\item \textbf{The closing half hour.} Trained on all 48 intervals, the full predictor set gains more
  over the HAR benchmark at 16:00 than in the main design (Table~\ref{tab:rh_train_arms}, Panel~A).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item ALL48: the change in 16:00 QLIKE is $\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}6.5$ to $\ensuremath{-}5.6$ for the
    three tree ensembles, each with $p < 0.001$, and $\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}2.6$ to $\ensuremath{-}1.8$
    for the penalized linear models, none significant at the 10\% level (the smallest, \ensuremath{p = 0.15}).
  \item RTH13: $\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}3.4$ to $3.3$, significant at the 5\% level for XGBoost
    only ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}3.4$, \ensuremath{p = 0.030}). Choosing the linear penalties on the 16:00 validation
    rows leaves every linear change insignificant at the 10\% level, in ALL48@16 and in RTH13@16, although in RTH13
    it lowers the 16:00 loss of the lasso's full-set forecast ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}5.4$,
    \ensuremath{p < 0.001}; Panel~C), whose HAR benchmark changes with it.
  \item A full-versus-HAR change compares two forecasts trained on the same sample, so it also moves with the HAR
    benchmark. Compared directly (Panel~C), the full-set forecasts trained on ALL48 have a lower 16:00 loss than
    those trained on RTH13 in all six classes ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}6.0$ to
    $\ensuremath{-}1.9$), significantly at the 5\% level in five.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{The average regular-hours bar.} On every bar, RTH13 is the most accurate sample: no other sample
  gives the full predictor set a lower every-bar loss in any class (Panels~C and~D test the pre-registered pairs).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The full-set forecasts trained on ALL48 have a higher every-bar QLIKE than those trained on RTH13 in all six
    classes ($\Delta\% = 1.9$ to $5.2$), each significant at the 1\% level
    (the largest, \ensuremath{p = 0.008}).
  \item The full predictor set lowers the every-bar loss significantly in every class under both samples, and by more
    under RTH13 in all six: $\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}6.2$ to $\ensuremath{-}5.4$ for the penalized linear models
    and $\ensuremath{-}14.0$ to $\ensuremath{-}11.1$ for the tree ensembles, against $\ensuremath{-}5.2$ to
    $\ensuremath{-}4.9$ and $\ensuremath{-}12.0$ to $\ensuremath{-}7.0$ under ALL48.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Data volume.} At equal calendar the samples differ in their numbers of training rows (144{,}000
  for ALL48, 39{,}000 for RTH13). The equal-row samples (Panel~D) hold the number of rows fixed and change the
  span and recency of the window instead.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item With 39{,}000 rows, as many as RTH13, ALL48-39k has a significantly lower 16:00 loss than RTH13 in
    two classes, the lasso and the random forest
    ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}3.6$ to $1.3$ across the six),
    against five for ALL48 with all its rows, and in every class its 16:00 loss relative to
    RTH13's is higher than ALL48's. Cutting ALL48 from 144{,}000 to 39{,}000 rows raises its 16:00 loss
    in all six classes ($\Delta\% = 1.7$ to $4.1$),
    significantly at the 5\% level in five. Much of ALL48's advantage at 16:00 thus
    goes with its larger number of rows. On every bar, ALL48-39k remains less accurate than RTH13 in all six classes
    ($\Delta\% = 2.7$ to $10.4$, each with $p < 0.001$).
  \item With 3{,}000 rows, ALL48-3k has a lower 16:00 loss than RTH13-3k in all six classes
    ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}8.1$ to $\ensuremath{-}3.3$, significantly at the
    5\% level in five) and a higher every-bar loss in all six
    ($\Delta\% = 2.7$ to $5.8$, each with
    $p < 0.001$), the same pattern as at equal calendar; the two windows span about 62.5 and
    231 trading days.
  \item Fewer rows also cost accuracy within the main sample: RTH13-3k has a higher loss than RTH13 at 16:00
    ($\Delta\% = 6.2$ to $12.3$) and on every bar
    ($\Delta\% = 2.7$ to $14.9$), each significant at the 1\% level.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{The trade.} The Sharpe ratio $\SR$ of the full-set sign strategy (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures};
  Panel~E) lies between 1.47 and 1.88 under RTH13 and between 1.25 and
  1.82 under ALL48. None of the 12 differences in $\SR$ between the full-set strategies
  of ALL48 or CLOSE and those of RTH13 is significant at the 5\% level under the \citet{LedoitWolf2008} test (the
  smallest, \ensuremath{p = 0.17}). For the tree ensembles, the full-set strategy's gain over the HAR benchmark's is
  significant at the 5\% level in two of the three classes under RTH13 and in none
  under ALL48.

\item \textbf{Caveats.} The tree configurations were chosen on an earlier design (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_tuning}) and,
  by the rule, are not re-tuned; with 3{,}000 rows (ALL48-3k, RTH13-3k) or 144{,}000 (ALL48) their
  sample-size parameters may not suit the window. The linear penalties are re-chosen in every sample. ALL48 differs
  from RTH13 in more than its rows: it adds the overnight indicator, keeps the early-close sessions, and computes its
  rolling scaling on its own rows.
\item \textbf{The main design is unchanged.} RTH13 was chosen before the comparison, following the literature cited
  above, and it is the sample under which the full predictor set is most accurate on the average regular-hours bar,
  the score of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}. At the 16:00 bar, training on all 48 intervals or on the close
  alone gives the full predictor set a larger gain over the HAR benchmark in every class
  (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_econ_last30} for the close), a gain significant for the tree ensembles under ALL48 and for
  every class under CLOSE. The closing-bar results of Sections~\ref{sec:rh_results} and~\ref{sec:rh_econ} are those
  of models estimated for the regular session as a whole, not for its last half hour.
\end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Test of a mean daily return.} For any daily return series $r_t$---either the return of an individual trading strategy or the return differential $\Delta_t$ between two strategies---observed on the $T = 614$ post-warmup days $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}), we test whether its mean is zero with the procedure that \citet{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018} recommend for the Newey--West estimator:
  \[
    t = \frac{\bar r}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega_r / T}},
    \qquad
    \hat\Omega_r = \sum_{|j| < S} \Bigl(1 - \frac{|j|}{S}\Bigr) \hat\gamma_j,
    \qquad
    \hat\gamma_j = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=|j|+1}^{T} (r_t - \bar r)(r_{t-|j|} - \bar r),
  \]
  with the Bartlett kernel, bandwidth $S = \lceil 1.3\, T^{1/2} \rceil = 33$, and fixed-$b$ critical values for $b = S/T$ \citep{KieferVogelsang2005}.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The autocovariances divide by $T$, with no small-sample factor; at lag truncation $S - 1$ the estimator equals the Newey--West variance of the previous item.
  \item This bandwidth is larger than that of conventional rules such as $0.75\, T^{1/3}$, which \citet{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018} obtain from the formula of \citet{Andrews1991} for a first-order autoregression with coefficient $0.25$. Combined with fixed-$b$ critical values, it reduces the size distortion of the test when the returns are serially correlated \citep{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018}.
  \item Under the null hypothesis and fixed $b$, the limiting distribution of $t$ is a functional of Brownian motion that depends only on the kernel and on $b$ \citep{KieferVogelsang2005}. We obtain its quantiles by simulation, computing the same statistic on 1{,}000{,}000 independent series of 1{,}000 i.i.d.\ standard normal draws with bandwidth $1{,}000\,b$. This gives the two-sided 5\% critical value 2.11 and the $p$-values reported in the text, in place of the standard normal value 1.96.

\item \textbf{Multiple-comparison procedures.} Each test above compares two forecasts, or two strategies, at a time,
  and Sections~\ref{sec:rh_results} and~\ref{sec:rh_econ} make many such comparisons. Three procedures account for
  their number; Tables~\ref{tab:rh_mcs} and~\ref{tab:rh_mcs_spa} report them (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing_mcs}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Model confidence set} \citep{HansenLundeNason2011}. Starting from a set $\mathcal M$ of forecasts with
    daily losses $L_{i,t}$, each step tests the equal predictive ability of the forecasts in $\mathcal M$ and, if it
    rejects, removes one of them. With $\bar d_{ij}$ the average of $L_{i,t} - L_{j,t}$ over $\mathcal O$ and
    $\bar d_{i\cdot}$ the average loss of forecast $i$ minus the average over $\mathcal M$, the two statistics are
    \[
      T_{\max} = \max_{i \in \mathcal M} t_{i\cdot}, \quad
      t_{i\cdot} = \frac{\bar d_{i\cdot}}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(\bar d_{i\cdot})}},
      \qquad
      T_R = \max_{i, j \in \mathcal M} |t_{ij}|, \quad
      t_{ij} = \frac{\bar d_{ij}}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(\bar d_{ij})}},
    \]
    and their elimination rules remove $\arg\max_i t_{i\cdot}$ and $\arg\max_i \max_j t_{ij}$, respectively. The
    variances and the null distributions of $T_{\max}$ and $T_R$ come from the bootstrap below, with the statistics
    recentred at their sample values. The elimination continues to the last forecast, so every forecast has an MCS
    $p$-value: the largest step $p$-value up to its removal, and one for the last forecast. The $(1-\alpha)$ model
    confidence set holds the forecasts whose $p$-value is at least $\alpha$; we report the 90\% and 75\% sets.
  \item \emph{Superior predictive ability} \citep{Hansen2005}. For a family of $K$ comparisons with daily
    differentials $d_{k,t}$, positive when the alternative $k$ is better than its comparison (the loss of the
    comparison minus that of the alternative, or the return of the alternative minus that of the comparison), the
    test of $H_0\colon \max_k \E[d_{k,t}] \le 0$ uses $T^{\mathrm{SPA}} = \max\bigl(0, \max_k \bar d_k/\hat\sigma_k\bigr)$,
    with $\hat\sigma_k$ the bootstrap standard deviation of $\bar d_k$. We report its consistent $p$-value.
  \item \emph{StepM} \citep{RomanoWolf2005}. The studentized step-down procedure tests the $K$ hypotheses
    $H_k\colon \E[d_{k,t}] \le 0$ and controls the familywise error rate, the probability of rejecting at least one
    true $H_k$. With $t_k = \bar d_k/\hat\sigma_k$ ordered as $t_{(1)} \ge \dots \ge t_{(K)}$ and
    $Z^{*}_k = (\bar d^{*}_k - \bar d_k)/\hat\sigma_k$ in a bootstrap sample, the adjusted $p$-value of the $j$-th
    hypothesis is
    \[
      \tilde p_{(j)} = \max_{i \le j} \Pr\nolimits^{*}\Bigl(\max_{l \ge i} Z^{*}_{(l)} \ge t_{(i)}\Bigr),
    \]

    $H_k\colon \E[d_{k,t}] = 0$, replaces $t_k$ and $Z^{*}_k$ by their absolute values. Beside each adjusted $p$-value

\section{Closing-interval models}
\label{app:rh_closing}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Scope.} The models of the main text are estimated on every regular-hours bar and forecast every bar.
  This section collects the models estimated on the closing half hour alone ($\mathcal I = \{c\}$, one observation
  a trading day): the closing-interval HAR benchmark, rebuilt under the current data chain, and the pooled models of
  Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} re-estimated on the closing half hour (the CLOSE sample). It also reports the accuracy of
  the pooled models' closing half hour on both evaluation spans and the multiple-comparison procedures, whose sets
  of the closing half hour include the closing-interval HAR benchmark.
\item \textbf{Spans.} Results for the closing half hour score its bar alone. Comparisons that involve the
  closing-interval models, whose forecasts start later, use the subset
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}} \subset \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ of the $T_{\mathrm{close}} = 1{,}082$ days from
  3 January 2020 to 30 April 2024 on which all of them exist, with a Newey--West lag of $6$; the
  option days of the application lie in it (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_strategy}).
  % 2026-10-26 (coordinator; author: no 16:00-bar results in the main text): moved here from Section 5 (Evaluation spans).
\item \textbf{Not reported.} The closing-interval linear models and tree ensembles of earlier drafts, a separate
  model set fitted under the earlier data rules with its own window, predictor set and tuning, are not reported;
  the CLOSE sample replaces them.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Model specification}
\label{app:rh_closing_sample}
\label{app:rh_closing_bench}
\label{app:rh_closing_predictors}
\begin{itemize}
% Moved from the parked subsection "Closing-interval HAR benchmark and estimation" (10_appendix.tex), lightly edited.
\item \textbf{The closing-interval HAR benchmark.} A HAR-type model in the spirit of \citet{Corsi2009}, not Corsi's
  daily HAR: OLS on the HAR components of the target at the horizons $\mathcal K$ and 16 calendar
  columns (22 columns in all), estimated on closing-interval observations only, over a rolling window of
  $W = 2{,}000$ trading days, and re-estimated every trading day. It has no exogenous series and no FOMC column.
  It is not the paper's benchmark, which is the pooled OLS on the HAR benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods}).
\item \textbf{Rebuilt under the current data chain.} The benchmark's forecasts in earlier drafts were built under the
  data rules in force before the data fixes of Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}. They are rebuilt with the same model and
  code, every data rule at its current setting.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Three rules change the benchmark's inputs. The diurnal factor of the target averages regular in-slot bars
    only, so the bars after the 13:00 close of an early-close session leave it, which moves the target and the HAR
    components for $n_{\mathrm{d}}$ trading days after each early close (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_samples}). The
    16:00 rows of the early-close sessions leave the design, as they leave the pooled design. The burn-in of the HAR
    components is dropped on the half-hour grid rather than on the series of closes, so the benchmark's estimation
    sample starts earlier and its forecasts cover $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ (first forecast 14 June 2006).
  \item The other data rules act on exogenous series only and do not reach a design without them.
  \item With the earlier rules switched back on, the code reproduces the earlier forecasts up to floating-point
    rounding.
  \item On the closing half hour of $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}}$ the rebuilt benchmark's average QLIKE loss is
    0.1025, against 0.1033 before the rebuild ($\DM = \ensuremath{-}0.86$,
    0.388), and its sign strategy takes the other position on 18 of the 614
    post-warmup days.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Its strategy.} The sign strategy on the benchmark's forecast (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_strategy}) has
  $\SR = 1.11$ at mid-quotes and 0.76 at quoted bid and ask prices, against the short straddle
  $\Delta\SR = 0.79$ (Ledoit--Wolf $p = 0.254$). The full-set strategies of the
  pooled models have the higher Sharpe ratio in 6 of the 6 model classes
  ($\Delta\SR = 0.43$ to $0.77$); 0 of these differences are
  significant at the 5\% level under the \citet{LedoitWolf2008} test (the smallest $p$, 0.093).
% 2026-10-28 (D19, standard pooled Sharpe): was "(bootstrap $p = \rhemPDShCiHarVsShort$)" and "under the bootstrap
% test".
\item \textbf{Models trained on the closing half hour (CLOSE).} A pre-registered comparison of training samples
  (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_robust_train}) re-estimated every pooled model of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} on the closing half
  hour alone.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Sample: the 16:00 rows of the main design, over a rolling window of 3{,}000 closes, refit at every
    close, on the design before the FOMC fixes of Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}.
  \item Predictors: those of the main design at the 16:00 bar (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}), computed on the full
    half-hour grid.
  \item Tuning: the frozen tree configurations of the main design, and the rule that chooses the linear penalties
    applied to the sample's own pre-sample rows (validation year 2013). A natively built CLOSE design
    (CLOSE-nat) checks the linear models.
  \item Scoring: the 16:00 bar of the 2{,}579 trading days from 2 January 2014 to 30 April 2024, the days of
    Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Training sample}
\label{sec:rh_econ_last30}
\label{sec:rh_results_pooled}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Against the main design.} Trained on the close alone, the full-set forecasts of the penalized linear
  models have a lower 16:00 loss than those of the main design ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}11.8$ to
  $\ensuremath{-}9.4$, each with $p < 0.001$); those of the tree ensembles do not differ significantly
  ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}2.2$ to $1.6$; the smallest $p$,
  \ensuremath{p = 0.42}; Table~\ref{tab:rh_train_arms}, Panel~C).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item For the trees, training on the close alone raises the 16:00 loss of the HAR benchmark (for LightGBM from
    0.1235 to 0.1313).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Full predictor set against the HAR benchmark.} Within CLOSE the full predictor set lowers the 16:00
  loss in all six classes (Panel~A).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}6.5$ to $\ensuremath{-}5.4$ for the penalized linear models and
    $\ensuremath{-}8.5$ to $\ensuremath{-}3.7$ for the tree ensembles, each with $p < 0.001$; CLOSE-nat
    gives the same result for the linear models ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}6.6$ to
    $\ensuremath{-}5.4$, each with $p < 0.001$).
  \item In the main design the same comparison gives $\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}3.4$ to $3.3$,
    significant at the 5\% level for XGBoost only (\ensuremath{p = 0.030}).
  \item A full-versus-HAR change compares two forecasts trained on the same sample, so it also moves with the HAR
    benchmark: for the trees, the larger change under CLOSE reflects their weaker HAR benchmark there (above).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{The window.} A follow-up run, specified in its own written rule before it was estimated,
  re-estimated CLOSE on windows of 1{,}000 to 3{,}500 closes (Panel~F). The full predictor set has the
  lower 16:00 loss in all 36 window and class pairs ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}6.7$ to
  $\ensuremath{-}1.5$ for the penalized linear models, $\ensuremath{-}8.5$ to $\ensuremath{-}2.1$ for the tree
  ensembles), significantly at the 5\% level in 32 of them and in every class from 2{,}000
  closes on.
\item \textbf{Equal numbers of rows.} CLOSE, with 3{,}000 rows, has a lower 16:00 loss than RTH13-3k, the
  main sample cut to the same number of rows, in all six classes ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}18.0$ to
  $\ensuremath{-}8.7$; the largest $p$, \ensuremath{p = 0.004}; Panel~D). Its window spans about
  12 years against about 231 trading days, so this comparison does not separate the
  choice of intervals from the span of the window.
\item \textbf{The trade} (Panel~E). The full-set sign strategies trained on CLOSE have $\SR$ from
  1.26 to 1.94, against 1.47 to 1.88 in the main design.
  % 2026-10-28 (D19; make_rehaul_train_arms.py rerun: the pooled ratio of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}, the
  % Ledoit-Wolf test): the item names the paper's ratio and test again; \rhtaNTreeShSigCl moved from two to one.
  % Was: "Here the Sharpe ratio is the equal-year mean of the yearly ratios $\SR_y$ of
  % Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}. The full-set sign strategies trained on CLOSE have ratios from ... in the main
  % design." and, below, "None of the \rhtaNDShTests{} differences in this ratio between the full-set strategies of
  % ALL48 or CLOSE and those of the main design is significant at the 5\% level under the paired bootstrap (the
  % smallest $p$, \rhtaDShPMin)."
  % 2026-10-28 (D19, standard pooled Sharpe; coordinator): make_rehaul_train_arms.py (\rhta...) still computes the
  % equal-year mean of the SR_y with the paired bootstrap; the text names it until the generator is rerun. Was: "The
  % full-set sign strategies trained on CLOSE have $\SR$ from ... in the main design." and, below, "None of the
  % \rhtaNDShTests{} differences in $\SR$ ... is significant at the 5\% level (the smallest $p$, \rhtaDShPMin)."
  \begin{itemize}
  \item None of the 12 differences in $\SR$ between the full-set strategies of ALL48 or CLOSE and those
    of the main design is significant at the 5\% level under the \citet{LedoitWolf2008} test (the smallest $p$,
    \ensuremath{p = 0.17}).
  \item For the tree ensembles, the full-set strategy's gain over the HAR benchmark's is significant at the 5\% level
    in one of the three classes under CLOSE, where the trees' HAR benchmark strategies have $\SR$
    from \ensuremath{-}0.03 to 0.40.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Caveats.} The tree configurations were chosen on an earlier design and, by the rule, are not
  re-tuned; with 3{,}000 rows their sample-size parameters may not suit the window
  (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_tuning}).
\item \textbf{Summary.} Training on the closing half hour alone lowers the 16:00 loss of the penalized linear models
  but not of the tree ensembles; within CLOSE the full predictor set beats the HAR benchmark in all six classes; and
  no Sharpe ratio differs significantly from the main design's.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Forecast accuracy}
\label{app:rh_closing_accuracy}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The table.} Table~\ref{tab:rh_close_accuracy} reports the 15:30 forecast of the closing half hour from
  the pooled models of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} on the 2{,}579 trading days of $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$,
  from 2 January 2014 to 30 April 2024 (Panel~A), and on $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}}$ (Panel~B).
\item \textbf{On $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$.} The full predictor set lowers the average QLIKE loss of the closing
  half hour in 3 of the 6 model classes.
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-26 (coordinator, D13): on the FOMC-patched design the elastic net's change is positive (NUMBERS report).
  % Was: "... for the three tree ensembles (...) and the elastic net ($\Delta\% = \rhcaPctEnetCloseSpan$); ..." and
  % "It raises the loss of ridge regression (...) and the lasso (...), neither significantly."
  \item It lowers it for the three tree ensembles ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}3.1$ to
    $\ensuremath{-}1.6$); the reduction is statistically significant at the 5\% level for XGBoost only
    ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}3.1$, $\DM = \ensuremath{-}2.01$, \ensuremath{p = 0.044}).
  \item It raises the loss of ridge regression ($\Delta\% = 1.8$, $\DM = 0.67$),
    the lasso ($\Delta\% = 4.2$, $\DM = 1.35$) and the elastic net
    ($\Delta\% = 0.6$), none significantly.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Against the OLS benchmark at 16:00.} The full-set LightGBM and XGBoost forecasts are significantly
  more accurate than the OLS on the HAR benchmark set at 16:00 as well ($\DM={}$$-$3.83 and
  $-$4.66).
\item \textbf{The realized moments account for the trees' gain at 16:00.} Added to the HAR benchmark set they
  change the trees' 16:00 loss by $-$3.4\% to $-$4.5\% ($\DM={}$$-$2.45
  or larger in absolute value), and the full set is significantly more accurate than the same class's HAR benchmark
  set plus realized moments in none of the six classes (its loss relative
  to that benchmark: 0.7\% for LightGBM, 1.4\% for XGBoost).
  % 2026-10-26 (coordinator; author: no 16:00-bar results in the main text): the two bullets above moved here from Section 6 (subsection "The closing half hour").
\item \textbf{On $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}}$.} The same comparison gives lower losses for the tree ensembles
  ($\Delta\% = \ensuremath{-}1.7$ to $\ensuremath{-}0.7$, none significant) and higher losses for the
  penalized linear models ($\Delta\% = 9.5$ to $15.2$, significant at the 5\%
  level for all three). % 2026-10-26 (coordinator, D13): was "for ridge regression and the lasso" (elastic net now p = 0.036)
\item \textbf{Why the linear models differ between the spans.} Their full-set change has opposite signs on the two
  halves of $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On 2014--2019 the full predictor set lowers their closing-half-hour loss ($\Delta\% =
    \ensuremath{-}4.1$, \ensuremath{-}2.3 and \ensuremath{-}4.8 for ridge regression, the lasso and
    the elastic net; $\DM = \ensuremath{-}1.42$, \ensuremath{-}0.67 and \ensuremath{-}1.80), and in
    4, 3 and 5 of the 6
    calendar years.
  \item On $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}}$ it raises their loss in 4 of the 5
    calendar years, most in 2023 ($\Delta\% = 32.0$ for ridge
    regression).
  \item Over the whole span the two halves offset, and no linear change is significant.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Against the closing-interval HAR benchmark.} The pooled forecasts are compared with it on
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{close}}$ in Appendix~\ref{app:rh_results_classes} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_close_accuracy},
  Panel~B), and jointly in Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing_mcs}.
\end{itemize}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:rh_intro}
% 2026-10-26 (author requirement, relayed by the coordinator): the bullet structure kept -- bold-lead items with

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Realized variance within the trading day.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Realized variance, the sum of squared high-frequency returns, made volatility observable and forecastable
    \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003, BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}, and the heterogeneous autoregressive
    (HAR) model of \citet{Corsi2009}, a regression of realized variance on its own averages over several past
    horizons, has become the benchmark for forecasting it.
  \item Within the trading day volatility follows a pronounced diurnal pattern \citep{AndersenBollerslev1997}, and
    pooled models that fit one forecasting equation across the intraday intervals, after a diurnal adjustment, have
    carried the approach to that horizon \citep{EngleSokalska2012,ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}. Like the HAR model,
    they forecast volatility from its own past; we ask what predictors beyond its lagged realized variances add.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Research question.} We investigate whether exogenous predictors improve pooled forecasts of the
  realized variance of front-month E-mini S\&P~500 futures on every regular-hours half-hour bar of the trading day.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item We call exogenous every predictor outside the HAR components of the target and the calendar dummies. The
    \rhdmNSeriesPooled{} exogenous series fall into \bkNBuckets{} groups drawn from the futures' own higher-order
    realized moments and trading activity; the intraday trading of the index's constituents, through their realized
    moments, liquidity and order-flow imbalance; option-implied volatility; the calendar of FOMC announcements; and
    alternative data, namely sentiment and attention on StockTwits and the net option vega bought by
    non-market-makers (volatility demand).
  \item Alternative data of this kind have mostly been used to forecast daily realized volatility
    \citep{AudrinoSigristBallinari2020,CaporinPoli2017}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Design.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Each model class is estimated as one pooled model on the \rhePoolNBars{} regular-hours bars of the day,
    $\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$ (bars ending 10:00 to 16:00 ET), as in the intraday volatility models of
    \citet{EngleSokalska2012} and \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}.
  \item Its predictors, the HAR components of the target and trailing averages of every exogenous series, are
    computed on the futures' full grid of \rhdmNIntervals{} half-hour intervals, overnight included, so that the
    forecasts use the information that accumulates outside regular hours \citep{StroudJohannes2014}.
  \item For bar $i \in \mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}$ of day $t$ the forecast is
    \[
      \hat y_{t,i} = f_{m,\mathcal X,\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}}(\bm x_{t,i}), \qquad
      \mathcal X \in \{\mathrm{HAR}, \mathrm{Full}\},
    \]
    for model classes $m$ from two families, the penalized linear models (ridge regression, the lasso and the
    elastic net) and the tree ensembles (LightGBM, XGBoost and the random forest). The exogenous series are the exact
    difference between the two predictor sets.
  \item Every model is re-estimated at every bar on a rolling window of \rhorWindowDays{} trading days
    ($\rhorWindowBars$ bars), with hyperparameters fixed before the evaluation span and then frozen
    (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Benchmark and evaluation.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The primary benchmark is ordinary least squares on the HAR benchmark set, pooled on the same bars (the OLS
    row of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}); on this set the penalized linear models choose penalties close to zero and
    reproduce its forecast.
  \item Every forecast is compared with this benchmark, and each class's full predictor set with the HAR benchmark
    set of the same class, the paired comparison that isolates what the exogenous series add.
  \item Accuracy is the average QLIKE loss over the \rhorNIntB{} regular-hours bars of the \rhorDays{} trading days
    from \rhorSpanStart{} to \rhorSpanEnd, with Diebold--Mariano tests on the daily average losses
    \citep{DieboldMariano1995}. QLIKE weighs an error relative to the forecast and, like squared error, ranks
    forecasts consistently despite noise in the realized-variance proxy \citep{Patton2011}.
  \end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Application to 0DTE straddles} (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On each day with a same-day SPXW expiration we buy or sell one zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) at-the-money
    straddle at 15:30 ET as the forecast of the closing bar's realized variance lies above or below the variance
    implied by the straddle's price; the straddle pays on the index's move over that half hour, not on its realized
    variance, so the forecast of the half hour's realized variance signals which side to take
    \citep{EngleHongKaneNoh1993,NohEngleKane1994}.
  \item Over \rheSzDays{} expiration days the full-set strategies beat the unconditional short straddle,
    significantly in \rhemFullVsShortSig{} of the \rhorAfPairs{} classes, but beat the strategy of the HAR benchmark
    significantly in \rhemFullVsOlsHarSig{} of them; their gain over the short straddle is earned on the
    \rhedLongPctMin--\rhedLongPctMax\% of days on which they buy and rests on each strategy's \rhedNTop{} best days,
    and none of them carries a significant market beta.
  \end{itemize}

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:rh_related}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Realized variance and the HAR model.} Realized variance, the sum of squared high-frequency returns,
  makes volatility observable and forecastable \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003,
  BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}, and the heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) model of \citet{Corsi2009}, which
  regresses next-day realized variance on its averages over the past day, week, and month, has become the benchmark
  for forecasting it. Its extensions add jumps \citep{AndersenBollerslevDiebold2007}, signed semivariances
  \citep{PattonSheppard2015}, leverage \citep{CorsiReno2012}, and the measurement error of realized variance
  \citep{BollerslevPattonQuaedvlieg2016}, and the panel HAR of \citet{BollerslevHoodHussLebedev2018} estimates a
  single pooled regression across a cross-section of assets. These are models of daily variance. We carry the HAR
  structure to the intraday interval, pool it across the intervals of one index rather than across assets, and ask
  how much a large set of exogenous predictors adds to it.
\item \textbf{Pooled intraday forecasting and overnight information.} Intraday volatility follows a pronounced
  U-shaped pattern across the trading session, and scaling intraday returns or realized variances by a diurnal
  factor is standard practice \citep{AndersenBollerslev1997,TaylorXu1997}; \citet{AndersenSuTodorovZhang2024}
  estimate this curve for the S\&P~500 futures around the clock and find that volatility outside U.S. trading hours
  matters more in the later part of their sample. With this scaling, one model can be estimated across the intervals
  of the regular session: \citet{EngleSokalska2012} estimate a multiplicative component GARCH model of intraday
  volatility, with daily, diurnal, and stochastic intraday components, pooled across a large cross-section of
  stocks, and \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024} fit machine-learning models of realized volatility across all
  intraday buckets of the day, with predictors built from realized volatility alone. Both leave the overnight return
  out of estimation, and so do we (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods}). Yet information from outside the session helps
  forecast it: after-hours realized variance \citep{ChenYuZivot2012} and overnight information, including the
  realized volatility of related assets that trade while the home market is closed \citep{TodorovaSoucek2014},
  improve volatility forecasts, and for the S\&P~500 futures \citet{StroudJohannes2014} argue that deleting the
  overnight returns removes important information. These studies forecast daily or session volatility; we carry the
  idea to the intraday interval by computing our predictors over the futures' full intraday grid, overnight
  intervals included (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}).
\item \textbf{Machine learning for realized volatility.} Applications of bagging, the lasso, boosting, random
  forests, and neural networks to realized volatility \citep{HillebrandMedeiros2010,AudrinoKnaus2016,
  MittnikRobinzonovSpindler2015,LuongDokuchaev2018,RahimikiaPoon2020} preceded the comparison of these methods with
  the HAR model for daily realized volatility in \citet{christensen2023machine}, much as \citet{gu2020empirical}
  compared linear, penalized, tree-based, and neural-network models for returns; \citet{BrancoRubesamZevallos2024}
  find that nonlinear models rarely beat linear ones. Most of this work targets daily volatility; we compare
  penalized linear models with tree ensembles on every regular-hours interval.
\item \textbf{Dense or sparse signals.} In macroeconomic, microeconomic, and financial data, the posterior over
  predictive models does not typically concentrate on a single sparse model \citep{GiannoneLenzaPrimiceri2021}, and
  a characteristics-sparse stochastic discount factor cannot adequately summarize the cross-section of expected
  stock returns \citep{KozakNagelSantosh2020}; \citet{ShenXiu2025} ask whether machine-learning methods can learn
  weak signals. That our exogenous signal is dense and weak, spread thinly over many series, is a hypothesis we
  test, not a premise: ridge regression suits a dense signal and the lasso a sparse one, and we compare penalized
  linear models with tree ensembles across the number of exogenous series and the length of the training window
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi}; Appendix~\ref{app:rh_fi_scaling}). Unlike the complex models of
  \citet{KellyMalamudZhou2024}, which have more parameters
% 2026-10-28 (v2 of Sections 6-7, author approved preliminarily): pointer for the v2 layout. Was: (Section~\ref{sec:rh_fi})
  than observations, ours have far fewer predictors than training observations.
  % 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): optional KMZ clause (coordinator: one clause; the author has not yet decided on
  % the complexity argument, plan "Pending author decisions"); delete the sentence if the author drops KMZ. No number
  % is quoted: the grid's c = P/T is at most \rhcxCMax (\rhcxCMaxMain for the full set at W = 3,000), macros of
  % generated/rehaul_complexity_numbers.tex, which the preamble does not \input today.
\item \textbf{Alternative data.} Sentiment, attention, and news measures have mostly been used to forecast daily
  realized volatility \citep{AudrinoSigristBallinari2020,CaporinPoli2017}; at the intraday horizon,
  \citet{BehrendtSchmidt2018} relate Twitter sentiment and activity to the intraday volatility of individual stocks.
  We ask what such data add to a pooled intraday model of the index's realized variance, next to the futures' own
  realized moments, the trading of the index's constituents, implied volatility, and the FOMC calendar.
\item \textbf{Economic evaluation of volatility forecasts and 0DTE options.} A long tradition ranks volatility
  forecasts by the profits of trading options on them, buying (selling) straddles when the price implied by the
  forecast exceeds (falls short of) the market price \citep{EngleHongKaneNoh1993,NohEngleKane1994,
  BandiRussellYang2008}; statistical gains need not survive transaction costs
  \citep{HarveyWhaley1992,ChanJhaKalimipalli2009}. Because the variance risk premium is positive on average
  \citep{CarrWu2009,BollerslevTauchenZhou2009}, zero-beta at-the-money straddles and delta-hedged index options lose
  money on average \citep{CovalShumway2001,BakshiKapadia2003}, which makes the unconditional short straddle the
  natural benchmark for a strategy that trades straddles on a variance forecast. A recent literature studies the
  pricing, trading, and volatility effects of zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options on the S\&P~500
  \citep{BandiFusariReno2023,BeckmeyerBrangerGayda2023,DimErakerVilkov2024}, and \citet{ChongTodorov2026} ask
  whether equity and 0DTE options markets agree about volatility and trade their disagreement. Nearest to our market
  and bar length, \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026} predict the half-hourly delta-hedged returns of S\&P~500 index
  options from contract characteristics, Greeks, and option-implied measures of the index's return distribution,
  and sort the contracts into long--short portfolios. Our forecasts belong to the realized volatility literature,
  and options enter only as an application: one 0DTE at-the-money straddle a day through the closing half hour,
  long or short as the forecast for that interval exceeds or falls short of the implied variance
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Data}
\label{sec:rh_data}
% 2026-10-17 (user): prose rewritten in the style of Zhang, Zhang, Cucuringu, and Qian (2024).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{E-mini futures and realized variance.} We obtain one-minute prices of the front-month E-mini S\&P~500
  futures contract (the most actively traded contract), which trades nearly 24 hours a day, from 1998 through
  \rhdsSampleEnd, and aggregate them on a grid of half-hour intervals. Trading days are indexed by $t = 1, \dots, T$
  and the half-hour intervals of day $t$ by $i = 1, \dots, M$; every interval is stamped by its end in Eastern time,
  and $i = c$ denotes the closing interval, 15:30--16:00~ET. With $r_{t,i,k}$ the one-minute log-price change of the
  front-month contract in the $k$-th non-missing minute of interval $(t,i)$, $k = 1, \dots, N_{t,i}$
  ($N_{t,i} \le 30$), the realized variance of the interval is \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003}
  \[
    \RV_{t,i} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{t,i}} r_{t,i,k}^2 ,
  \]
  which we forecast on every regular-hours interval, the bars ending 10:00 to 16:00~ET
  (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}).
\item \textbf{Exogenous series.} The pooled models use \rhdmNSeriesPooled{} exogenous series in \bkNBuckets{} groups.
  Appendix Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_dictionary} defines each series, and Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_sources} gives the
  sources and the construction.
  % 2026-10-26 (integration, JFEc): the display of the seven sums and the sentence that names them moved to Appendix
  % app:rh_dp_sources (A_data_predictors.tex).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Realized moments} (\bkSizeMom{} series): one-minute sums of the futures over the interval other than
    $\RV_{t,i}$, the target: the sums of the returns, of their absolute values, cubes and fourth powers, the positive
    realized semivariance, the bipower variation and the first-order realized autocovariance.
  \item \textbf{Liquidity} (\bkSizeLiq{} series): the futures volume, the number of observed minutes
    $N_{t,i}$\ifrawseries{} (\sername{numobs})\fi, and equal- and value-weighted cross-sectional averages over the
    S\&P~500 constituents of turnover (total, buyer- and seller-initiated), the effective and quoted spreads, and
    order-flow imbalance.
  \item \textbf{Equal- and value-weighted market moments} (\bkSizeMew{} and \bkSizeMvw{} series): the same averages of
    realized moments of the constituents' 5-minute returns.
  \item \textbf{Sentiment} (\bkSizeSent{} series): StockTwits attention (posts in the half hour), the sentiment score of
    the posts tagged bullish or bearish, and their number.
  \item \textbf{Implied volatility} (\bkSizeIv{} series): the Cboe VIX, VIX3M and VVIX indices.
  \item \textbf{Volatility demand} (\bkSizeVd{} series): the net vega bought by customers other than market makers in
    Cboe option volume.
  \item \textbf{FOMC} (\bkSizeFomc{} series): an indicator for a scheduled Federal Open Market Committee statement on
    day $t$ and the proximity measures $1/(1+n^{+}_{t,i})$ and $1/(1+n^{-}_{t,i})$, with $n^{+}_{t,i}$ and
    $n^{-}_{t,i}$ the number of intervals until the next and since the last scheduled statement. The proximity
    measures follow the pre-announced meeting calendar, so all three series are known before the interval begins;
    the meeting scheduled for \rhdsFomcSchedMeeting{} is the next statement until the action announced on
    \rhdsFomcReplaced{} replaced it (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_fomc}).
  \end{itemize}
  Our data end on \rhdsSampleEnd. The file of the implied volatility indices ends on \rhdsVixVendorLast{} and is
  extended with the hourly closes of a free feed; the FOMC release file ends with the statement of \rhdsFomcFileLast{}
  and is completed with the \rhdsFomcAdded{} scheduled statements that follow; the volatility-demand feed ends on
  \rhdsVdLast{} (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_sources}).
\item \textbf{Interval grid, sessions and cleaning.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The interval grid $\mathcal{G}$ holds the intervals with an observed realized variance outside the weekend
    break, Friday 20:00 to Sunday 18:30. Lag operators step back through $\mathcal{G}$, overnight sessions included:
    $(t, i - j)$ is the $j$-th interval of $\mathcal{G}$ before $(t, i)$, which may lie on an earlier day.
  \item Early-close sessions stay in $\mathcal{G}$ but leave the estimation and evaluation samples of the pooled
    models and the option-trading sample; their intervals after the 13:00~ET close also leave the window of the
    target's diurnal factor (Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}).
  \item On NYSE holidays the E-mini trades a shortened session that ends at about 13:00~ET. The regular-hours intervals
    of these sessions stay in $\mathcal{G}$, in the \rhorNBars-bar estimation sample and in the window of the target's
    diurnal factor, but are not scored; dropping them from the sample and the window changes the every-bar
    comparisons of the full predictor set with the HAR benchmark by \rhholEffCABarPpRng{} percentage points in the
    linear models (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_robust_holiday}).
  \item A print outside the domain of its series, such as a nonpositive spread or futures volume, is set to missing.
    For each exogenous series $u$ we record the availability indicator $a_{t,i} = \mathbf{1}\{u \text{ observed in }
    (t,i)\}$ before any filling, forward-fill $u$ over at most \rhdsFfillCap{} intervals to compute its trailing
    statistics, and impute every interval with $a_{t,i} = 0$ (step~4 of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}). A trailing
    average that holds no observed interval enters at its neutral value (step~6), as the averages of the
    volatility-demand series do after their feed stops (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_dp_sessions}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Samples.} Appendix Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_samples} lists the samples. The estimation samples and the
  evaluation span are set out in Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_setup}, the option-trading sample in
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_strategy}, and the sample of the closing-interval models in
  Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing_sample}.
\end{itemize}
